Store submission pre-processors transform component CSS into standardized @scope blocks to prevent cross-component style bleeding.

title: W3C CSS Conditional Rules Level 4: @supports Feature Queries, Selector Queries, and Progressive UI Degradation
summary: Super-app mini-apps run across diverse device fleets ranging from budget legacy Android devices with older System WebView builds to flagship devices running modern Chromium/WebKit rendering engines. Hardcoding cutting-edge CSS features (e.g., subgrid, color-mix(), anchor positioning) causes complete rendering breakdowns on older engines if not properly protected. The W3C CSS Conditional Rules Level 4 specification standardizes the '@supports' rule with support for property queries, boolean logic, and 'selector()' conditional tests.
key_points: Defines '@supports' condition testing for CSS property:value pairs, including compound 'and', 'or', and 'not' boolean operators.
Introduces 'selector()' condition to test browser support for modern pseudo-classes (e.g., '@supports selector(:has(div))').
Enables progressive enhancement: mini-apps deliver baseline functional layouts to low-end devices while unlocking fluid animations on modern hardware.
Super-app container injects feature detection polyfills and provides CSS testing suites during mini-app store package validation.
Store quality gates enforce that mini-apps using modern visual effects implement robust @supports fallback paths for older WebView engines.

title: W3C CSS Scoping Module Level 1: Shadow DOM Style Encapsulation, :host Pseudo-Class, and Slotted Component Protection
summary: Shadow DOM provides true DOM and style boundary encapsulation, but component authors must selectively style host elements and project slotted content without compromising isolation. The W3C CSS Scoping Module Level 1 specifies the pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements used to pierce and customize Shadow DOM boundaries—specifically ':host', ':host()', ':host-context()', and '::slotted()'. In a super-app container, these scoping primitives ensure that host application themes can gracefully customize mini-app widgets without penetrating internal private DOM hierarchies.
key_points: Specifies ':host' pseudo-class to style the shadow host element from within the shadow tree, and ':host(selector)' for state-dependent host styling.
Defines '::slotted()' pseudo-element allowing shadow root styles to style elements distributed through <slot> insertion points without modifying outside styles.
Enforces strict boundary isolation: normal selectors inside a shadow tree cannot match elements outside the shadow root, and outer selectors cannot match inner elements.
Prevents CSS selector injection attacks: untrusted user-generated content rendered inside a mini-app cannot target host application UI elements.
Super-app UI component SDK relies on CSS Scoping Level 1 to provide themable, hermetically sealed form inputs and modal dialogs across all mini-apps.

title: NIST SP 800-218 SSDF: Mini-App Developer Security Verification, Toolchain Attestation & Provenance Gating
summary: To prevent supply chain poisoning and malicious code infiltration into super-app ecosystems, store governance must hold third-party mini-app developers to established software security practices. NIST Special Publication 800-218 defines the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, organizing software security into four foundational groups: Prepare the Organization (PO), Protect the Software (PS), Produce Well-Secured Software (PW), and Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV). Enterprise super-app stores use SSDF as the normative audit framework for enterprise developer onboarding.
key_points: Mandates developer environment preparation: toolchain hardening, role-based access control, and mandatory multi-factor authentication (PO group).
Enforces software protection: integrity verification of code repositories, build pipelines, and cryptographically signed release commits (PS group).
Requires well-secured software production: automated static analysis (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA) for third-party npm packages, and secure coding training (PW group).
Establishes vulnerability response procedures: documented incident response plans, CVE tracking, and rapid patch delivery timelines (RV group).
Store submission portal mandates self-attestation or third-party audit reports conforming to NIST SP 800-218 for tier-1 financial and healthcare mini-apps.

title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 C-SCRM: Super-App Third-Party Ecosystem Risk Tiers & Supplier Integrity Auditing
summary: A super-app ecosystem acts as an operational supply chain aggregator where third-party vulnerabilities directly compromise host platform integrity and user data. NIST Special Publication 800-161 Revision 1 (Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations) provides an enterprise methodology for managing ICT supply chain risks across system life cycle phases. The standard structures C-SCRM into enterprise, mission/business process, and operational tiers, providing risk assessment templates, supplier vetting criteria, and continuous monitoring controls.
key_points: Establishes 3-tier C-SCRM risk governance: Organization Level (policies & risk tolerance), Mission Level (critical service dependencies), and Operational Level (package vetting & runtime monitoring).
Classifies mini-apps into supply chain risk tiers based on access to user PII, payment tokens, device sensors, and network privileges.
Mandates formal vendor assessment: legal ownership verification, historical security breach analysis, and country-of-origin hardware/software dependencies.
Enforces continuous supply chain monitoring: automated vulnerability feeds for all upstream libraries declared in mini-app Software Bills of Materials (SBOM).
Provides termination and rapid de-provisioning protocols: super-app operator retains unilateral authority to quarantine or revoke high-risk supplier mini-apps.

title: OWASP MASVS v2.0: Host Container Hardening Matrix (MASVS-STORAGE, CRYPTO, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE)
summary: The host native mobile application (Android/iOS) wrapping the super-app runtime represents the ultimate security perimeter for all embedded mini-apps. The OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) Version 2.0 establishes a comprehensive baseline of security requirements across six core domains: Storage, Cryptography, Authentication, Network, Platform Interaction, Code Quality, and Resilience against reverse engineering and tampering.
key_points: MASVS-STORAGE: Prohibits unencrypted sensitive data in SharedPreferences, NSUserDefaults, SQLite, or external shared storage; mandates Android Keystore / iOS Keychain.
MASVS-CRYPTO: Enforces modern authenticated encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), forbids deprecated algorithms (DES, SHA-1, ECB mode), and verifies secure key generation.
MASVS-NETWORK: Mandates TLS 1.3/1.2, certificate pinning / transparency checks, and complete blocking of cleartext HTTP traffic across all container WebViews.
MASVS-PLATFORM: Secures IPC boundaries (Intents, BroadcastReceivers, URL schemes, Pasteboard access, FileProviders) against unauthorized third-party invocation.
MASVS-RESILIENCE: Implements anti-tampering, root/jailbreak detection, emulator detection, integrity checks, and active debugger evasion to defend the super-app runtime.

title: IETF RFC 9052 / RFC 9053 COSE: Compact Binary Signatures & Encryption for Resource-Constrained Mini-App Bundles
summary: While JSON Web Signatures (JWS) and JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are widely used for web authentication, their base64url encoding and text parsing impose excessive memory and compute overhead on constrained mobile devices and embedded IoT super-app runtimes. IETF RFC 9052 (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption - COSE: Structures and Process) and RFC 9053 (Algorithms) define compact binary representations for cryptographically signed (COSE_Sign, COSE_Sign1) and encrypted (COSE_Encrypt, COSE_Encrypt0) data objects based on Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR - RFC 8949).
key_points: Defines COSE_Sign1 structure providing single-signature digital verification with zero-copy binary CBOR serialization.
Significantly reduces bundle metadata overhead: COSE headers and signatures occupy roughly 50-70% less byte volume than equivalent JWS/JWT envelopes.
Supports modern elliptic curve cryptographic algorithms: Ed25519 (EdDSA), ECDSA with P-256/P-384, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD.
Super-app package distribution uses COSE_Sign1 to sign package manifests, Web Bundles, and delta-patch chunks at the byte level.
Mobile container runtime verifies COSE signatures using native C/Rust cryptographic bindings before extracting or mounting mini-app asset directories.

title: IETF RFC 9116 security.txt: Standardized Vulnerability Disclosure Policy Publication for Mini-App Publishers and Host Stores
summary: Security researchers and users discovering critical vulnerabilities in third-party mini-apps or the host super-app store frequently lack a clear, secure channel to contact responsible security teams, resulting in public zero-day disclosure or unaddressed exploits. IETF RFC 9116 standardizes 'security.txt', a machine-readable text file deployed under the '/.well-known/' directory path that explicitly defines security contact details, encryption keys, vulnerability disclosure policies, hiring notices, and preferred languages.
key_points: Mandates placement at '/.well-known/security.txt' containing mandatory 'Contact' and 'Expires' fields.
Supports 'Encryption' directive linking to PGP/GPG public keys for encrypted vulnerability reporting via email or web portals.
Includes 'Policy' field pointing to safe-harbor bug bounty rules and responsible vulnerability disclosure commitments.
Super-app store operator hosts an authoritative security.txt for the overarching platform and container SDKs.
Store submission requirements mandate that enterprise mini-app publishers publish and maintain a valid security.txt on their canonical web domain.

title: W3C Web Speech API: SpeechRecognition & SpeechSynthesis Lifecycle, Microphone Arbitration, and Acoustic Privacy
summary: Voice-driven multimodal interaction enables hands-free navigation, conversational AI, and accessibility within super-apps. The W3C Web Speech API specification defines JavaScript interfaces for speech recognition (SpeechRecognition) and speech synthesis (SpeechSynthesis). Because continuous acoustic monitoring presents severe privacy risks (surreptitious recording and speaker profiling), host containers must enforce strict transient user activation, visual listening indicators, continuous audio session timeouts, and granular background audio isolation.
key_points: Defines SpeechRecognition event lifecycle: onaudiostart, onsoundstart, onspeechstart, onresult, onspeechend, and onerror.
Specifies SpeechGrammarList and SpeechRecognitionResultList supporting confidence scoring and alternative recognition candidates.
Enforces SpeechSynthesis utterance controls: SpeechSynthesisUtterance rate, pitch, volume, and voice selection across platform TTS engines.
Super-app container gates speech recognition behind runtime micro-permissions, showing persistent system status bar recording badges.
Container automatically aborts recognition sessions (SpeechRecognition.abort()) when mini-apps navigate to background or lose viewport focus.

title: W3C EditContext API: Decoupled Text Input, Canvas IME Composition, and Non-DOM Virtualized Editor Sandboxing
summary: Building high-performance collaborative editors, spreadsheets, games, and document tools inside mini-apps has traditionally required hidden contenteditable DOM nodes or transparent textareas to capture user keystrokes and IME composition. This approach causes severe DOM synchronization race conditions, accessibility failures, and mobile virtual keyboard glitches. The W3C EditContext API standardizes an abstract text input model that directly connects custom canvas or virtualized renderers to OS Input Method Editors (IMEs) without touching the DOM tree.
key_points: Decouples text input processing from DOM elements, establishing a direct bidirectional bridge between JavaScript rendering loops and native OS IMEs.
Provides granular composition lifecycle events: textupdate, textformatupdate, characterboundsupdate, and compositionstart/end.
Enables seamless complex script input (Vietnamese Telex/VNI, Chinese Pinyin, Japanese Kana, Arabic) in WebGL/Canvas-based mini-apps.
Exposes updateText(), updateSelection(), and updateControlBounds() allowing the native virtual keyboard to position candidate windows accurately.
Eliminates hidden DOM hack vulnerabilities, preventing third-party mini-apps from desynchronizing editor state or triggering layout reflow loops.

title: WHATWG Fullscreen Living Standard: requestFullscreen() Mediation, User Activation Gating, and Escape Gesture Guarantees
summary: Immersive video streaming, gaming, and kiosk mini-apps require full display utilization. However, unrestricted fullscreen transitions allow malicious mini-apps to spoof system UI, phishing logins, or lock users into inescapable traps. The WHATWG Fullscreen Living Standard defines the programmatic API for entering (Element.requestFullscreen()) and exiting (Document.exitFullscreen()) fullscreen mode, enforcing strict transient user activation prerequisites, Permissions Policy delegation, and non-overridable hardware escape affordances.
key_points: Specifies Element.requestFullscreen() options (navigationUI: 'auto' | 'show' | 'hide') requiring transient user activation (user gesture).
Enforces Permissions Policy 'fullscreen' feature directive; cross-origin mini-app iframes cannot enter fullscreen without explicit 'allow="fullscreen"'.
Fires fullscreenchange and fullscreenerror events on Document and Element targets during state transitions.
Super-app host container renders an un-interceptable system overlay banner ('Press Back or swipe down to exit') during initial fullscreen entry.
Host platform reserves native hardware back gestures and status-bar reveals, guaranteeing users can escape hijacked mini-app viewports at all times.

title: WICG Keyboard Lock API: Fullscreen System Key Capture, Chord Reservation, and Mandatory Exit Affordance Protection
summary: When mini-apps run complex immersive games, virtual desktop clients, or terminal emulators in fullscreen mode, native operating system shortcuts (such as Escape, Alt+Tab, Cmd+Tab, or browser navigation chords) are normally intercepted by the host platform, disrupting the user experience. The WICG Keyboard Lock API enables fullscreen web applications to capture specific key codes or all available keyboard events via navigator.keyboard.lock(). Host super-apps must enforce strict security boundaries to prevent malicious entrapment.
key_points: Provides navigator.keyboard.lock([keyCodes]) and navigator.keyboard.unlock() methods, callable strictly within active fullscreen mode.
Permits filtering of specific key chords (e.g., 'KeyW', 'KeyA', 'KeyS', 'KeyD', 'Escape') or locking the entire keyboard matrix.
Enforces mandatory host fallback: user pressing and holding the Escape key for 2 seconds instantly breaks the lock and terminates fullscreen mode.
Super-app store review restricts Keyboard Lock API entitlements to verified gaming, remote-desktop, and creative kiosk mini-app categories.
Container audits prevent mini-apps from suppressing emergency OS-level task-switching gestures or physical power/home button sequences.

title: W3C Screen Orientation API: Programmatic Orientation Locking, Angle Telemetry, and Cross-Platform Rotation Policies
summary: Mini-apps span diverse UX paradigms—from portrait-only fintech workflows to landscape-only high-definition games and document scanners. Abrupt device rotations disrupt rendering geometry and trigger unnecessary re-layouts. The W3C Screen Orientation API standardizes reading the current screen orientation type/angle and locking the display to specific orientations (screen.orientation.lock()) such as 'portrait-primary', 'portrait-secondary', 'landscape-primary', or 'landscape-secondary'.
key_points: Exposes ScreenOrientation interface with 'type' ('portrait-primary'/'landscape-primary'/etc.) and 'angle' (0, 90, 180, 270 degrees) properties.
Provides asynchronous screen.orientation.lock(orientation) and synchronous screen.orientation.unlock() APIs.
Fires 'change' event when physical or programmatic rotation occurs, enabling dynamic responsive layout adjustments.
Enforces Permissions Policy 'screen-wake-lock' and fullscreen prerequisites on mobile browsers before permitting orientation locking.
Super-app manifest allows developers to declare default 'orientation' in manifest.json, which the host container enforces during launch.

title: GSMA Open Gateway: Universal Network API Federation, Carrier Identity Verification, and Anti-Fraud SIM Swap Gating
summary: Super-apps operating in emerging and developed markets require direct telecommunications carrier integration for frictionless SIM-based user onboarding, fraud detection, and carrier billing. The GSMA Open Gateway initiative standardizes a global framework of universal network APIs, transforming telecom operator networks into open, standardized programmable platforms. Implemented via CAMARA project APIs, it provides carrier-grade identity verification, device location confirmation, and SIM swap detection directly to super-app containers.
key_points: Defines universal northbound API specifications implemented across Tier-1 global mobile network operators (MNOs).
Exposes Number Verification API: verifies user phone number possession over mobile cellular data without insecure SMS OTPs.
Integrates SIM Swap API: checks whether a subscriber's SIM card was swapped recently (e.g., within 24-72 hours) before processing high-value fintech transactions.
Provides Device Location Verification API: confirms device presence within a specific geographical cell without accessing GPS coordinates.
Super-app backend mediates Open Gateway tokens, granting mini-apps scoped access while protecting subscriber MSISDN privacy.

title: Linux Foundation CAMARA Project: Telco API Open Source Standardization, QoS-on-Demand, and Carrier Billing Abstraction
summary: To prevent fragmentation across telecommunications operators, the Linux Foundation's CAMARA project acts as the official open-source code repository and working group developing the technical API implementations for GSMA Open Gateway. CAMARA harmonizes API definitions across AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and global telcos, establishing standardized OpenAPI 3.0 schemas for Quality-on-Demand (QoD), Carrier Billing, Device Status, and Network Slicing.
key_points: Harmonizes carrier API definitions across major cloud hyperscalers and telecommunications operators.
Defines Quality on Demand (QoD) API: dynamically requests low-latency, high-bandwidth network profiles for interactive cloud gaming or video mini-apps.
Standardizes Carrier Billing API: abstracts direct operator billing (DCB) across diverse telcos through unified JSON REST endpoints.
Provides Device Reachability and Roaming Status APIs to adapt mini-app data sync strategies based on user connection state.
Super-app host container SDK maps CAMARA REST endpoints into lightweight JavaScript API wrappers for authorized mini-app developers.

title: IETF RFC 8470: Using Early Data in HTTP (TLS 1.3 0-RTT), Replay Mitigation, and Idempotency Gateway Validation
summary: Launching mini-apps on mobile devices across 3G/4G/5G networks suffers significant latency overhead from TLS handshakes. TLS 1.3 introduces 0-RTT Early Data, allowing clients to send HTTP request payloads in the initial cryptographic flight. However, 0-RTT data is vulnerable to network replay attacks, where malicious eavesdroppers re-transmit recorded packets. IETF RFC 8470 defines HTTP protocol mechanics for safely utilizing early data, standardizing the 'Early-Data: 1' request header and the HTTP 425 (Too Early) response code.
key_points: Establishes strict rules: only safe HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) without side effects should be sent in 0-RTT early data.
Intermediary proxies and gateways append 'Early-Data: 1' header when forwarding requests received in early data to backend services.
Servers return HTTP status '425 Too Early' if a request received in early data cannot be safely processed or risks non-idempotent side effects.
Client network stacks automatically retry requests rejected with 425 after the full 1-RTT TLS handshake completes, with zero user disruption.
Super-app network stack enables 0-RTT for initial bundle manifest downloads, reducing mini-app cold start latency by 30-50%.

title: IETF RFC 9205: Architectural Best Practices for Building Protocols with HTTP (Method Semantics, URI Design, and Extensibility)
summary: Super-app mini-app platforms define extensive suites of Open APIs, bridge protocols, and cloud sync services. Ad-hoc API design leads to broken caching, security loopholes, and protocol brittleness. IETF RFC 9205 (BCP 56 - Building Protocols with HTTP) establishes authoritative architectural guidance for protocol designers using HTTP as an application layer substrate, standardizing method semantics, status code usage, header handling, URI design, payload structures, and state management.
key_points: Prohibits overloading HTTP methods (e.g., using GET for state-mutating requests or POST for pure cacheable data retrieval).
Mandates proper HTTP status code semantics over custom application error envelopes masked behind HTTP 200 OK responses.
Enforces standard header prefixing conventions: discourages deprecated 'X-' headers in favor of standardized HTTP structured fields (RFC 8941/9651).
Specifies URI namespace governance: host platforms must avoid hardcoding path hierarchies that prevent future protocol evolution.
Super-app API review board adopts RFC 9205 as the mandatory design guideline for all partner Open APIs and mini-app platform endpoints.

title: IETF RFC 9218: Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP (Priority Header & Urgency/Incremental Multiplexing)
summary: When multiple mini-apps, images, scripts, and real-time feeds compete for limited mobile bandwidth across HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connections, poor scheduling causes head-of-line blocking and stuttering UI. IETF RFC 9218 standardizes an extensible prioritization scheme for HTTP requests, replacing complex HTTP/2 dependency trees with a simple, robust priority scheme using the 'Priority' header field and PRIORITY_UPDATE frames.
key_points: Defines two orthogonal parameters: 'urgency' (integer 0-7, where 0 is highest priority and 7 is lowest) and 'incremental' (boolean 'i' flag).
Specifies 'Priority: u=0, i' for progressive rendering of critical UI assets, and 'Priority: u=6' for background analytics beacons.
Supports dynamic client prioritization updates mid-stream via HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE extension frames.
Enables super-app container network schedulers to dynamically adjust resource priority as users scroll, minimizing layout shifts.
Eliminates bandwidth starvation: background mini-app sync tasks never degrade the network responsiveness of the foreground active mini-app.

title: NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism for Quantum-Resistant Mini-App Transport & Sessions
summary: Emerging quantum computing architectures threaten classical public key cryptography (RSA, ECDHE) with 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks against sensitive mobile sessions and payment tokens. In August 2024, NIST officially published FIPS 203 (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard), standardizing ML-KEM (derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber) as the primary post-quantum standard for general encryption and key exchange across enterprise networks.
key_points: Standardizes three security parameter sets: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024, providing quantum resistance based on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE) problem.
ML-KEM-768 provides security roughly equivalent to AES-192, serving as the recommended default for hybrid post-quantum TLS 1.3 (e.g., X25519MLKEM768).
Super-app edge gateways implement hybrid post-quantum TLS key encapsulation, protecting mini-app API traffic against future quantum decryption.
Key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) produces compact ciphertexts (~1088 bytes for ML-KEM-768), well within standard mobile packet MTU limits.
Store submission infrastructure begins piloting post-quantum package encryption keys for long-lived enterprise document and financial mini-apps.

title: NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm for Quantum-Resistant Package Signing
summary: Classical digital signature schemes (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519) securing mini-app software bundles and publisher certificates will become insecure once cryptographically relevant quantum computers exist. NIST FIPS 204 standardizes ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) as the primary post-quantum standard for digital signatures, ensuring long-term non-repudiation and software integrity.
key_points: Specifies parameter sets: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87 based on Module Short Integer Solution (M-SIS) lattice hardness.
ML-DSA-65 provides Category 3 security (comparable to AES-192), generating signatures of ~3293 bytes and public keys of ~1952 bytes.
Designed for general software distribution signing, code provenance attestation, and digital identity certificates.
Super-app store release pipeline initiates dual-signing (hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65) for mini-app archive manifests and package bundles.
Native container runtime embeds post-quantum cryptographic libraries (liboqs / BoringSSL) to verify ML-DSA signatures prior to code execution.

title: NIST FIPS 205 SLH-DSA: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard for Long-Term Root CA & Trust Anchor Portability
summary: While lattice-based cryptography is highly efficient, having a mathematically diverse cryptographic backup is essential in case lattice assumptions face unexpected algebraic breakthroughs. NIST FIPS 205 standardizes SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, derived from SPHINCS+), relying exclusively on the security properties of cryptographic hash functions (SHA-2, SHAKE) rather than lattice or number-theoretic assumptions.
key_points: Stateless hash-based architecture eliminates the dangerous state-synchronization vulnerabilities inherent in stateful hash signatures (LMS/XMSS).
Relies strictly on pre-image and collision resistance of standard hash functions (SHA-256 / SHAKE-256), offering exceptional theoretical resilience.
Produces larger signatures (7-49 KB) and slower signing times, making it ideal for high-security root CAs and offline package signing rather than high-frequency TLS.
Super-app store operator employs SLH-DSA for its offline root signing keys, guaranteeing that platform trust anchors remain cryptographically sound for decades.
Provides an independent cryptographic safety net, enabling store governance to transition seamlessly if lattice algorithms are compromised.

title: WICG Secure Curves in Web Cryptography: Ed25519 and X25519 Algorithms for High-Performance Mini-App Key Operations
summary: The original W3C Web Cryptography API omitted modern, high-performance Edwards-curve cryptography (Curve25519 / Ed25519), forcing developers to rely on NIST curves (P-256) or heavy pure-JavaScript libraries for modern decentralized protocols and end-to-end messaging. The WICG Secure Curves in Web Cryptography specification standardizes Ed25519 digital signatures and X25519 key agreement within the native SubtleCrypto interface.
standards: WICG Secure Curves in Web Cryptography
key_points: Extends SubtleCrypto with { name: 'Ed25519' } algorithm identifier for sign() and verify() operations.
Extends SubtleCrypto with { name: 'X25519' } algorithm identifier for deriveKey() and deriveBits() key agreement.
Offers complete immunity against timing side-channel attacks through constant-time native implementation in browser engines.
Provides compact 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures, drastically outperforming RSA and P-256 in memory and CPU footprint.
Enables mini-apps to implement end-to-end encrypted messaging, decentralized identity (DID) verification, and fast client-side transaction signing.

title: IETF RFC 8439: ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols (High-Throughput Mobile AEAD without Hardware AES Acceleration)
summary: While AES-GCM is standard for authenticated encryption, low-cost mobile devices and budget smartphones common in emerging markets often lack dedicated hardware AES acceleration instructions (ARMv8 Cryptography Extensions). On such hardware, software AES implementations suffer severe performance degradation and vulnerability to cache-timing attacks. IETF RFC 8439 standardizes the ChaCha20 stream cipher and Poly1305 authenticator as an AEAD construction optimized for fast, constant-time execution on general-purpose CPUs.
key_points: Specifies ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) using a 256-bit key and 96-bit nonce.
Executes in strictly constant time on all CPU architectures, entirely eliminating cache-timing side-channel vulnerabilities inherent in software AES.
Delivers up to 3x higher encryption throughput compared to unaccelerated software AES on entry-level mobile devices.
Standardized as a mandatory cipher suite in TLS 1.3 and widely adopted for mobile VPNs, WireGuard, and local storage encryption.
Super-app container automatically negotiates ChaCha20-Poly1305 for mini-app local cache encryption on devices lacking hardware AES acceleration.

title: W3C/MDN Background Fetch API: ServiceWorker Background Transfers & Persistent UI
standard: W3C / WHATWG / MDN Background Fetch API Living Standard
key_takeaways: Provides BackgroundFetchManager and BackgroundFetchRegistration on ServiceWorkerRegistration for long-running asset downloads (game bundles, audio, document packs) that persist even after tabs or the mini-app UI are closed
Mandates container-managed persistent system UI alerting users to ongoing background downloads with title, icons, and cancel affordance
Enforces strict downloadTotal byte limits, immediately aborting the transfer if cumulative payload size exceeds developer-declared totals
Dispatches functional backgroundfetchsuccess, backgroundfetchfail, and backgroundfetchabort events to the Service Worker for deterministic cache storage and state settlement
Eliminates mobile container crashes and memory pressure caused by trying to keep active WebViews alive in background processes during bulk asset downloads
store_governance_rules: Store submission must audit mini-app backgroundFetch downloadTotal declarations against package storage quotas (max 150MB per mini-app without explicit user approval)
Container host must provide unified notification progress bars in the super-app notification drawer for all active background fetch operations
Mini-apps must handle backgroundfetchabort gracefully, ensuring partial byte ranges do not corrupt local persistent caches
Background fetch permission must be gated behind 'background-fetch' feature policy and revoked automatically upon mini-app uninstallation
Super-app background watchdog must terminate any background fetch task stalling on zero-throughput connections exceeding 180 seconds
detail: The Background Fetch API addresses a critical architectural challenge in super-app mobile runtimes: managing large-volume asset and media downloads without keeping the mini-app foreground WebView alive. When a mini-app initiates backgroundFetch.fetch(id, requests, options), the native container or browser host decouples network execution from the rendering thread. The host displays a native progress notification containing developer-provided icons and titles, allowing the user to track progress or cancel the operation. Crucially, downloadTotal provides an upper bound that prevents unbounded bandwidth and disk exhaustion; exceeding this threshold aborts the request immediately. Upon completion, the container wakes the Service Worker, firing backgroundfetchsuccess or backgroundfetchfail, enabling safe off-thread persistence into Cache Storage or IndexedDB.

title: WICG Periodic Background Synchronization: Engagement-Gated Background Execution
standard: WICG Web Periodic Background Synchronization Specification
key_takeaways: Defines PeriodicSyncManager for scheduled background synchronization of fresh catalog, feeds, and cache manifests without active user interaction
Calculates effective minimum sync interval as origin minimum interval plus a user-agent defined penalty based on the user's Engagement Score
Enforces system power, battery status, and unmetered network preconditions before dispatching periodicsync events to Service Workers
Prevents background execution abuse, crypto-mining, and covert tracking by capping background execution duration and frequency
Provides an unmetered Wi-Fi bias, deferring heavy sync routines until the device is connected to non-cellular networks
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps requesting periodic-background-sync must declare min_interval (minimum allowed interval is 12 hours for tier-2/tier-3 mini-apps; 4 hours for certified enterprise tools)
Super-app host container must calculate Site Engagement Scores per mini-app; mini-apps with zero engagement over 7 days are suspended from periodic sync
Container must enforce execution timeout of 30 seconds for periodicsync event handlers, forcibly terminating unresponsive Service Worker instances
Periodic sync execution is prohibited when device battery is below 20% unless actively connected to an external charging source
Developers must document all data fetched during periodic sync; background analytics telemetry during periodic sync is strictly forbidden
detail: WICG Periodic Background Sync allows progressive web applications and mini-apps to keep their content fresh by scheduling periodic network synchronizations in the background. To protect mobile devices against resource exhaustion, battery drain, and covert location tracking, the specification mandates an adaptive scheduling algorithm. The host container dynamically adjusts the execution frequency based on user engagement metrics: highly frequented mini-apps receive frequent sync windows, while seldom-used mini-apps have their interval pushed to Infinity. In a super-app ecosystem, this API must be coupled with OS-level WorkManager (Android) and BGAppRefresh (iOS) constructs to ensure execution aligns with host battery conservation profiles.

title: W3C Badging API: Document & Application Unread Badge Governance
standard: W3C Badging API W3C Recommendation / Working Draft
key_takeaways: Standardizes navigator.setAppBadge(contents) and navigator.clearAppBadge() for setting subtle unread notification counts on application icons and taskbars
Sanitizes badge contents, requiring positive integers (unsigned long long) while rejecting negative numbers and treating zero as an explicit badge clear
Supports flag badges (setAppBadge() without parameters) for unnumbered attention indicators without displaying misleading numeric quantities
Provides origin-scoped badge isolation, ensuring mini-app badges reflect only their internal unread state without contaminating the host super-app badge
Prevents deceptive dark patterns where applications set astronomical unread counts to coerce user engagement
store_governance_rules: Super-app catalog UI must map mini-app badges to in-app mini-app drawer/grid icons, displaying numeric badges up to a cap of 99 (rendering '99+' for larger values)
Mini-apps are strictly prohibited from using badge APIs to display promotional discounts, currency amounts, or artificial urgency indicators
Host container must automatically clear a mini-app's badge upon launch or when the user marks all notifications as read in the system drawer
Badging API access requires active notification permissions or store certification for productivity and messaging categories
Automated store linting must flag mini-apps invoking setAppBadge in tight loops or setting badges without corresponding backend push events
detail: The W3C Badging API provides web applications and mini-apps with a standardized mechanism to inform users of pending actions or unread messages without sending intrusive push notifications. In a super-app architecture, mini-apps execute within a sub-container; therefore, badging must be mediated by the host shell. The host container multiplexes badges from multiple installed mini-apps: aggregating total priority notifications onto the main super-app launcher icon while maintaining discrete badges on individual mini-app icons within the super-app app drawer. Sanitization prevents deceptive practices such as setting artificial badge counts of 9999 to trick users into opening marketing campaigns.

title: W3C Battery Status API: Thermal Energy Adaptation & Fingerprint Mitigation
standard: W3C Battery Status API Specification
key_takeaways: Exposes BatteryManager interface providing charging status, chargingTime, dischargingTime, and level (0.0 to 1.0)
Allows mini-apps to adapt execution strategies, degrading frame rates, pausing background polling, and deferring non-essential compute when battery is low
Identifies high-entropy device fingerprinting risks arising from sub-millisecond precision battery level and discharge timing measurements
Mandates privacy protections including coarse quantization of battery levels (e.g. rounding to nearest 1% or 5%) and clamping discharge time estimations
Recommends gating access or returning simulated default values (charging=true, level=1.0) to untrusted embedded third-party contexts
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps must not utilize Battery Status API attributes as entropy sources for device fingerprinting or cross-mini-app tracking
Host container must virtualize navigator.getBattery(), quantizing battery level to 5% increments and spoofing chargingTime/dischargingTime to fixed intervals
Mini-apps certified for heavy graphics or offline compute must implement automatic low-power degradation when battery level drops below 15%
Store security audit scans AST for battery event listener registrations combined with canvas or WebGL fingerprinting scripts, failing non-compliant submissions
Host container must restrict battery status access to foreground active top-level mini-app documents, returning inert dummy objects in iframes
detail: The W3C Battery Status API enables client-side web applications to monitor host battery parameters to deliver energy-efficient user experiences. While beneficial for throttling background syncing, reducing animation frame rates, or autosaving state before battery exhaustion, the API was historically exploited for cross-site fingerprinting due to micro-variations in battery discharge curves. Within a super-app container, the native host must intercept navigator.getBattery(), delivering a quantized, privacy-preserving proxy that strips microsecond-level timing entropy while preserving the macro status needed for legitimate energy conservation and green computing policies.

title: W3C Service Workers: Deterministic Offline Lifecycle & Cache Isolation
standard: W3C Service Workers Living Standard
key_takeaways: Defines the event-driven worker execution model operating independently of window browsing contexts, managing offline caching and network routing
Enforces strict three-phase lifecycle: Installing (precaching assets), Waiting (waiting for existing client tabs to close), and Active (controlling clients)
Highlights security risks of self.skipWaiting() and Clients.claim(), which can cause version mismatch bugs and resource race conditions across concurrent sessions
Mandates cross-origin isolation and partitioned CacheStorage, preventing mini-apps from accessing or poisoning another mini-app's cached responses
Establishes byte-to-byte script comparison rules: Service Worker scripts are re-checked at least every 24 hours, triggering automatic background updates
store_governance_rules: Mini-app packages must register Service Workers within their designated origin scope, strictly bounded to the mini-app's sandbox path
Mini-app updates must not execute uncoordinated skipWaiting() calls that corrupt active database schemas in ongoing user sessions
Host container must purge orphaned Service Worker registrations and CacheStorage allocations upon mini-app deletion or store revoking
Store packaging pipeline must validate that Service Worker install event handlers complete within a 15-second budget to prevent installation lockups
Mini-app Service Workers must respect host-injected Content-Security-Policy headers, restricting fetch interception to declared mini-app domains
detail: The W3C Service Workers specification represents the foundational substrate for offline web applications and mini-app execution. By acting as a programmable client-side network proxy, a Service Worker intercepts fetch requests, manages the Cache API, and coordinates background events. In multi-tenant super-app containers, strict governance of the Service Worker lifecycle is paramount. The container must enforce origin-bound storage partitioning, prevent unauthorized cross-origin request interception, and regulate updates. Improper use of skipWaiting() can inject breaking script changes while a user is actively completing a checkout flow; the store guidelines enforce staged activation and deterministic cache rotation.

title: IETF RFC 9530: Digest Fields (Content-Digest & Repr-Digest) for HTTP Message Integrity
standard: IETF RFC 9530 Proposed Standard (Obsoletes RFC 3230)
key_takeaways: Defines modern HTTP fields Content-Digest and Repr-Digest using Structured Fields (RFC 8941) dictionary syntax with binary byte sequences
Disambiguates content integrity (Content-Digest over transferred message body bytes) from representation integrity (Repr-Digest over complete payload resource)
Standardizes Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest preference headers, enabling clients and gateways to negotiate hashing algorithms (sha-256, sha-512) and relative weights (0-10)
Formally obsoletes RFC 3230 (Digest and Want-Digest) which suffered from severe interoperability ambiguities regarding transfer-coding and content-encoding
Provides the foundational payload integrity layer required for RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures in enterprise and financial API transactions
store_governance_rules: All payment, balance inquiry, and user profile state-changing APIs between mini-apps and super-app gateways must include Content-Digest with sha-256 or sha-512
Super-app API reverse proxy must validate Content-Digest against received body bytes before routing requests to core banking / commerce backend microservices
Gateways must reject requests containing unsupported or deprecated hashing algorithms (e.g., md5, sha-1) with HTTP 400 Bad Request
Mini-app SDKs must implement RFC 9530 structured dictionary formatting, encoding binary digests via colon-delimited base64 strings (:...:)
Automated store API contracts require upstream developer servers to support Want-Repr-Digest negotiation for large catalog and digital asset sync endpoints
detail: IETF RFC 9530 establishes a modernized, unambiguous framework for communicating cryptographic digests of HTTP content and representations. Historical implementations relying on RFC 3230 frequently broke in production when intermediate proxies applied gzip or brotli compression, because RFC 3230 confused instance data with transport content. RFC 9530 resolves this by splitting the contract: Content-Digest verifies the exact bytes transmitted on the wire, whereas Repr-Digest verifies the underlying resource representation regardless of transfer encodings. In a super-app financial ecosystem, Content-Digest provides non-negotiable end-to-end tamper detection across mini-app client SDKs and backend settlement gateways.

title: IETF RFC 8941: Structured Field Values for HTTP Syntax Validation & Gateway Hygiene
standard: IETF RFC 8941 Proposed Standard
key_takeaways: Establishes a rigorous, standardized data model for HTTP headers: Items, Lists, and Dictionaries with strict type parsing
Defines strongly-typed primitive data types including Integers, Decimals, Strings, Tokens, Byte Sequences, and Booleans
Eliminates bespoke, fragile regex parsing and ad-hoc header serialization across client runtimes, reverse proxies, and microservices
Prevents HTTP request smuggling, header injection, and parameter confusion attacks arising from delimiter mismatches
Forms the structural syntax bedrock for modern web specifications including RFC 9530 Digest Fields, RFC 9421 HTTP Signatures, and Client Hints
store_governance_rules: All proprietary super-app custom headers (e.g., SuperApp-MiniApp-Context, SuperApp-Auth-Params) must conform to RFC 8941 Structured Fields syntax
API Gateway ingress firewalls must parse and re-serialize incoming structured headers, stripping malformed fields or tokens with illegal characters
Mini-app client native bridges must validate structured dictionary keys, enforcing lowercase token constraints (a-z, 0-9, _, -, *, /)
Store submission linting parses mini-app declared webhook headers, rejecting schemas with custom unstructured comma-delimited strings
Container proxy layers must leverage zero-copy structured field parsers to minimize CPU serialization overhead in high-throughput RPC routing
detail: For decades, HTTP header parsing was plagued by inconsistent formatting, undefined whitespace rules, and varying quote escaping semantics, leading to widespread vulnerabilities such as HTTP request smuggling and cache poisoning. RFC 8941 defines Structured Field Values, providing an explicit, unambiguous type system and canonical parsing algorithm for HTTP header fields. In an enterprise super-app store where thousands of third-party mini-apps interact with host APIs, enforcing RFC 8941 on all authorization, context propagation, and signature headers guarantees deterministic parsing across heterogeneous technology stacks.

title: IETF RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures for Non-Repudiable Webhook & Transaction Integrity
standard: IETF RFC 9421 Proposed Standard
key_takeaways: Defines standard HTTP fields Signature and Signature-Input for cryptographic signing of HTTP requests and responses
Enables fine-grained parameterization of signed components: HTTP methods, target URIs, specific header fields, and RFC 9530 content digests
Specifies mandatory signature metadata including key identifier (keyid), algorithm (alg), creation timestamp (created), and expiration (expires)
Prevents man-in-the-middle tampering, message replay attacks, and non-repudiation disputes across distributed multi-party ecosystems
Replaces insecure, vendor-locked webhook HMAC implementations with an open, cryptographically robust standard supporting asymmetric keys (ed25519, ecdsa-p256)
store_governance_rules: All asynchronous store webhooks (order status updates, merchant refund callbacks, developer license revocations) must be signed conforming to RFC 9421
Signature-Input must bind @method, @target-uri, content-digest, and date/created fields to guarantee end-to-end request integrity
Gateways must enforce signature freshness, rejecting any HTTP message where (current_time - created) exceeds 300 seconds (clock skew tolerance)
Developer merchant consoles must register public keys (Ed25519 or ES256) for webhook signature verification, with automated 90-day rotation workflows
Super-app SDK client payment verification must validate the host platform's RFC 9421 signature on payment confirmation payloads
detail: RFC 9421 provides an end-to-end cryptographic signing mechanism for HTTP messages, decoupling message integrity and sender authentication from the underlying transport layer. Unlike TLS, which only protects data in transit between immediate hops, HTTP Message Signatures survive multi-hop routing through proxies, CDNs, and API gateways. For super-app mini-app stores processing sensitive commerce transactions, refunds, and webhook callbacks, RFC 9421 ensures non-repudiation: developers cannot claim an order cancellation or transaction settlement was forged or altered by an intermediary.

title: OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0: JSON Schema 2020-12 & First-Class Webhooks Governance
standard: OpenAPI Initiative / Linux Foundation OAS 3.1.0
key_takeaways: Fully aligns OpenAPI schemas with the complete JSON Schema 2020-12 specification, enabling advanced polymorphism, $defs, and prefixItems
Introduces top-level 'webhooks' metadata, formalizing asynchronous event-driven outbound API contracts outside the traditional request/response tree
Supports Mutual TLS (mTLS) and OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange security schemes as native declaration primitives in API service definitions
Enables automated, bidirectional contract testing and gateway mock validation between super-app host core and third-party mini-app backends
Standardizes content encoding, multipart payload validation, and schema reusability across enterprise service meshes
store_governance_rules: Third-party mini-app developers providing enterprise backend integrations must submit an OAS 3.1.0 compliant OpenAPI document during store review
All asynchronous event webhooks received or transmitted by mini-apps must be formally defined in the OpenAPI webhooks dictionary
Store CI/CD ingestion pipeline automatically generates mock servers and executes contract-fuzzing against developer endpoints based on the OAS document
OpenAPI definitions must not declare HTTP endpoints; all paths must mandate HTTPS with TLS 1.3 or 1.2 strict cipher suites
Store registry exports an aggregated, versioned OAS 3.1.0 catalog enabling automated SDK client generation for Flutter, iOS, and Android containers
detail: The OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 marked a transformative milestone by establishing 100% dialect compatibility with JSON Schema 2020-12 and introducing native support for Webhooks. In modern super-app ecosystems, mini-apps do not operate merely as self-contained client scripts; they interface with enterprise backends and event streams. Mandating OAS 3.1.0 contract definitions allows the super-app platform to automate gateway schema validation, detect breaking API changes prior to production release, and simulate webhook delivery during automated store vetting.

title: IETF RFC 7807: Problem Details for HTTP APIs & Anti-Leakage Error Standardization
standard: IETF RFC 7807 Proposed Standard (Updated by RFC 9457)
key_takeaways: Defines application/problem+json and application/problem+xml standardized media types for communicating API error details

Specifies core problem object members: type (URI reference identifying problem type), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (human explanation), and instance (URI identifying specific occurrence)
Allows extension members to convey machine-readable context without breaking generic client error handlers
Prevents information leakage, stack trace disclosure, and internal infrastructure exposure in public and partner-facing error payloads
Facilitates consistent client-side error handling, localized user messaging, and automated incident correlation across distributed microservices
store_governance_rules: All super-app gateway error responses returned to mini-apps must use Content-Type: application/problem+json conforming to RFC 7807
Mini-app backend APIs interacting with the super-app container must adopt RFC 7807 format for all 4xx and 5xx responses
Gateway error handlers must sanitize error bodies, stripping SQL exceptions, database connection strings, server IP addresses, and stack traces
Every problem details object must include an 'instance' URI containing a unique tracing request-id for correlated developer support tickets
Store automated security testing injects malformed payloads across all declared endpoints, verifying that gateways never return raw 500 HTML debug pages
detail: RFC 7807 (and its successor RFC 9457) establishes a uniform syntax and semantics for communicating machine-readable error details across HTTP APIs. In heterogeneous super-app platforms, disparate backend services often return conflicting error structures (some returning raw strings, others HTML stack traces or ad-hoc JSON). By enforcing RFC 7807 application/problem+json contracts across all store gateway APIs and third-party mini-app integrations, the platform ensures predictable client-side error recovery while safeguarding sensitive backend topology from malicious reconnaissance.

title: OWASP CycloneDX v1.6: Full-Stack SBOM, CBOM & Component Integrity Verification
standard: OWASP CycloneDX Specification v1.6 / ECMA-424
key_takeaways: Provides an advanced, machine-readable software bill of materials standard covering applications, libraries, frameworks, containers, and firmware
Introduces Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM), capturing cryptographic algorithms, key lengths, certificates, and post-quantum readiness across dependencies
Includes Operations Bill of Materials (OBOM) and Software-as-a-Service Bill of Materials (SaaSBOM) for cloud endpoint and runtime dependency tracking
Supports component hashes (SHA-256, SHA-512, BLAKE3) and package URL (purl) identifiers for automated vulnerability matching against national databases
Integrates digital signatures (JSF / XML Signature) directly into the SBOM document, ensuring non-repudiation and tamper detection
store_governance_rules: Store submission pipeline requires mini-app packages to bundle a signed CycloneDX JSON SBOM (schema version 1.5 or 1.6) documenting all npm/gradle/cocoapods dependencies
Store security gates automatically analyze declared CBOM entries, flagging outdated cryptographic algorithms (e.g. SHA-1, 1024-bit RSA, MD5) as blocking defects
Component purl declarations are matched continuously against OSV and CVE feeds; critical unpatched CVEs trigger automated developer remediation warnings
The platform retains historical CycloneDX SBOMs across all published versions to maintain full audit traceability for enterprise compliance
Mini-apps incorporating proprietary third-party commercial SDKs must include vendor-signed component attestations within the primary SBOM
detail: OWASP CycloneDX is a purpose-built software supply chain standard designed specifically for application security analysis and risk reduction. Unlike earlier inventory formats, CycloneDX v1.6 encompasses the entire modern software lifecycle, extending beyond simple open-source licenses to include Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) and runtime services (SaaSBOM). For super-app mini-app stores hosting thousands of third-party plugins, CycloneDX enables automated, continuous supply chain vulnerability monitoring. The store platform ingests the developer's CycloneDX document during the review pipeline, auditing cryptographic compliance and flagging vulnerable transitive dependencies before user exposure.

title: Linux Foundation SPDX 3.0: Package Composition Analysis & IP Licensing Compliance
standard: Linux Foundation / ISO/IEC 5962:2021 SPDX 3.0
key_takeaways: Standardizes the exchange of software package metadata, licensing terms, copyrights, and provenance relationships across multi-tier supply chains
Introduces modular architecture in SPDX 3.0: Core profile, Software profile, Licensing profile, Security profile, and AI profile
Enables precise tracking of dependency relationships: DEPENDS_ON, CONTAINS, GENERATES, DESCRIBES, and DYNAMIC_LINK
Provides standardized SPDX License Identifiers (e.g. Apache-2.0, MIT, GPL-3.0-only) preventing legal ambiguity and intellectual property conflicts
Facilitates automated open-source license compliance audits, isolating copyleft viral licenses (e.g., AGPL-3.0) that could compromise proprietary host IP
store_governance_rules: Store review engine runs automated SPDX license compliance validation against all mini-app binary packages and source bundles
Mini-apps containing AGPL-3.0 or GPL-3.0-only linked dependencies must not access proprietary super-app core host SDK bridges without legal clearance
SPDX 3.0 documents must accompany all enterprise-tier mini-app releases, published with canonical package verification codes
Dependencies lacking recognized SPDX license identifiers or declared as 'unlicensed' are rejected during automated store ingestion
Store operator console provides developers with an interactive license risk report during pre-submission dry-run validation
detail: Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) is an open international standard (ISO/IEC 5962) for communicating software bill of materials information, provenance, and licensing details. SPDX 3.0 modernizes the framework through a graph-based modular architecture, dividing metadata into specialized profiles. In a commercial super-app marketplace, license compliance is a critical legal safeguard. If a third-party mini-app incorporates strong copyleft code (such as GPL or AGPL) that statically links to the super-app host container libraries, the host could face intellectual property contamination claims. Automated SPDX parsing ensures complete license transparency and legal risk containment.

title: OpenSSF SLSA v1.0: Supply-Chain Levels for Software Artifacts & Hermetic Build Provenance
standard: OpenSSF Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) v1.0
key_takeaways: Defines a security framework of progressively increasing levels (Build L1 to L3) to protect software artifacts against tampering and supply chain attacks
Specifies verifiable provenance format detailing how an artifact was built, including source repo, commit hash, builder identity, and input parameters
Requires Build L2 to mandate hosted, authenticated build platforms that generate tamper-evident provenance signed by the build service
Requires Build L3 to enforce hermetic (isolated) builds and ephemeral build environments, preventing build-time network access and artifact manipulation
Mitigates compromised developer workstation attacks, stolen credentials, and malicious source injection during the compilation pipeline
store_governance_rules: All enterprise, banking, and government mini-apps must achieve SLSA Build L2 or L3 compliance, providing verifiable build provenance
Store ingestion gateway validates build provenance signatures using Sigstore cosign or container-approved root CAs before binary unpacking
Provenance metadata must prove that artifacts were generated from declared public or approved private Git repositories without local developer overrides
Build environments used by certified mini-app development agencies must be authenticated and isolated from external uncontrolled network access
Store badge displays verified 'SLSA L3 Hermetic Build' verification indicators on developer profiles to promote ecosystem supply chain maturity
detail: The OpenSSF SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework establishes an industry-standard hierarchy for software artifact integrity and build security. As attacks shifting from runtime exploitation to upstream developer infrastructure proliferate, validating the build provenance of mini-app bundles becomes indispensable. SLSA v1.0 establishes clear requirements: Build Level 1 requires automated builds and provenance; Level 2 requires hosted, authenticated builders and tamper-evident signed provenance; Level 3 enforces hermetic environments where external network dependencies cannot alter build output. This prevents a compromised developer laptop from distributing weaponized mini-app packages to millions of super-app users.

title: OpenVEX Specification: Machine-Readable Vulnerability Exploitability Exchange for Store Triage
standard: OpenVEX Specification / Linux Foundation OpenSSF Working Group
key_takeaways: Defines a lightweight, machine-readable JSON format for asserting the actual exploitability of known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in specific software components
Establishes four standardized status classifications: not_affected, affected, fixed, and under_investigation

Provides an authoritative justification taxonomy for not_affected status: component_not_present, inline_mitigations_already_exist, vulnerable_code_cannot_be_controlled_by_adversary, vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path, and vulnerable_code_not_present
Eliminates false-positive fatigue where scanner alerts block legitimate mini-app releases due to dead code or unused transitive libraries
Enables cryptographic signing of VEX statements by software publishers and independent security auditing firms
store_governance_rules: Developers contesting automated store CVE blocking flags must submit a signed OpenVEX statement detailing the exact non-exploitability justification
Store review engine accepts OpenVEX justifications only when accompanied by static call-graph proof or verified container mitigation boundaries
OpenVEX statements with status 'under_investigation' grant a temporary 14-day conditional release window for non-critical severity issues
The super-app security operations center maintains a centralized VEX repository documenting platform-level mitigations for common mobile runtime CVEs
Store operator console automatically resolves false positives across all mini-apps once a platform-wide OpenVEX assertion is approved by security leads
detail: While SBOMs provide exhaustive visibility into software components, automated scanners routinely flag vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies whose vulnerable functions are never called (dead code) or are mitigated by host container sandboxes. This produces severe false-positive fatigue, stalling release cycles. OpenVEX solves this by providing a standardized, interoperable format for developers and vendors to declare whether a vulnerability is genuinely exploitable. In a super-app mini-app store review workflow, signed OpenVEX documents enable automated triage, allowing developers to justify harmless findings while focusing remediation efforts exclusively on actual risks.

title: in-toto Framework: Cryptographically Chained Supply Chain Layout Policies & Step Attestation
standard: in-toto Supply Chain Security Specification / CNCF Graduated Standard
key_takeaways: Defines a cryptographically verifiable framework enforcing integrity across the entire software delivery pipeline from commit to deployment
Establishes supply chain 'layouts' defined by project owners, specifying required steps, authorized functionaries (keys), and artifact transit rules
Generates cryptographically signed 'link' metadata for every build step (checkout, dependency resolution, linting, compilation, packaging, security scan)
Enforces artifact matching rules, verifying that outputs of step N (e.g., compiled JS bundle) match the exact inputs to step N+1 (e.g., package signing)
Detects and blocks rogue intermediate modifications, unauthorized pipeline tool injection, and out-of-band artifact tampering
store_governance_rules: High-security financial and utility mini-apps must provide an in-toto link metadata chain covering Git commit, CI build, and package bundling
Store verification engine evaluates the developer's declared in-toto layout against submitted link attestations prior to store publication
Any discrepancy between step input/output hashes (e.g. unexpected files injected between compile and signing) aborts release immediately
Functionary public keys authorized to sign pipeline links must be pinned in the developer organization's store portal registry
Super-app CI/CD template provides zero-configuration in-toto link generation for developers utilizing official super-app build CLI tools
detail: in-toto provides a comprehensive, end-to-end framework to guarantee the integrity of the software supply chain. While point solutions verify source code or individual binary hashes, in-toto glues the entire development and build process together into a cryptographically verified chain of custody. A project owner authors a 'layout' that defines what steps must be performed, who is authorized to perform them, and how artifacts must match between steps. When applied to super-app mini-app stores, in-toto ensures that the exact code committed to version control is what was tested, scanned, compiled, and bundled, completely preventing tampering during transit.

title: TC39 ShadowRealm: Distinct Global Evaluation & Controlled Cross-Realm Callables
standard: ECMAScript / TC39 ShadowRealm Proposal (Stage 2.7)
key_takeaways: Introduces ShadowRealm constructor providing a distinct global execution environment with its own built-ins and global object
Establishes a strict boundary preventing object identity exposure between the incubating realm and the inner shadow realm
Restricts values crossing the realm boundary strictly to primitives or wrapped callables (custom [[Call]] internal methods)
Provides synchronous code evaluation via shadowRealm.evaluate() and asynchronous dynamic module loading via shadowRealm.importValue()
Eliminates prototype pollution and scope escalation risks by preventing direct reference sharing to host objects
store_governance_rules: Host container runtime isolates mini-app third-party analytics and ad plugins into dedicated ShadowRealm instances
Wrapped callables crossing the ShadowRealm boundary must be strictly argument-validated and sanitized by host bridge wrappers
Direct passing of mutable DOM nodes, Window handles, or native JSAPI host objects across realm boundaries is strictly forbidden
Store security linter verifies that plugin code running in guest realms cannot access or mutate the incubating application realm globals
Host containers maintain separate memory telemetry for each ShadowRealm to enforce strict per-plugin memory allocation ceilings
detail: The TC39 ShadowRealm specification provides a standardized, high-performance mechanism for evaluating untrusted or third-party JavaScript code in a distinct global execution context. Unlike iframes or full worker threads, ShadowRealm executes on the same thread without the overhead of a complete DOM window, yet guarantees complete global object isolation. Crucially, the realm boundary only permits primitives (strings, numbers, booleans, symbols, bigints, undefined, null) and wrapped callable functions to cross. This prevents malicious third-party plugins within a mini-app from polluting host prototypes, exfiltrating global variables, or hijacking native bridge interfaces.

title: Endo SES: Hardened JavaScript & Object-Capability (ocaps) Sandboxing
standard: Endo Secure ECMAScript (SES) Specification / Agoric Ocap Architecture
key_takeaways: Transforms standard JavaScript into a secure, deterministic object-capability (ocap) environment via lockdown()
Deep-freezes all primordial intrinsics (Object.prototype, Array.prototype, Function.prototype, Math, etc.) to eliminate prototype tampering
Provides Compartment instances with isolated global scopes, customizable module loaders, and attenuated ambient endowments
Replaces ambient authority (e.g., direct network or storage access) with explicitly granted, revocable capability references
Enforces strict defensive consistency, ensuring that untrusted guest code cannot modify or inspect adjacent tenant code
store_governance_rules: Container JavaScript runtime must invoke lockdown() at host startup before evaluating any untrusted mini-app script
Each mini-app is instantiated within an isolated Compartment endowed only with authorized host bridge capability stubs
Primordial prototype mutation attempts within guest compartments trigger runtime security alerts and automated sandbox termination
Dangerous ambient properties (such as eval, Function constructor, or global process/window properties) are stripped from guest compartments
Store submission scanner requires third-party component vendors to prove compatibility with deeply frozen primordial prototypes
detail: Endo SES (Secure ECMAScript) extends the JavaScript language into an object-capability system by combining primordial freezing with isolated execution compartments. By executing lockdown(), SES recursively freezes all shared JavaScript prototypes, preventing any code from performing prototype pollution attacks. Compartments allow the host container to execute untrusted mini-app code with a tailored global object, providing access only to attenuated capabilities rather than ambient authority. This paradigm is essential for enterprise super-apps, allowing untrusted partner mini-apps to run within the same JavaScript VM while strictly isolating tenant state.

title: ShadowRealm Dynamic Module Virtualization & Static Capability Attenuation
standard: ECMAScript / TC39 ShadowRealm Module Loading Specification
key_takeaways: Specifies ShadowRealm.prototype.importValue(specifier, bindingName) for asynchronous module import inside the sandbox
Guarantees that imported modules execute entirely within the target realm without leaking module namespace objects
Allows host container to implement synthetic module specifiers and virtual module resolution graphs for guest realms
Enforces capability attenuation by intercepting module resolution requests and denying access to sensitive host modules
Returns a promise resolving to a primitive or wrapped callable, preventing direct access to the module namespace object
store_governance_rules: Host container intercepts all module specifiers loaded via importValue(), mapping standard mini-app APIs to sandboxed stubs
Attempts by guest modules to dynamically import native host modules (e.g. '@superapp/native-bridge') without permission are denied
Store review pipeline audits mini-app dynamic module loading graphs to ensure all entry points are declaratively declared
All imported callable exports from mini-app plugins must be wrapped with host schema-validating argument interceptors
Memory consumed by dynamically imported modules inside a ShadowRealm is accounted toward the mini-app's sandbox quota
detail: ShadowRealm's importValue API provides a secure foundation for module virtualization in super-app environments. When a mini-app dynamically loads third-party plugins or components, importValue ensures the target module executes strictly within the isolated realm. The returned value is restricted to primitives or wrapped callables, ensuring that the module's internal lexical scope and prototype references remain strictly confined. The host platform leverages this mechanism to dynamically attenuate capabilities, providing developers with powerful modularity without exposing the super-app host container to code execution vulnerabilities.

title: Endo Compartments: Attenuated Bridge Proxies & Revocable Capability Handles
standard: Endo / SES Compartment Architecture / RFC 9205 Alignment
key_takeaways: Defines Compartment constructors allowing precise attenuation of system capabilities through proxy wrappers
Implements the principle of least authority (POLA) by replacing broad APIs with narrow, purpose-specific function closures
Supports revocable capability handles via Proxy.revocable(), enabling instantaneous revocation of permissions at runtime
Isolates module namespaces between co-located components, preventing inter-plugin variable sniffing or interference
Provides deterministic execution environments suitable for auditing, testing, and high-assurance multi-tenant execution
store_governance_rules: All privileged host capabilities (geolocation, camera, bluetooth) granted to mini-apps must be delivered as revocable capability handles
When a user revokes mini-app permissions via the super-app UI, the host runtime immediately revokes the corresponding Proxy handle
Attenuated bridge proxies must validate argument types and ranges before forwarding invocation requests to native bridge layers
Direct access to raw platform bridge dispatchers is blocked; all communication must traverse verified Compartment wrappers
Store compliance certification requires multi-tenant plugins to operate exclusively through attenuated capability handles
detail: Endo Compartments provide the operational mechanism for enforcing the Principle of Least Authority (POLA) in super-app architectures. Rather than granting a mini-app full access to a native bridge interface, the host constructs an attenuated proxy within a Compartment. If a mini-app requires location access only for city-level services, the proxy can coarsen coordinates or restrict call frequency. Furthermore, by wrapping bridge functions in revocable proxies, the super-app can instantly sever a mini-app's access to sensitive device sensors upon backgrounding or user permission withdrawal, eliminating lingering execution hazards.

title: W3C CSP Level 3: 'report-sample' Directives & Automated Script Sandbox Telemetry
standard: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 / Candidate Recommendation
key_takeaways: Defines the 'report-sample' CSP expression allowing violation reports to capture the first 40 characters of offending inline scripts
Enables rapid diagnostic triage of dynamic code injection and eval attempts in violation reports
Enforces strict script-src and script-src-elem isolation, blocking unauthorized third-party script tags and un-hashed inline code
Integrates with the W3C Reporting API for out-of-band delivery of CSP violation reports to store monitoring endpoints
Provides standardized JSON violation payloads with blocked-uri, violated-directive, original-policy, and script-sample fields
store_governance_rules: Store container enforces CSP Level 3 with 'script-src 'self' 'report-sample'' across all hosted mini-app WebViews
Any dynamic code injection or unauthorized inline script execution is logged and dispatched to the super-app security SOC
Violation reports containing 'report-sample' payloads are automatically analyzed by store bots to detect active XSS exploitation
Mini-apps exceeding five CSP report-sample violations per 1,000 sessions are automatically flagged for security re-review
Store developer console surfaces real-time CSP violation samples to assist developers in eliminating legacy inline scripts
detail: W3C Content Security Policy (CSP) Level 3 introduces the 'report-sample' directive, which enriches security violation reporting by attaching a truncated snippet of the offending code. When combined with strict script execution policies, this mechanism provides the super-app host container with immediate, actionable telemetry regarding script injection attempts or policy bypasses within mini-app WebViews. In addition to blocking malicious execution, automated collection and aggregation of these samples enable store operators to rapidly detect zero-day exploits, misconfigured analytics SDKs, and unauthorized runtime code modifications across the entire ecosystem.

title: W3C Global Privacy Control: Sec-GPC HTTP Header & Universal Opt-Out Signaling
standard: W3C Global Privacy Control (GPC) Specification / W3C Draft
key_takeaways: Defines the Sec-GPC HTTP request header conveying a user's universal preference to opt out of data selling and sharing
Specifies strict wire format: the Sec-GPC header field value MUST be exactly the character '1'
Prohibits multiple Sec-GPC headers in a single request and forbids Sec-GPC within HTTP trailers
Mandates that servers treat Sec-GPC: 1 as a legally binding opt-out signal under regulations like CCPA/CPRA and GDPR
Specifies user-agent requirements to ensure GPC signals reflect genuine, unambiguous affirmative user choices
store_governance_rules: Super-app host container automatically injects 'Sec-GPC: 1' into all outbound HTTP requests made by mini-apps when user enables privacy mode
Mini-app backend servers and integrated advertising networks must respect Sec-GPC: 1 as an automated opt-out of data sale/sharing
Store compliance audits verify that mini-app analytics endpoints do not transmit cross-context tracking identifiers when Sec-GPC: 1 is set
Mini-apps operating in regulated jurisdictions (California, Colorado, EU) must document GPC signal compliance in their privacy disclosures
The store developer console provides a simulated Sec-GPC testing environment to validate compliance before app submission
detail: The W3C Global Privacy Control (GPC) specification standardizes an automated, universal opt-out mechanism across web platforms. Under modern privacy frameworks such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA), Colorado Privacy Act (CPA), and European GDPR, users have the legal right to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal data. By transmitting the 'Sec-GPC: 1' header with every network request, the super-app container communicates the user's binding privacy choice to both mini-app frontends and backend servers, establishing an automated compliance layer across third-party services.

title: W3C GPC DOM API: navigator.globalPrivacyControl & Client-Side SDK Mediation
standard: W3C Global Privacy Control (GPC) DOM API Specification
key_takeaways: Exposes navigator.globalPrivacyControl as a boolean property across Window and WorkerGlobalScope environments
Returns true if the user has asserted a global privacy control preference, and false/undefined otherwise
Enables client-side JavaScript analytics and advertising libraries to immediately adapt data collection behaviors
Ensures consistency between HTTP network layer signals (Sec-GPC) and DOM runtime execution environments
Specifies that navigator.globalPrivacyControl must be read-only and immutable to untrusted page scripts
store_governance_rules: Super-app WebView runtime pre-populates navigator.globalPrivacyControl based on the user's centralized super-app privacy settings
Client-side SDKs embedded in mini-apps must inspect navigator.globalPrivacyControl prior to initializing user tracking or ad profiling
Attempts by mini-app scripts to overwrite, shadow, or delete navigator.globalPrivacyControl are blocked by the host runtime
Mini-apps submitting for store review undergo automated runtime checks ensuring SDKs suppress third-party cookies when GPC is true
Store guidelines mandate that mini-app consent banners must reflect the pre-existing GPC state without presenting redundant opt-out prompts
detail: The W3C GPC DOM API complements HTTP header signaling by exposing navigator.globalPrivacyControl directly to client-side scripts. In a super-app architecture where mini-apps embed third-party analytics, monetization, and tracking SDKs, this API allows libraries to immediately detect user privacy preferences upon script execution. The super-app host container ensures that navigator.globalPrivacyControl is deeply integrated with the user's profile settings, guaranteeing that client-side tracking is automatically suppressed without requiring complex banner interactions on every mini-app launch.

title: GPC Support Resource: /.well-known/gpc.json Server-Side Compliance Declaration
standard: W3C Global Privacy Control Specification / GPC Support Resource
key_takeaways: Specifies a standardized server-side discovery document hosted at /.well-known/gpc.json
Defines JSON schema containing 'gpc' boolean indicator and optional 'lastUpdate' date string
Enables web applications and API servers to publicly assert their active recognition and processing of GPC signals
Allows automated compliance crawlers and store review bots to verify publisher adherence to privacy mandates
Provides legal and technical non-repudiation proving the publisher's commitment to user privacy standards
