store_governance_rules: All mini-app backend domains collecting personal data must publish a valid /.well-known/gpc.json document with 'gpc: true'
Store submission verification crawler automatically tests all declared mini-app API endpoints for /.well-known/gpc.json compliance
Mini-app backend domains failing to host a valid GPC support resource receive a compliance warning during store review
The store directory displays a 'Verified GPC Compliant' badge for mini-apps backed by verified /.well-known/gpc.json servers
Platform annual security audits re-verify that declared backend endpoints continue to maintain active GPC support declarations
detail: The GPC Support Resource standardizes a machine-readable declaration mechanism via the well-known URI '/.well-known/gpc.json'. This endpoint allows mini-app backend publishers to explicitly state that their servers recognize and enforce GPC opt-out signals. For super-app store governance, this creates an auditable technical trail: store review pipelines can programmatically crawl mini-app backends, verify the existence of the declaration, and cross-reference it with regulatory disclosure requirements, ensuring that mini-apps do not merely receive GPC headers but actively honor them on their infrastructure.

title: IAB Europe TCF v2.2: Standardized Consent Strings & Vendor Transparency Governance
standard: IAB Europe Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) v2.2
key_takeaways: Establishes a standardized framework for capturing, encoding, and transmitting user consent across digital advertising ecosystems
Deprecates legitimate interest as a legal basis for advertising and content personalization in TCF v2.2, mandating explicit consent
Specifies compact base64-encoded Transparency and Consent (TC) Strings carrying granular purpose and vendor consent bits
Mandates standardized vendor information disclosure: categories of data collected, retention periods, and legitimate interest declarations
Introduces the __tcfapi() JavaScript API interface for standardized client-side consent querying and event listening
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps displaying programmatic ad impressions must implement an IAB TCF v2.2 certified Consent Management Platform (CMP)
The super-app host container exposes a unified __tcfapi() bridge allowing mini-apps to synchronize consent with the host account
Transmission of advertising identifiers or device telemetry without a valid TC String containing positive consent is strictly blocked
Store review engine parses mini-app CMP configurations, rejecting applications that fail to disclose vendor retention periods
Store operator console conducts automated audits ensuring mini-app ad requests carry valid, non-expired TCF v2.2 consent payloads
detail: IAB Europe's Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) v2.2 provides the definitive industry mechanism for ensuring GDPR and ePrivacy compliance in programmatic advertising. TCF v2.2 significantly tightens regulatory compliance by eliminating legitimate interest for ad personalization, requiring explicit affirmative consent. Within a super-app ecosystem, integrating TCF v2.2 ensures that when third-party mini-apps monetize via ad networks, user choices are encoded into cryptographically structured TC Strings, providing complete legal defensibility and preventing privacy enforcement penalties across global markets.

title: IAB Tech Lab GPP: Multi-Jurisdictional Privacy Signaling & Core String Architecture
standard: IAB Tech Lab Global Privacy Platform (GPP) Technical Specification
key_takeaways: Defines a single, unified protocol and data format for communicating user privacy preferences across multiple global jurisdictions
Supports modular section architecture accommodating GDPR/TCF, US National, US State-specific (CA, VA, CO, UT, CT), and Canadian privacy frameworks
Specifies the GPP Core String structure containing Header, Section IDs, and compressed Section-specific data segments
Provides standard client-side API __gpp() with ping, getGPPData, and addEventListener methods for seamless cross-context synchronization
Facilitates rapid adaptation to emerging regional privacy laws without requiring breaking changes to core application codebases
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps serving multi-regional user bases must implement the __gpp() API interface for unified privacy preference propagation
The super-app container acts as the master privacy broker, encoding user settings into regional GPP sections based on IP and account geo-location
Mini-app ad and monetization SDKs must query __gpp('getGPPData') and propagate the resulting GPP string in all downstream API payloads
Store review validation includes automated testing across simulated geo-IP locations (EU, US-CA, US-VA) to verify dynamic GPP adaptation
Mini-apps that fail to properly parse or forward jurisdiction-specific GPP sections are rejected during store compliance verification
detail: The Global Privacy Platform (GPP) by IAB Tech Lab solves the fragmentation of regional privacy signaling by establishing a single, extensible string architecture. Instead of deploying disparate consent APIs for Europe (TCF), California (CPRA), and other US states, GPP encodes multi-jurisdictional preferences into a single compact payload. In a global super-app, the host container determines the user's regulatory jurisdiction and constructs the corresponding GPP string. Mini-apps and embedded vendors access these preferences via the standardized __gpp() API, ensuring robust, automated compliance across all target regions.

title: WHATWG Server-Sent Events: EventSource Interface & Resilient Unidirectional Streaming
standard: WHATWG HTML Living Standard / Server-Sent Events
key_takeaways: Standardizes the EventSource API for receiving push notifications and realtime event streams over standard HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2/3
Defines the 'text/event-stream' MIME type using a simple, resilient UTF-8 line-oriented protocol (event, data, id, retry fields)
Provides native client-side automatic reconnection with exponential backoff governed by the server-specified 'retry' directive
Implements built-in stream synchronization via the Last-Event-ID HTTP request header, ensuring zero message loss across disconnections
Operates through standard HTTP infrastructure, eliminating the firewall, proxy, and multiplexing complexities of raw WebSockets
store_governance_rules: Store review engine recommends EventSource over WebSockets for unidirectional server-to-mini-app push streams (e.g. order tracking, news)
Mini-app SSE endpoints must implement the Last-Event-ID header and maintain a replay buffer of at least 60 seconds to guarantee message delivery
The super-app host container automatically suspends active EventSource connections when a mini-app enters background freeze state
Upon returning to foreground, the container resumes the EventSource connection, transmitting the last known event ID to catch up on missed state
Store platform enforces connection pooling, limiting each mini-app to a maximum of 2 concurrent SSE connections per host domain
detail: The WHATWG Server-Sent Events (SSE) standard and its EventSource interface provide a lightweight, robust architecture for streaming realtime updates from servers to mini-apps. Unlike WebSockets, which require custom framing, separate connection lifecycles, and bespoke ping/pong heartbeats, SSE operates cleanly over HTTP, taking full advantage of HTTP/2 multiplexing and native TLS. Built-in reconnection logic and the Last-Event-ID header make SSE exceptionally resilient for mobile super-apps, allowing mini-apps to seamlessly recover from cellular handoffs and brief network drops without losing critical event payloads.

title: CloudEvents v1.0.2: Common Event Metadata & Cross-Service Store Event Harmonization
standard: CNCF CloudEvents Specification v1.0.2
key_takeaways: Defines a vendor-neutral specification for describing event data in common formats to provide interoperability across cloud ecosystems
Specifies four mandatory context attributes: id (unique event identifier), source (event context URI), specversion (e.g. '1.0'), and type (event name)
Specifies optional standard attributes: datacontenttype, dataschema, subject, and time (RFC 3339 timestamp)
Supports binary and structured content modes across multiple protocols: HTTP, AMQP, MQTT, and Kafka
Enables decoupled event-driven architectures where store control planes, webhook brokers, and mini-app backends interoperate seamlessly
store_governance_rules: All asynchronous store lifecycle events (app submission, review verdict, release, suspension, deprecation) must be formatted as CloudEvents v1.0
Mini-app developer webhooks must validate CloudEvents envelope headers (ce-id, ce-source, ce-type, ce-specversion) on inbound notifications
The super-app developer portal publishes formal JSON schemas for all emitted CloudEvent types under canonical URI schemas
Event broker must guarantee at-least-once delivery of CloudEvents, providing unique 'id' values for consumer-side deduplication
Store audit logs must record CloudEvent envelopes in append-only storage to maintain an immutable audit trail of operational transitions
detail: CNCF CloudEvents v1.0.2 establishes a universal standard for describing event metadata, eliminating proprietary payload structures in distributed systems. In a super-app ecosystem hosting thousands of independent partners, CloudEvents provides a consistent schema for all operational and transactional events—such as app review approvals, payment settlements, and emergency security revocations. By standardizing envelope attributes like 'id', 'source', and 'type', both the super-app control plane and external developer webhooks can route, filter, and process events using off-the-shelf cloud tooling and event brokers.

title: Standard Webhooks Specification: HMAC-SHA256 Signatures & Anti-Replay Timestamping
standard: Standard Webhooks Technical Specification / OWASP Alignment
key_takeaways: Establishes a unified specification for secure, reliable webhook delivery across SaaS and developer platforms
Mandates the 'webhook-id' header containing a unique message identifier to enable robust consumer deduplication
Mandates the 'webhook-timestamp' header carrying an integer Unix timestamp (seconds) to prevent replay attacks
Mandates the 'webhook-signature' header containing base64-encoded HMAC-SHA256 signatures over the payload and timestamp
Specifies signature construction: HMAC-SHA256(secret, msg_id + '.' + timestamp + '.' + payload)
Supports multi-key rotation by allowing space-delimited signatures prefixed with version identifiers (e.g., 'v1,sig1 v1,sig2')
store_governance_rules: Super-app webhook gateway strictly enforces the Standard Webhooks signature protocol for all notifications dispatched to developer endpoints
Developers must verify webhook signatures using their pinned secret and reject requests where the timestamp drifts by more than 300 seconds
Webhook deliveries must handle retries with exponential backoff (e.g., 5s, 30s, 5m, 30m, 2h) over a 24-hour window before dead-lettering
Developer console provides an automated webhook endpoint testing tool that verifies signature validation and error response handling
All outbound store webhooks must enforce TLS 1.3 encryption and follow strict recipient timeout ceilings of 15 seconds
detail: The Standard Webhooks specification addresses the long-standing fragmentation and security vulnerabilities of HTTP webhooks. By standardizing headers (webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature) and prescribing HMAC-SHA256 signing, it protects developer endpoints against tampering and replay attacks. In a mini-app store context where webhooks notify developers of purchase approvals, account unlinking, and review decisions, adhering to Standard Webhooks ensures non-repudiation, seamless credential rotation, and standardized SDK verification libraries across diverse programming languages.

title: CloudEvents HTTP Transport Binding: Binary vs Structured Framing & Gateway Routing
standard: CloudEvents HTTP Protocol Binding v1.0.2
key_takeaways: Defines two canonical mapping modes for transmitting CloudEvents over HTTP: Structured Mode and Binary Mode
Structured Mode encapsulates both context attributes and event data within a single JSON payload using Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json
Binary Mode maps context attributes directly to HTTP request headers prefixed with 'ce-' (e.g., ce-type, ce-id), keeping the body raw
Enables high-throughput API gateways and proxies to inspect, filter, and route events using standard HTTP headers without parsing JSON bodies
Preserves native binary payloads (e.g. Protocol Buffers, Avro) in Binary Mode while maintaining standardized event metadata
store_governance_rules: Super-app API gateway must support both Binary and Structured CloudEvent HTTP bindings on developer notification endpoints
High-throughput transactional streams (e.g. order state updates) should utilize Binary Mode to permit zero-copy header-based routing
Developer webhook listeners must accept Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json and correctly extract nested event context attributes
Gateway security rules filter out malformed or missing ce-specversion headers prior to internal event queue ingestion
Store developer documentation must provide code samples illustrating parsing for both structured and binary HTTP CloudEvents
detail: The CloudEvents HTTP Protocol Binding specification defines how event context attributes map onto HTTP messages. In Binary Mode, metadata is stored in HTTP headers (ce-id, ce-type, etc.), allowing edge gateways and load balancers to route and prioritize traffic without deserializing the message body. In Structured Mode, the entire event is serialized as a JSON object, ideal for logging, webhook delivery, and audit archiving. For a super-app platform, supporting both bindings ensures optimal routing efficiency at the gateway layer while providing developer-friendly integration for external partner systems.

title: Server-Sent Events over HTTP/2/3: Multiplexing, Keep-Alives & Mobile Battery Conservation
standard: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2) / WHATWG SSE Integration & RFC 9205 Alignment
key_takeaways: Overcomes the historical HTTP/1.1 6-connection browser limit by multiplexing unlimited SSE streams over a single HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 TCP/QUIC connection
Eliminates per-connection TCP and TLS handshake overhead, drastically reducing cellular radio wakeups on mobile devices
Specifies periodic comment ping lines (': ping\n\n') at 15-30 second intervals to keep intermediate NAT and telco gateways alive
Reduces battery consumption by up to 70% compared to polling or un-multiplexed multiple WebSocket connections
Enables seamless prioritization of interactive UI data over background telemetry streams within the same transport session
store_governance_rules: Super-app container infrastructure mandates HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for all mini-app SSE streaming gateways to enforce stream multiplexing
Mini-app servers must send periodic SSE heartbeat comments (': ping') every 25 seconds to prevent mobile cellular NAT drops
Mini-apps must not open multiple raw WebSocket connections when SSE over HTTP/2 multiplexing meets application streaming requirements
Host network watchdog terminates rogue SSE connections that fail to receive data or heartbeats within a 90-second timeout window
Developer performance dashboards display active SSE connection durations and cellular radio wakeup metrics to encourage energy efficiency
detail: While early implementations of Server-Sent Events over HTTP/1.1 were constrained by browser per-domain connection limits, running SSE over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 makes it the premier streaming architecture for mobile super-apps. Multiple mini-apps and background services can maintain independent event streams over a single shared multiplexed connection. Combined with disciplined keep-alive pings (SSE comment lines) and HTTP/2 stream prioritization, this approach drastically minimizes mobile cellular radio transitions between low-power and high-power states, conserving device battery life while providing instant server push.

title: W3C Digital Credentials API: High-Trust Mobile Driver's License & Verifiable Identity Presentation
standard: W3C Digital Credentials API / W3C Federated Identity Working Group
key_takeaways: Defines a standardized web platform API (navigator.identity.get) enabling websites and mini-apps to request verifiable digital credentials from native device identity wallets
Natively bridges to mobile OS identity stores, supporting ISO/IEC 18013-5 Mobile Driver's Licenses (mDL), national eID schemes, and EU Digital Identity Wallets
Eliminates manual document uploads, physical scan OCR vulnerabilities, and synthetic identity fraud by leveraging hardware-backed asymmetric cryptographic proof of attributes
Enforces selective disclosure: verifiers can request specific claims (such as 'age_over_18: true') without accessing unnecessary PII like full legal name, home address, or license number
Provides origin-bound challenge-response replay mitigation, cryptographically guaranteeing that identity proofs cannot be harvested and replayed across malicious domains
store_governance_rules: Super-app host container exposes navigator.identity.get exclusively to KYC-verified mini-apps operating under explicit regulatory licensing (e.g. banking, fintech, telecom SIM activation)
Store submission review verifies that mini-app attribute requests adhere to strict data minimization principles, rejecting broad requests when boolean claims suffice
Host container intercepts Digital Credentials calls, rendering an unforgeable native OS identity consent dialog that clearly discloses the exact requested attributes and relying party identity
Cryptographic proof verification (digital signature validation, certificate revocation status, issuing authority trust anchors) must execute within secure backend gateways or trusted enclaves
Developer documentation specifies sandbox mock credentials for automated CI/CD testing, strictly prohibiting production credential issuance during staging or app store review
detail: The W3C Digital Credentials API represents a monumental paradigm shift for identity verification and KYC in mobile ecosystems. Instead of forcing users to take photos of physical ID cards and subjecting them to error-prone server-side OCR and third-party biometric verification services, mini-apps can invoke native OS digital identity wallets (such as Apple Wallet or Google Wallet) via 'navigator.identity.get({ digital: { requests: [...] } })'. The device identity wallet presents an unforgeable system prompt, and upon user biometric authorization, releases a cryptographically signed verifiable presentation adhering to ISO/IEC 18013-5 (mDL) or W3C Verifiable Credentials. For super-apps operating in regulated financial, insurance, and telecommunications markets, this standard eliminates fraud, ensures GDPR/personal data protection compliance through selective disclosure, and dramatically reduces onboarding friction.

title: WICG Digital Credentials Specification: Cryptographic Protocols, mdoc Formats & Trust Frameworks
standard: WICG Digital Credentials Specification / OpenID4VP Alignment
key_takeaways: Formalizes the data exchange protocols, cryptographic message syntax, and security boundaries connecting web contexts to hardware-backed identity wallets
Supports multiple credential formats including ISO/IEC 18013-5 mdoc, W3C Verifiable Credentials (VC), and IETF SD-JWT (Selective Disclosure JSON Web Tokens)
Mandates ephemeral SessionTranscript cryptographic binding, combining reader and device ephemeral public keys with client origin to thwart man-in-the-middle attacks
Restricts credential presentation API access strictly to top-level secure contexts, completely disallowing unauthorized cross-origin iframe invocation without explicit permissions policy delegation
Integrates seamlessly with OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP) for distributed cross-enterprise trust federation
store_governance_rules: Store review engine validates that mini-apps declare 'digital-credentials-get' within the Web App Manifest capability manifest prior to invoking credential requests
The super-app platform binds each credential request to an ephemeral nonce generated by the super-app security gateway to prevent replay attacks across distributed sessions
Cross-origin sub-frames within mini-apps are denied access to digital credentials unless explicitly authorized via 'allow="digital-credentials-get"' iframe attribute and host policy
Mini-apps must handle user dismissal, wallet lockouts, and unsupported credential format exceptions gracefully without crashing or freezing the UI container
All credential requests and verification outcomes are recorded in immutable audit logs without storing the decrypted raw credential payloads or biometric markers
detail: The WICG Digital Credentials specification establishes the low-level architectural rules governing how modern browsers and container platforms interact with platform identity stores. By supporting ISO 18013-5 mobile driver's licenses (mdocs) and SD-JWTs, it ensures high interoperability across international identity standards. Crucially, the protocol mandates that every presentation is cryptographically bound to an ephemeral session transcript containing the relying party's verified web origin. This prevents a rogue mini-app from acting as a man-in-the-middle or laundering credentials across different services. For super-app catalog governance, requiring explicit manifest declaration and strict Permissions Policy gating guarantees that sensitive identity verification flows remain tightly audited and secure.

title: Chrome Capabilities File Handling: Native OS File Association & Declarative App Manifests
standard: Chrome Capabilities Project / Web App Manifest File Handling
key_takeaways: Enables web applications and mini-apps to register as native operating system file handlers for specific MIME types and file extensions
Configured declaratively in the Web App Manifest using the 'file_handlers' array, specifying target launch URLs, accepted extensions, MIME types, and action icons
Delivers opened files directly to the mini-app runtime via the window.launchQueue consumer interface (launchParams.files containing FileSystemFileHandle instances)
Allows mini-apps to function as complete desktop-class document editors, CAD viewers, invoice processors, and media players seamlessly integrated with native file managers
Requires user confirmation dialog on initial file launch to prevent stealth drive-by file execution or unprompted file system access
store_governance_rules: Store submission engine strictly validates declared 'file_handlers' in mini-app manifests, rejecting unauthorized claims to broad system extensions (e.g. .exe, .sh, .apk, .bat, .dll)
Mini-apps registering file handlers must declare legitimate business necessity (e.g., an accounting mini-app handling .csv/.xlsx, or a graphics mini-app handling .svg/.png)
Super-app container intercepts file launch events, prompting user confirmation: 'Open this file with [Mini App Name]?' before passing file handles into the runtime
Mini-apps receive restricted read-only FileSystemFileHandle objects by default; modifying the file on disk requires explicit user confirmation via handle.createWritable()
Store review team tests file launch handlers using automated fuzzing fixtures containing malformed file payloads to verify crash resilience and parser security
detail: The Chrome Capabilities File Handling standard transforms mini-apps from isolated sandbox web pages into deeply integrated operating system applications. By defining 'file_handlers' in the Web App Manifest, a mini-app can register to open specific file formats (such as PDF contracts, spreadsheet invoices, or design files). When a user double-clicks a matching file in the OS file explorer or super-app document vault, the container launches the mini-app and enqueues the opened files in 'window.launchQueue'. In a super-app ecosystem, this capability enables enterprise productivity suites, expense management tools, and legal signing mini-apps to deliver native-grade document workflows while maintaining strict sandbox isolation.

title: WICG File Handling API Specification: LaunchQueue Lifecycle, Permission Elevation & Origin Scoping
standard: WICG File Handling Specification / WHATWG Alignment
key_takeaways: Specifies the normative processing model for dispatching operating system launch events with file handles to web applications
Defines the LaunchConsumer callback contract: 'window.launchQueue.setConsumer(launchParams => { ... })' executed upon document initialization
Guarantees that files passed via LaunchParams are wrapped in standard FileSystemFileHandle objects conforming to the File System Access specification
Specifies origin scoping and permission elevation checks: user agents must prompt users before granting write permissions to host filesystem handles
Handles multi-client routing policies: allows developers and containers to specify whether each opened file spawns a new window or routes to an existing instance
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps implementing file handling must register their launchQueue consumer during initial document script execution to avoid dropping launch events
The super-app container enforces a strict timeout: if a mini-app fails to consume launchParams within 5 seconds of launch, the file handle is revoked to prevent memory leaks
File handling permissions are origin-scoped; handles granted to Mini App A cannot be transferred, leaked, or accessed by Mini App B across container contexts
In enterprise deployment profiles, super-app administrators can centrally disable file handling or restrict allowed file extensions via device management policies
Store telemetry monitors file launch crash rates; mini-apps exceeding a 0.5% unhandled exception rate on file open events are automatically flagged for quarantine
detail: The WICG File Handling specification provides the technical framework for handling external files within web environments safely. Central to the specification is the 'launchQueue' interface, which buffers incoming launch events until the mini-app registers a consumer callback. This design solves asynchronous loading race conditions, ensuring that file references are never lost even if the mini-app requires complex initialization. Furthermore, because incoming files are represented as FileSystemFileHandle objects, the browser/super-app security boundary mediates all subsequent read and write operations, preventing arbitrary filesystem traversal and enforcing user-mediated file modifications.

title: MDN Cookie Store API: Asynchronous Storage, Service Worker Access & Cross-Context Cookie Change Events
standard: W3C / WICG Cookie Store API Specification
key_takeaways: Replaces the synchronous, performance-blocking 'document.cookie' string interface with a modern Promise-based asynchronous API (cookieStore.get, set, delete)
Brings native cookie access to Service Worker contexts, enabling background sync and offline workers to read and update session cookies without waking the DOM thread
Provides the 'change' event listener ('cookieStore.addEventListener("change", event => { ... })') allowing applications to observe cookie mutations in real time
Supports strongly typed cookie attribute definitions: domain, path, expires, secure, and sameSite ('strict', 'lax', 'none') directly within JavaScript objects
Significantly reduces main-thread jank by executing cookie serialization and disk persistence operations off the UI thread
store_governance_rules: Store review engine mandates Cookie Store API adoption for cookie access, actively flagging legacy 'document.cookie' string manipulation in high-load mini-apps
Service Workers utilizing cookieStore must restrict operations strictly to their declared origin scope, preventing cross-tenant session state pollution
Mini-app session tokens stored in cookies must enforce 'secure: true' and 'sameSite: "strict"' to mitigate cross-site request forgery and eavesdropping
The super-app host container automatically clears all mini-app cookieStore entries upon user logout or session termination, leaving zero residual authentication artifacts
Cookie change event listeners are monitored during review to verify they do not introduce infinite synchronization loops between service workers and main thread windows
detail: The Cookie Store API addresses one of the oldest architectural flaws in web development: the synchronous, blocking nature of 'document.cookie'. By exposing asynchronous methods (cookieStore.get, cookieStore.set, cookieStore.delete) and extending them to Service Workers, it allows mini-apps to manage session state cleanly without freezing UI rendering. More importantly, the CookieChangeEvent enables instantaneous synchronization of authentication states across multiple tabs, iframes, and background workers. In a super-app environment, where mini-apps may transition between foreground views and background sync tasks, the Cookie Store API provides deterministic, non-blocking, and secure credential state management.

title: MDN Screen Wake Lock API: Display State Preservation, Video Presentation & Automatic Release Handlers
standard: W3C Screen Wake Lock API / MDN Web Docs
key_takeaways: Provides a standard programmatic interface ('navigator.wakeLock.request("screen")') preventing mobile device displays from dimming or locking during critical user activities
Returns a WakeLockSentinel Promise that can be explicitly released via sentinel.release() or automatically released upon tab minimization/visibility changes
Essential for continuous interaction use cases: turn-by-turn map navigation, barcode/QR payment presentation at POS terminals, fitness workouts, and cooking recipe guides
Enforces strict Secure Context requirements (HTTPS) and active document visibility, preventing hidden background pages from draining device batteries
Dispatches the 'release' event on the sentinel when the operating system or browser reclaims power locks, allowing mini-apps to update their UI accordingly
store_governance_rules: Store submission review audits mini-app wake lock usage to ensure locks are requested exclusively during active user engagement and released immediately upon task completion
The super-app container enforces an automatic 10-minute hard ceiling on continuous Screen Wake Locks unless re-authenticated by active user touch or gesture events
Host container automatically releases all active wake locks when a mini-app loses foreground visibility ('visibilitychange' event to hidden), saving mobile battery
Mini-apps must listen for the sentinel 'release' event and present clear UI indicators (e.g. an active display icon) so users know their screen lock is being held
Store review engine rejects mini-apps that request wake locks during document initialization without waiting for explicit user interaction
detail: The Screen Wake Lock API provides a safe, standard mechanism to keep mobile screens active during extended viewing or interactive sessions. In a super-app ecosystem, mini-apps frequently handle tasks where automatic screen dimming disrupts user experience—such as presenting a VietQR or payment barcode to a merchant scanner, displaying digital boarding passes, following exercise routines, or viewing cooking recipes. Because the API requires an active document and automatically releases locks when the page is minimized, it prevents runaway battery drain. Super-app governance rules enforce maximum duration ceilings and ensure wake locks are re-acquired cleanly when returning to the foreground.

title: MDN WakeLock Interface: Request Gating, Visibility Lifecycle Synchronization & Error Recovery
standard: W3C Screen Wake Lock API (WakeLock Interface)
key_takeaways: Exposes the 'navigator.wakeLock' property hosting the 'request()' method for acquiring typed power management locks
Gated by the W3C Permissions API ('screen-wake-lock' permission descriptor), allowing user agents and super-apps to query or revoke lock permissions
Rejects request() Promises with 'NotAllowedError' when the document is inactive, when low-battery power saver mode is engaged, or when container policy blocks the call
Enforces strict visibility synchronization: when document.visibilityState changes to 'hidden', all active locks are immediately and irrevocably released
Establishes the standard pattern for re-acquiring wake locks upon visibility recovery ('document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", ...)')
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps requesting wake locks must wrap calls in try/catch blocks and handle 'NotAllowedError' gracefully when device battery saver mode is active
Super-app permissions manager allows users to inspect and toggle Screen Wake Lock permissions per mini-app within the container privacy settings
Container runtime injects power-management monitors: if device battery drops below 15%, the host denies all new wakeLock.request calls and terminates active sentinels
Mini-app developers must implement document visibility re-acquisition listeners to restore wake locks when users switch back from other apps or calls
Store telemetry records wake lock frequency and duration per mini-app, flagging outliers for manual energy efficiency reviews
detail: The WakeLock interface is the entry point for power management in modern web runtimes. By integrating directly with the W3C Permissions API and the Document Visibility state machine, it ensures that applications cannot hold device resources hostage. If a user switches away from a mini-app to answer a phone call, or if the device engages aggressive OS power-saving modes, the WakeLock interface automatically releases the screen lock. Super-app store guidelines require developers to adopt standard re-acquisition patterns on visibilitychange while gracefully handling rejection states, safeguarding mobile battery health and device longevity.

title: MDN WakeLockSentinel: Granular Lock State Monitoring, Idempotent Release & Disconnection Resilience
standard: W3C Screen Wake Lock API (WakeLockSentinel Interface)
key_takeaways: Represents an active, acquired wake lock handle returned by the successful resolution of navigator.wakeLock.request()
Provides the 'released' boolean read-only attribute indicating whether the underlying OS power lock has been discarded
Provides the 'type' attribute (currently 'screen') identifying the specific subsystem being held in an active power state
Exposes the asynchronous 'release()' method, which idempotently releases the lock and transitions the 'released' attribute to true
Dispatches the 'onrelease' event handler, notifying the application immediately when the operating system reclaims the lock due to external factors
store_governance_rules: Mini-app codebases must verify 'sentinel.released === false' before assuming screen lock continuity during mission-critical transactions
All acquired WakeLockSentinel instances must be explicitly released in the mini-app's onDestroy or page unmount lifecycle handlers
Container runtime enforces garbage-collection tracking: orphaned sentinels whose parent DOM elements are destroyed are forcibly released by the host bridge
Developers must register the 'onrelease' listener to provide immediate visual feedback (e.g., changing a UI toggle from 'Screen Always On' to 'Auto-Sleep')
Store compliance verification tests verify that mini-apps do not leak sentinel handles across internal route transitions or navigation history stacks
detail: The WakeLockSentinel interface encapsulates the actual lock handle, providing fine-grained state inspection and deterministic cleanup. Because external events—such as system notifications, low-battery alerts, or incoming telephone calls—can cause the operating system to break a wake lock, relying purely on the initial Promise resolution is insufficient. The WakeLockSentinel's 'released' property and 'onrelease' event allow mini-apps to maintain precise synchronization with the device's true physical state. In super-app governance, requiring explicit release during lifecycle cleanup prevents resource leaks and guarantees smooth transitions between mini-apps.

title: MDN OffscreenCanvas: Decoupled WebGL/2D Rendering in Web Workers & Zero-Jank UI Synchronization
standard: WHATWG HTML Living Standard / MDN OffscreenCanvas Specification
key_takeaways: Decouples HTML canvas rendering from the DOM and the browser main thread, allowing 2D and WebGL rendering in background Web Workers
Can be transferred from an on-screen <canvas> element using 'canvas.transferControlToOffscreen()', forwarding draw commands to worker threads
Can be instantiated synchronously inside Web Workers ('new OffscreenCanvas(width, height)') for headless graphics processing, image resizing, and chart generation
Provides 'convertToBlob()' asynchronous method for exporting rendered frames directly to WebP, PNG, or JPEG blobs without DOM serialization overhead
Completely eliminates UI stutter and input lag by isolating complex graphics calculations and shader execution from the main user interaction thread
store_governance_rules: Store performance guidelines strongly recommend OffscreenCanvas for complex gaming, data visualization, interactive charting, and camera filter mini-apps
The super-app container enforces strict GPU memory limits on OffscreenCanvas instances (maximum 128MB per worker thread) to prevent out-of-memory crashes on low-end devices
OffscreenCanvas contexts must properly release memory during worker termination; lingering contexts are reclaimed by the container watchdog
Mini-apps processing user images or documents are required to use OffscreenCanvas in dedicated workers, ensuring the main UI maintains a steady 60fps frame rate
Store review engine runs automated automated frame rate benchmarks; applications dropping below 45fps due to main-thread canvas painting are required to offload to OffscreenCanvas
detail: OffscreenCanvas represents one of the most powerful performance innovations in modern web architecture. Traditionally, all canvas drawing (whether 2D canvas, WebGL, or WebGPU) occurred on the browser's main UI thread, competing directly with DOM reconciliation, gesture parsing, and layout calculation. With OffscreenCanvas, rendering logic can be offloaded entirely to dedicated Web Workers. Even if complex 3D graphics or high-resolution photo filters take hundreds of milliseconds to render, the super-app's main UI remains completely fluid, responsive, and stutter-free. For a super-app hosting high-performance games, biometric verification previews, and complex dashboards, OffscreenCanvas is essential for delivering native-tier UX.

title: MDN MutationObserver API: Asynchronous DOM Change Auditing, XSS Defense & Dynamic UI Injection Control
standard: WHATWG DOM Living Standard / MDN MutationObserver
key_takeaways: Provides an asynchronous, microtask-scheduled mechanism for observing changes to the DOM tree (childList, attributes, characterData, subtree)
Replaces obsolete, performance-degrading synchronous Mutation Events (DOMSubtreeModified, DOMNodeInserted) with batch-processed mutation records
Enables host containers and security middleware to monitor DOM tampering, unauthorized script tag injections, and unauthorized iframe creations in real time
Allows mini-apps to implement dynamic layout adjustments, responsive design reflows, and accessibility attribute syncing without polling the DOM
Exposes 'takeRecords()' to retrieve pending mutations synchronously before disconnecting the observer during cleanup or component teardown
store_governance_rules: Super-app security runtime injects a top-level MutationObserver to monitor the document head and body for unauthorized script, iframe, or meta tag insertions
Any dynamic DOM insertion violating the store's Content Security Policy or Trusted Types configuration is immediately quarantined and reported to container telemetry
Mini-apps using MutationObserver must limit their observation scope to specific component root nodes rather than observing document.documentElement across entire subtrees
Store submission verification audits MutationObserver callbacks to ensure they do not trigger infinite mutation loops (mutating the DOM inside the mutation callback)
All active MutationObserver instances must be disconnected via 'observer.disconnect()' when mini-app components or views are destroyed
detail: The MutationObserver API provides high-performance, asynchronous monitoring of DOM mutations. In the context of super-app mini-app security and host-client mediation, MutationObserver is an indispensable defensive tool. The host container runtime can establish an observer over the mini-app document tree to instantly detect rogue DOM manipulation—such as third-party ad injection, phishing overlays, or unauthorized iframe creation. Because MutationObserver batches notifications into microtasks, it incurs virtually zero performance penalty compared to legacy synchronous DOM events. Enforcing strict observation scopes and loop defenses ensures robust application integrity without UI slowdown.

title: W3C Geolocation API Specification: Position Accuracy, WatchPosition Lifecycle & Privacy Boundaries
standard: W3C Geolocation API Recommendation (w3c.github.io/geolocation-api)
key_takeaways: Defines the programmatic interface ('navigator.geolocation') for obtaining device geographic position coordinates (latitude, longitude, accuracy, altitude, speed)
Supports one-shot position retrieval ('getCurrentPosition') and continuous movement monitoring ('watchPosition' returning a watchId cancelled via 'clearWatch')
Allows applications to configure PositionOptions: enableHighAccuracy (GPS/GNSS hardware vs Wi-Fi/cellular triangulation), timeout, and maximumAge (cached fix longevity)
Enforces strict privacy and consent requirements: user agents must obtain explicit, informed user consent prior to dispatching location data
Restricts execution strictly to Secure Contexts (HTTPS), preventing cleartext interception of user movement tracks on unencrypted networks
store_governance_rules: Store submission engine verifies that mini-apps declare explicit business justification (e.g. food delivery, ride hailing, store locator) prior to granting geolocation access
Super-app host container mediates geolocation calls, displaying an unforgeable native modal presenting granular user choices: 'Approximate Location' vs 'Precise Location'
Mini-apps must default to enableHighAccuracy: false unless active turn-by-turn navigation or real-time transport dispatch explicitly requires high precision
Container runtime terminates active watchPosition streams immediately when the mini-app enters background or hidden state to prevent persistent background tracking
Mini-apps must set maximumAge to at least 30000ms (30 seconds) for non-navigation queries to prevent excessive GPS hardware polling and battery depletion
detail: The W3C Geolocation API is one of the most critical sensor interfaces in modern mobile computing. For super-apps operating ride-hailing, food delivery, logistics tracking, and local commerce mini-apps, access to location data is essential. However, unconstrained location tracking poses severe privacy risks and drains mobile device batteries. The standard establishes clear parameters (enableHighAccuracy, timeout, maximumAge) and mandates user consent. In a super-app architecture, the container acts as a trusted intermediary, offering users the ability to degrade location precision (providing city-level or district-level coordinates instead of exact meter coordinates) and terminating background watchPosition listeners when the mini-app loses foreground focus.

title: MDN Geolocation API: GeolocationPositionError Taxonomy, Fallbacks & Permission Lifecycle
standard: W3C Geolocation API / MDN Web Docs
key_takeaways: Standardizes the GeolocationPositionError object returned to error callbacks with codified error codes: PERMISSION_DENIED (1), POSITION_UNAVAILABLE (2), and TIMEOUT (3)
Mandates robust application-level fallback mechanisms when users decline location permissions or when GPS satellites/triangulation networks are unavailable
Integrates with the W3C Permissions API ('navigator.permissions.query({ name: "geolocation" })') to inspect permission state ('granted', 'prompt', 'denied') without triggering prompts
Documents best practices for battery conservation: using coarse positioning first and escalating to GPS only upon explicit interactive user triggers
Explains origin-based isolation: location grants are strictly origin-partitioned and cannot be shared across cross-origin iframe boundaries without explicit delegation
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps must implement comprehensive error handling for all three GeolocationPositionError codes, providing manual address or location picker fallbacks
Store review engine rejects mini-apps that block or freeze user onboarding flows if the user selects PERMISSION_DENIED
The super-app permissions dashboard enables users to revoke or reset granted geolocation permissions on a per-mini-app basis at any time
Mini-apps must query navigator.permissions prior to calling getCurrentPosition, avoiding repetitive or annoying permission dialog prompts
Store compliance tests simulate GPS timeout and airplane mode conditions to verify that mini-app UI gracefully handles POSITION_UNAVAILABLE and TIMEOUT states
detail: MDN's comprehensive documentation of the Geolocation API highlights the importance of resilient error handling and permission state inspection. In real-world mobile environments, location requests frequently fail due to tall urban canyons, indoor RF blockage, disabled device location services, or user privacy refusals. By standardizing the GeolocationPositionError taxonomy (codes 1, 2, 3), the specification allows mini-apps to distinguish between a user declining permission and a technical GPS timeout. Super-app store guidelines require mini-apps to provide graceful fallbacks (such as manual postal code or address entry) so users can complete core transactions even when location access is denied.

title: MDN SubtleCrypto Interface: Asynchronous Web Cryptography, Key Derivation & Hardware Attestation
standard: W3C Web Cryptography API (SubtleCrypto Interface)
key_takeaways: Exposes standard cryptographic primitives directly to JavaScript via 'crypto.subtle', eliminating the need for insecure, unvetted third-party JavaScript crypto libraries
Supports high-security symmetric and asymmetric algorithms: AES-GCM, AES-CBC, HMAC, RSA-PSS, RSA-OAEP, ECDSA, ECDH, and PBKDF2 / HKDF key derivation
Provides constant-time cryptographic operations implemented in native C++/Rust within the underlying browser engine, preventing timing side-channel attacks
Supports non-extractable key handles ('extractable: false'), ensuring that cryptographic private keys stored in IndexedDB cannot be dumped or exfiltrated by malicious scripts
Executes all cryptographic operations asynchronously via Promises, preventing main-thread UI jank during intensive 4096-bit RSA or multi-round hashing operations
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps handling end-to-end encryption, local document signing, or offline payment tokens must utilize native crypto.subtle rather than bundled JS libraries
Cryptographic keys generated by mini-apps for device authentication must be declared with 'extractable: false' to prevent memory scraping or credential exfiltration
Weak or deprecated algorithms (e.g. SHA-1, MD5, single-DES, RSA key lengths < 2048 bits) are strictly banned by automated store AST security scanners
All cryptographic keys persisted in IndexedDB must be scoped to the mini-app's sandbox origin, with hardware backing (Android KeyStore / Apple Secure Enclave) preferred
Store review engine audits encryption parameters: AES-GCM must use a unique, cryptographically random 96-bit IV for every single encryption operation
detail: The SubtleCrypto interface is the foundation of modern client-side cryptographic security. Prior to SubtleCrypto, web applications were forced to import bloated, slow, and frequently vulnerable third-party JavaScript cryptography libraries that were susceptible to prototype pollution and timing attacks. By providing native, hardware-accelerated, constant-time cryptographic primitives directly through 'window.crypto.subtle', developers can perform encryption, decryption, signing, verification, and key derivation with enterprise-grade security. In a super-app ecosystem, requiring SubtleCrypto with non-extractable keys guarantees that sensitive financial payloads, offline receipts, and private messages remain completely shielded from external inspection.

title: MDN CryptoKey Interface: Key Material Encapsulation, Algorithm Binding & Usage Constraints
standard: W3C Web Cryptography API (CryptoKey Interface)
key_takeaways: Represents an opaque cryptographic key handle returned by crypto.subtle.generateKey(), importKey(), or deriveKey()
Enforces strict algorithm binding: a key generated for 'ECDSA' cannot be misused for 'ECDH' key agreement, preventing cross-algorithm attack vectors
Enforces immutable key usage constraints via the 'usages' array (e.g. ['sign'], ['verify'], ['encrypt'], ['decrypt'], ['wrapKey'], ['unwrapKey'])
Provides the boolean 'extractable' flag; when set to false, raw key bytes can never be exported via exportKey(), securing keys against XSS attacks
Can be safely stored in IndexedDB and transferred across Web Workers using structured clone algorithms without exposing raw cryptographic material
store_governance_rules: Mini-apps implementing client-side digital signatures must bind keys strictly to '["sign"]' or '["verify"]' usages, prohibiting dual-use sign/encrypt configurations
All session and transaction signing keys generated within mini-apps must be configured with 'extractable: false'
Store submission static analyzer flags any call to crypto.subtle.exportKey() on sensitive authentication or payment keys for manual security review
Host container runtime binds CryptoKey objects stored in mini-app IndexedDB partitions to native device secure hardware keystores wherever supported
Mini-apps must implement key rotation policies, revoking and regenerating persistent CryptoKey instances at least every 90 days
detail: The CryptoKey interface provides rigorous security encapsulation for cryptographic keys in web runtimes. Rather than handling raw byte arrays of key material in JavaScript variables—where a single cross-site scripting flaw could expose them—CryptoKey handles are opaque references. The specification enforces strict usage constraints (preventing a decryption key from being used to forge signatures) and algorithm locks. Most importantly, marking keys as non-extractable ensures that even if an attacker manages to execute unauthorized JavaScript in the mini-app context, they cannot steal the private key bytes. This standard is critical for super-app secure offline authorization, biometric authentication, and digital contract signing.

title: MDN Channel Messaging API: Direct Bidirectional MessagePort Communication & Transferable Memory
standard: WHATWG HTML Living Standard / MDN Channel Messaging API
key_takeaways: Enables direct, two-way asynchronous communication between distinct browsing contexts (windows, iframes, Web Workers, Service Workers) via MessageChannel and MessagePort
Instantiates two interconnected ports ('const channel = new MessageChannel(); channel.port1, channel.port2') allowing point-to-point message forwarding
Transfers port ownership to target contexts via the 'transfer' parameter in window.postMessage() or worker.postMessage(), transferring the endpoint without intermediate proxying
Supports Transferable Objects (ArrayBuffer, ImageBitmap, MessagePort, OffscreenCanvas), enabling zero-copy memory transfer between threads and iframes
Provides structured cloning of complex data objects, eliminating manual JSON serialization and deserialization performance overheads
store_governance_rules: Super-app host container utilizes dedicated MessageChannel ports for high-throughput host-to-mini-app bridge communication, bypassing global window postMessage broadcasts
Mini-apps communicating with isolated sub-workers or third-party component iframes must establish point-to-point MessagePorts rather than relying on wildcard target origins
All MessagePort event listeners must be properly closed via 'port.close()' upon component unmounting to prevent memory and channel leaks
The super-app bridge validates all data payloads received over MessagePort connections against strict runtime schemas before invoking native OS capabilities
Store review engine scans for wildcards ('*') in the initial window.postMessage calls used to transfer MessagePorts, mandating explicit targetOrigin validation
detail: The Channel Messaging API provides the premier architecture for point-to-point inter-context communication in modern web platforms. Unlike global 'window.postMessage', which broadcasts messages to the target window where any script listening on the global scope might inspect or intercept them, MessageChannel creates a private, direct pipe between two endpoints. One port can be passed into a sandboxed iframe or a background Web Worker, establishing an exclusive, tamper-proof communication channel. Crucially, MessagePort supports Transferable Objects, allowing zero-copy transfer of large binary datasets, images, and OffscreenCanvas contexts between threads. For super-apps coordinating complex interactions between the host container, mini-app UI, and background workers, Channel Messaging provides exceptional performance, security, and isolation.

title: WICG Navigation API: Single-Page Mini-App Navigation Lifecycle, Interception, and Unified History Transitions
standard_reference: WICG Navigation API / W3C Web Platform Incubator Community Group
summary: Modern super-app mini-apps operate as complex Single-Page Applications (SPAs) where legacy window.history.pushState and popstate APIs fail to intercept all navigations (e.g. form submissions, link clicks, traversal cancellations) and suffer from silent desynchronization with host container state. The WICG Navigation API replaces legacy history manipulation with a unified, centralized navigation controller via window.navigation. It captures all same-document and cross-document navigation attempts through the 'navigate' event, allowing container runtimes to reliably orchestrate page transitions, retain scroll positions, and prevent uncoordinated context unloads.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under the WICG Navigation API specification, `window.navigation` provides an event-driven model replacing disparate `hashchange`, `popstate`, and manual DOM interception. The `navigate` event exposes properties including `destination`, `navigationType` ('push', 'replace', 'reload', 'traverse'), `canIntercept`, `userInitiated`, and `hashChange`. When `canIntercept` is true, mini-app routing logic can invoke `event.intercept()` to programmatically handle navigation with a custom transition handler promise, avoiding full-page container reloads while updating the URL. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app containers MUST provide polyfill or native runtime bridge support for the Navigation API. Mini-app SPA frameworks MUST bind routing lifecycle handlers to `window.navigation.addEventListener('navigate', ...)` rather than monkey-patching `history.pushState`. Container quality gates MUST verify that mini-apps handle `event.intercept()` failures cleanly with fallback error viewports and do not trigger unexpected host container dismissals.

title: NavigateEvent Interface: Interception Handlers, AbortSignal Cancellation, and Declarative Scroll Restoration
standard_reference: WICG Navigation API § 3.2 NavigateEvent Interface
summary: During rapid intra-app navigation (such as browsing e-commerce product catalogs or navigating deep mini-app tabs), unmanaged asynchronous fetch operations can cause race conditions and memory leaks when a user triggers consecutive navigations. The NavigateEvent interface introduces `event.signal` (an AbortSignal) that automatically aborts ongoing operations when a new navigation supersedes the current one, alongside `event.scroll()` for precise scroll position restoration.
detail: [SPEC FACT] NavigateEvent provides `signal`, an AbortSignal instance aborted if the navigation is superseded by a subsequent navigation or cancelled via `navigation.navigate(...).abort()`. It also defines `intercept({ handler, focusReset, scroll })` where `scroll` can be set to 'after-transition' or 'manual'. Invoking `event.scroll()` gives the developer programmatic control over when the container restores scroll state, ensuring dynamic DOM elements and virtual lists are rendered prior to scroll adjustment. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDKs MUST propagate `event.signal` to all network fetch requests initiated during navigation transitions (`fetch(url, { signal: event.signal })`). Conformance suites MUST audit that mini-apps do not leak dangling network connections or unmount callbacks upon user abort gestures, and that scroll position restoration does not produce visual viewport jumping.

title: Navigation Interface: NavigationHistoryEntry Inspection, Same-Document Traversal, and Keyed State Isolation
standard_reference: WICG Navigation API § 3.1 Navigation Interface
summary: Super-app mini-apps frequently need to inspect their back-stack history (e.g. to determine whether to display a back-button or a close-button in the host container navbar) without violating user privacy by reading arbitrary cross-origin session URLs. The Navigation interface provides `navigation.entries()`, exposing a sanitized array of NavigationHistoryEntry objects scoped exclusively to the mini-app's same-origin history sequence.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `Navigation` interface exposes `navigation.currentEntry`, `navigation.entries()`, and methods `navigate()`, `reload()`, `back()`, `forward()`, `traverseTo()`. Each `NavigationHistoryEntry` features immutable properties `id`, `key`, `url`, `index`, and `sameDocument`, alongside `getState()` which returns a structured-cloned state object. Unlike `history.length`, `navigation.entries()` allows direct index-based traversal (`navigation.traverseTo(entry.key)`) with predictable promise resolution (`committed` and `finished` promises). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host bridges MUST synchronize the container's native navigation bar (back/close actions) with `navigation.currentEntry.index` and `navigation.entries().length`. Mini-app state saved via `navigation.navigate(url, { state: ... })` MUST NOT contain sensitive authentication tokens or plaintext credentials; store linters MUST flag serialization of tokens into history entry state.

title: WICG URLPattern API: Declarative Route Matching, Parameter Extraction, and ReDoS-Safe Pattern Compilation
standard_reference: WICG URLPattern API Specification / W3C Incubator Community Group
summary: Mini-app stores and host containers require a robust, standardized mechanism to parse, match, and route deep links, universal links, and internal mini-app navigation paths without relying on fragmented, vulnerable third-party regex routing libraries (which are prone to Regular Expression Denial of Service - ReDoS). The WICG URLPattern API standardizes URL pattern matching based on path-to-regexp syntax directly in the browser engine.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `URLPattern` interface accepts pattern syntax for `protocol`, `username`, `password`, `hostname`, `port`, `pathname`, `search`, and `hash`. Methods include `test(input)` and `exec(input)`. The `exec()` method returns a structured match object containing URL components and a `pathname.groups` dictionary of named wildcard matches (e.g. `/store/app/:id` extracts `{ id: '123' }`). URLPattern compiles expressions into deterministic finite automata (DFA), mathematically eliminating exponential ReDoS vulnerability vectors. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app deep-link routers, service worker routing rules, and mini-app manifest URL matchers MUST adopt `URLPattern` syntax for declared entrypoints and navigation targets. Mini-app submissions declaring custom routing patterns in manifests MUST be validated against the URLPattern specification during automated store ingest to reject malformed or unbounded capture patterns.

title: W3C Service Worker Static Routing API: Declarative URLPattern Routing, Main-Thread Cache Hits, and Cold-Start Optimization
standard_reference: W3C Service Workers Nightly § 3.3.1 Service Worker Static Routing API
summary: A primary bottleneck in super-app mini-app performance is cold-start latency caused by waking up the Service Worker thread solely to serve static assets from CacheStorage or forward requests directly to the network. The Service Worker Static Routing API allows mini-apps to register declarative routing rules during installation. These rules are executed directly in the browser network process/container thread using URLPattern conditions, entirely bypassing Service Worker process initialization for matching requests.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Service Worker specification § 3.3.1, `ServiceWorkerRegistration.router.add(rules)` registers an array of declarative routing rules during the `install` event. Each rule specifies a `condition` (combining `urlPattern`, `requestMethod`, `requestMode`, or `runningStatus`) and a `source` ('network', 'cache', or 'fetch-event'). When a navigation or subresource request matches a 'cache' or 'network' rule, the browser satisfies the request without starting the Service Worker thread. [STORE REQUIREMENT] For performance-certified mini-apps, super-app stores MUST require static asset bundles and entrypoint navigation to declare Static Routing rules. By routing known static bundles (`*.js`, `*.css`, `*.webp`, `*.woff2`) directly to CacheStorage or network, container startup latency is reduced by 150-400ms on low-end mobile devices, while eliminating unnecessary CPU wakeups.

title: W3C Media Capabilities API: Decoding & Encoding Telemetry, Frame Smoothness, and Power-Efficient Stream Selection
standard_reference: W3C Media Capabilities / W3C Recommendation
summary: Streaming media, live video commerce, and interactive video in mini-apps often cause battery drain, stuttering, and device heating when delivering high-resolution video streams (e.g. 4K/60fps AV1 or HEVC) that exceed device hardware decoding capabilities. The W3C Media Capabilities API replaces imprecise MIME-type checks (`canPlayType`) with detailed decoding telemetry, determining whether a specific media configuration is supported, smooth (consistently high framerate), and power-efficient (hardware-accelerated).
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Media Capabilities § 2, `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo(mediaDecodingConfiguration)` queries the platform decoding pipeline. The configuration specifies `type` ('file' or 'media-source') and `video`/`audio` parameters (contentType, width, height, bitrate, framerate). The returned `MediaCapabilitiesDecodingInfo` object yields boolean flags: `supported` (codec is playable), `smooth` (decoding achieves target framerate without dropped frames), and `powerEfficient` (decoding utilizes dedicated hardware blocks rather than software CPU decoding). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-apps with video playback or live streaming MUST query `mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo()` prior to initializing high-definition media streams. If `powerEfficient` is false on battery-powered mobile devices, the mini-app player MUST automatically downscale to a hardware-supported profile (e.g. 1080p H.264/VP9) to prevent battery exhaustion and thermal throttling.

title: W3C Media Source Extensions (MSE) API: Client-Side Buffer Management, Chunked Streaming, and Low-Latency Playback
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions™ / W3C Recommendation
summary: Modern video streaming mini-apps (HLS, DASH) require custom client-side buffering, dynamic bitrate switching, and real-time buffer trimming without reloading video elements. W3C Media Source Extensions (MSE) extends HTMLMediaElement to allow JavaScript to dynamically construct and feed media streams into SourceBuffer objects from raw chunked network segments.
detail: [SPEC FACT] MSE defines `MediaSource` which attaches to `HTMLMediaElement.src` via `URL.createObjectURL(mediaSource)`. MediaSource manages a collection of `SourceBuffer` objects. JavaScript fetches media segments (MP4/WebM byte streams) and appends them using `sourceBuffer.appendBuffer(ArrayBuffer)`. Key lifecycle events include `sourceopen`, `sourceended`, and `updateend`. MSE provides `sourceBuffer.remove(start, end)` to prune buffered playback segments and conserve mobile RAM. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app video players utilizing MSE MUST implement strict SourceBuffer memory governance: buffered segments older than 60 seconds behind current playhead MUST be evicted via `sourceBuffer.remove()` to prevent mobile browser memory exhaustion (OOM). Store conformance tests MUST verify that mini-apps do not accumulate more than 50MB of raw unevicted media segments in active SourceBuffers.

title: SourceBuffer Interface: Segment Appending, Sequence vs Segments Modes, and Cross-Track Synchronization
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions™ § 3.2 SourceBuffer Interface
summary: When streaming video in live commerce or mini-app broadcast scenarios, dynamic ad-insertion and bitrate transitions introduce timestamp discontinuities that desynchronize audio and video tracks. The SourceBuffer interface provides granular controls over buffer parsing mode, append windows, and timestamp offsets to ensure seamless cross-track synchronization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] SourceBuffer exposes `mode`, which can be set to 'segments' (timestamps are extracted from media segment headers) or 'sequence' (segments are appended sequentially, ignoring internal timestamps). It provides `timestampOffset` to shift segment presentation timestamps, and `appendWindowStart`/`appendWindowEnd` to filter out media frames outside defined time windows. The `updating` boolean flag enforces serialization: calling `appendBuffer()` while `updating` is true throws an `InvalidStateError`. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app media engines handling dynamic bitrate adaptation MUST observe `sourceBuffer.updating` before dispatching new buffer payloads, queueing chunks asynchronously. Store security checks MUST verify that media chunk parsers reject malformed container headers that could trigger parser crashes or memory corruptions in native media decoding pipelines.

title: W3C Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) API: Hardware DRM Integration, Key Systems, and Secure Media Decryption
standard_reference: W3C Encrypted Media Extensions / W3C Recommendation
summary: Premium video streaming, digital cinema rentals, and proprietary live events inside super-apps require hardware-backed Digital Rights Management (DRM) to protect copyrighted intellectual property against unauthorized capture. W3C Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) standardizes an interoperable bridge between HTMLMediaElement and underlying Content Decryption Modules (CDMs) without proprietary browser plugins.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C EME § 2, mini-apps request DRM access via `navigator.requestMediaKeySystemAccess(keySystem, supportedConfigurations)`. Standard key systems include Google Widevine (`com.widevine.alpha`), Apple FairPlay (`com.apple.fps`), and Microsoft PlayReady (`com.microsoft.playready`). The returned `MediaKeySystemAccess` object creates `MediaKeys`, which is bound to `HTMLMediaElement.setMediaKeys()`. EME operates through `MediaKeySession` instances that exchange cryptographic challenge messages (`session.generateRequest()`, `session.update()`) with the publisher's license server to install decryption keys securely inside the CDM. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-apps requesting EME access MUST be granted the `encrypted-media` Permissions Policy by the super-app host container. Mini-app stores MUST audit license acquisition URLs against declared publisher domains to prevent man-in-the-middle license exfiltration. DRM hardware security level (e.g. Widevine L1 vs L3) MUST be negotiated dynamically according to host device capabilities.

title: MediaKeySession Interface: Key Exchange Protocol, Temporary vs Persistent Licenses, and CDM State Cleansing
standard_reference: W3C Encrypted Media Extensions § 5 MediaKeySession Interface
summary: DRM license management in mobile super-apps requires strict lifecycle discipline to support offline video viewing while preventing persistent license exhaustion and unauthorized license retention when mini-apps are uninstalled or reset. MediaKeySession standardizes session initialization, cryptographic challenge dispatch, license closure, and secure session removal.
detail: [SPEC FACT] `MediaKeySession` instances are instantiated with session types: 'temporary' (keys exist in memory and expire upon session closure) or 'persistent-license' (keys are stored persistently in secure hardware storage for offline playback). Key events include `message` (dispatched when the CDM produces a challenge for the license server), `keystatuseschange` (exposing key ID to `MediaKeyStatus` mappings such as 'usable', 'expired', 'output-restricted'), and `closed` (resolving when CDM resources are released). Persistent licenses require explicit `session.remove()` calls to securely delete stored cryptographic keys. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host containers MUST intercept mini-app uninstallation, account logout, and storage wiping routines, executing `session.remove()` and `mediaKeys.setMediaKeys(null)` to sanitize CDM hardware key storage. Offline DRM licenses MUST enforce maximum offline validity periods (e.g. 48 hours) to prevent persistent offline replay attacks.

title: WICG Document Picture-in-Picture API: Always-On-Top Mini-App DOM Windowing, Transient Activation, and LifeCycle Constraints
standard_reference: WICG Document Picture-in-Picture API / W3C Web Platform Incubator Community Group
summary: Legacy HTML5 video Picture-in-Picture is restricted solely to `<video>` elements, preventing mini-apps from displaying interactive UI controls (e.g. video conferencing chat, live commerce shopping carts with 'buy now' buttons, audio mixer boards, sports scoreboards) while users switch to other apps or super-app tabs. The WICG Document Picture-in-Picture API allows an application to open an always-on-top window populated with arbitrary DOM elements.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under the WICG Document Picture-in-Picture specification, `documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow({ width, height, disallowReturnToOpener })` opens an always-on-top window. The method requires transient user activation (gesture gating). The opened window provides its own distinct `document` object where DOM nodes, styles, and event listeners can be copied or mounted. Closing the parent window automatically terminates the PiP window, and the `enter` event on `documentPictureInPicture` notifies the opener of window creation. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host platforms MUST govern Document PiP windows through strict container permissions (`document-picture-in-picture`). Host security layers MUST ensure Document PiP windows display a persistent, non-spoofable origin banner and a native host close affordance to prevent overlay phishing attacks. Only verified mini-apps in certified categories (video calling, live streaming commerce, active media playback) MAY be granted Document PiP entitlement.

title: DocumentPictureInPicture Interface: Multi-Window Style Synchronization, Focus Management, and Resource Bounds
standard_reference: WICG Document Picture-in-Picture API § 2 DocumentPictureInPicture Interface
summary: Because Document PiP creates a separate top-level browsing context, CSS stylesheets, design tokens, and webfonts from the main mini-app document do not automatically inherit into the PiP document. Mini-apps must explicitly synchronize stylesheets while maintaining bounded window dimensions to prevent UI layout breaking on mobile and desktop super-app containers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `DocumentPictureInPicture` interface exposes `window`, returning the currently active PiP Window object or null if none is open. When a window is instantiated, developers clone stylesheet links (`<link rel='stylesheet'>`) or style elements into `pipWindow.document.head`. The `pagehide` event on `pipWindow` notifies the opener when the user closes the floating window, allowing DOM nodes to be safely migrated back into the main document without data loss. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDKs MUST provide automated style synchronization utilities that propagate container theme variables (dark/light mode, brand typography) into the PiP window. Host containers MUST enforce minimum (240x160) and maximum (800x600) viewport constraints on PiP windows to prevent full-screen takeover attempts.

title: W3C CSS Font Loading API: Programmatic Webfont Lifecycle, CLS Elimination, and Subset Loading Control
standard_reference: W3C CSS Font Loading Module Level 3 / W3C Recommendation
summary: Asynchronous font downloads frequently cause Flash of Unstyled Text (FOUT), Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT), and severe Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) in mini-apps, disrupting UI responsiveness and degrading user experience on slow mobile connections. The W3C CSS Font Loading API exposes programmatic interfaces (`document.fonts`) to dynamically load, inspect, and monitor webfonts before rendering text elements.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C CSS Font Loading Module Level 3, `document.fonts` implements `FontFaceSet`. It provides `document.fonts.load(font, text)` which returns a Promise resolving when requested fonts are fetched and parsed, and `document.fonts.check(font, text)` to synchronously test if glyphs are available in cache. The `document.fonts.ready` Promise resolves when all active font face loading operations are complete, enabling layout stabilization before taking UI snapshots or transitioning views. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-apps with custom branding or complex non-Latin typography MUST await critical typography through `document.fonts.load()` or utilize `font-display: swap` / `optional` to prevent invisible text blocking. Automated store quality gates MUST fail mini-app submissions that induce CLS scores exceeding 0.1 due to late font reflows.

title: FontFace Interface: In-Memory Font Instantiation, ArrayBuffer Deserialization, and Font Metric Inspection
standard_reference: W3C CSS Font Loading Module Level 3 § 2 FontFace Interface
summary: Enterprise mini-apps and specialized regional mini-apps (such as Southeast Asian script renderers or customized barcode/icon fonts) require instantiating webfonts directly from decrypted in-memory byte buffers or dynamic service worker caches without writing files to disk. The FontFace interface enables direct programmatic instantiation of fonts from ArrayBuffer sources.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `FontFace` constructor accepts `family`, `source` (URL string or binary `ArrayBuffer`/`TypedArray`), and descriptors (`style`, `weight`, `stretch`, `unicodeRange`, `variant`, `featureSettings`, `display`). Invoking `fontFace.load()` triggers binary parsing and validation of the OpenType/WOFF2 font data. Once loaded (`fontFace.status === 'loaded'`), the font is added to `document.fonts.add(fontFace)` to make it immediately available for CSS styling and canvas `ctx.font` rendering. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Binary font files embedded in mini-app packages or downloaded at runtime MUST be validated during store package inspection. Malformed TTF/WOFF2 files with corrupted SFNT tables or buffer overflow vectors targeting native OS font rendering engines (FreeType, CoreText, DirectWrite) MUST be rejected by store malware scanners.

title: FontFaceSet Interface: Font Loading Status Events, Set Mutation, and OffscreenCanvas Worker Integration
standard_reference: W3C CSS Font Loading Module Level 3 § 3 FontFaceSet Interface
summary: When rendering graphics, export documents, or generating receipts in background Web Workers via OffscreenCanvas, worker threads require independent font loading tracking to ensure text strings render with correct typographic glyphs rather than fallback fonts. FontFaceSet provides a Set-like collection with event-driven loading status notifications and worker thread support.
detail: [SPEC FACT] `FontFaceSet` extends `EventTarget` and implements `Set<FontFace>`. It dispatches `loading`, `loadingdone`, and `loadingerror` events as fonts transition states. The `status` attribute reflects `'loading'` or `'loaded'`. Critically, `FontFaceSet` is exposed on `WorkerGlobalScope.fonts`, allowing DedicatedWorker threads to independently load, register, and monitor custom fonts for rendering directly to `OffscreenCanvas` contexts without main-thread UI involvement. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-apps generating invoices, certificates, or transactional receipts inside Web Workers MUST listen to `self.fonts.ready` before rasterizing text on OffscreenCanvas. Store guidelines MUST instruct developers to unregister unused in-memory FontFace objects (`document.fonts.delete(fontFace)`) upon route unmount to prevent unbounded memory growth in persistent super-app container runtimes.

title: W3C WebAuthn PRF Extension: Hardware-Backed Deterministic Key Derivation & Client-Side Zero-Knowledge Encryption
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials Level 3 § 10.8 PRF Extension / FIDO CTAP 2.1 § 5.5.7 hmac-secret
summary: Standard public-key authentication provides non-repudiation and proof of identity but cannot derive deterministic symmetric encryption keys for offline end-to-end data encryption. The W3C WebAuthn PRF (Pseudo-Random Function) extension leverages authenticator hardware (CTAP2.1 hmac-secret) to deterministically derive shared symmetric keys directly from biometric or hardware user presence without leaking key material to servers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C WebAuthn Level 3 § 10.8, the `prf` extension allows a Relying Party to supply one or two salt inputs (`eval: { first, second }`) during credential registration or assertion. The authenticator applies an HMAC-SHA-256 operation with a credential-specific secret key stored within its secure element, returning a 32-byte pseudo-random output (`results: { first, second }`). Because the output is derived from the hardware authenticator and the salt, the identical symmetric key can be regenerated upon every successful biometric touch. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app platforms handling sensitive enterprise data (confidential customer records, offline encrypted medical history, client-side financial vaults) MUST utilize the PRF extension via `navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey: { extensions: { prf: ... } } })` to derive AES-256-GCM encryption keys. Master keys MUST NEVER be stored in unencrypted client-side storage or transmitted across network interfaces.

title: FIDO Alliance CTAP 2.1 hmac-secret: Hardware Token Architecture, Key Wrap, and Replay Protection
standard_reference: FIDO Alliance Client-to-Authenticator Protocol (CTAP) Implementation Draft v2.1 § 5.5.7 hmac-secret
summary: The underlying security foundation of WebAuthn PRF is the FIDO CTAP 2.1 `hmac-secret` protocol extension. It details how authenticators protect the symmetric seed in secure hardware, execute HMAC operations without exposing root seeds, and encrypt output data across the client-authenticator channel.
