detail: [SPEC FACT] Under CTAP 2.1 § 5.5.7, authenticators supporting `hmac-secret` create a 32-byte random secret (`CredRandom`) during credential creation, storing it either in internal persistent hardware storage or encrypting it inside the credential ID wrapper (Key Wrap mechanism). During assertion, the host client sends an encrypted salt using a Diffie-Hellman shared secret negotiated via ECDH over curve P-256. The authenticator computes `HMAC-SHA-256(CredRandom, Salt)` and returns the ciphertext. This guarantees that eavesdroppers on USB, NFC, or BLE buses cannot intercept the derived cryptographic seed. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app native containers providing WebAuthn bridge interfaces MUST verify that the client-to-authenticator channel enforces CTAP 2.1 ECDH channel encryption. Host SDKs MUST fail closed and return standardized error codes if an authenticator does not support hardware-backed `hmac-secret` when a financial mini-app demands zero-knowledge encryption.

title: PublicKeyCredential getClientExtensionResults(): PRF Output Processing and Key Derivation Function (HKDF) Pipelines
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 § 5.7.5 Extension Processing
summary: Once the authenticator completes biometric verification and PRF computation, the browser client exposes the derived 32-byte pseudo-random seed via `credential.getClientExtensionResults().prf`. Mini-apps must pipe this raw output into standardized key derivation functions (HKDF) to generate operational encryption and integrity keys.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `PublicKeyCredential.prototype.getClientExtensionResults()` method returns an object containing the `prf` property. When successful, `results.prf.results.first` provides an `ArrayBuffer` containing 32 cryptographically strong pseudo-random bytes. Developers ingest this buffer into WebCrypto `crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', prfOutput, 'HKDF', false, ['deriveKey'])` to derive distinct AES-GCM encryption keys and HMAC integrity keys using domain-specific info strings. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer guidelines MUST mandate using HKDF (RFC 5869) to separate derived keys by context (e.g. 'offline-db-encryption' vs 'auth-token-seal'). Storing raw PRF output directly as a symmetric key is prohibited by store security audits because direct reuse of PRF outputs across different cryptographic primitives compromises key separation.

title: Zero-Knowledge Local Storage Architecture: Combining WebAuthn PRF with IndexedDB and OPFS
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication / Chrome Status Feature #5141362703892480 (WebAuthn PRF)
summary: Combining WebAuthn PRF with local storage mechanisms (Origin Private File System / OPFS and IndexedDB) enables mini-apps to create zero-knowledge encrypted vaults on client devices. This architecture guarantees that even if a physical device is compromised or container storage is backed up, encrypted data cannot be decrypted without physical biometric interaction.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In a zero-knowledge mini-app vault pattern, the application stores encrypted database files (e.g. SQLite compiled to Wasm running on OPFS) encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The encryption key never resides in persistent flash memory. On app launch, the mini-app invokes `navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey: { extensions: { prf: { eval: { first: saltBuffer } } } } })`. Upon user biometric presence, PRF returns the 32-byte secret, derives the AES key into volatile RAM, decrypts the SQLite database into memory, and zeroizes key material upon app backgrounding or session timeout. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms in regulated banking, fintech, and healthcare domains SHOULD certify this zero-knowledge local storage pattern. Store review guidelines MUST verify that mini-apps claiming 'end-to-end local encryption' do not store decryption passphrases or unencrypted master seeds in unpartitioned Web Storage (localStorage).

title: Cryptographic Key Recovery Governance: Managing Device Loss, Authenticator Replacement, and Re-Encryption Flows
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 / Enterprise Passkey Deployment Guidelines
summary: Because WebAuthn PRF output is bound to a specific hardware authenticator credential, losing the physical authenticator or switching devices prevents direct regeneration of the PRF symmetric key. Mini-app platforms must establish secure multi-key wrapping recovery protocols.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To support multi-device synchronization and device loss recovery without compromising zero-knowledge security, applications implement an envelope encryption scheme: a randomly generated Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts the actual data, while a Key Encryption Key (KEK) derived from WebAuthn PRF wraps (encrypts) the DEK. When a user registers a secondary passkey or backup authenticator, the DEK is decrypted using the active PRF key and re-wrapped with the new authenticator's PRF key. Alternatively, an encrypted recovery escrow blob is synchronized across cloud backups. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store compliance policies MUST require apps implementing PRF encryption to present a verified recovery mechanism (secondary passkey binding, multi-party threshold recovery, or secure escrow passphrases). Apps that lock user data permanently upon single-token loss without user warning fail store usability and resilience audits.

title: WICG Web App Manifest Scope Extensions: Declarative Multi-Origin Application Boundaries & Verification Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Web App Manifest Incubations § Scope Extensions / Chrome Status Feature #5752614244188160
summary: Historically, a mini-app or progressive web application is strictly confined to a single origin defined by its manifest `scope` property. Navigating to an auxiliary subdomain (e.g. `auth.example.com`, `checkout.example.com`, or regional domains `example.vn`) forces the container to launch an external browser or display out-of-scope window chrome. The WICG Scope Extensions specification allows an app to expand its navigation scope across multiple origins through declarative, cryptographically verified two-way associations.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WICG Manifest Scope Extensions, the manifest defines `scope_extensions: [ { origin: 'https://auth.example.com' }, { origin: 'https://*.partner.com' } ]`. Crucially, to prevent malicious scope hijacking of arbitrary domains, the target origins MUST reciprocate trust by hosting a declarative verification file at `/.well-known/web-app-origin-association`. The association file explicitly declares the allowed mini-app manifest URL. Browsers and container runtimes only extend the execution scope if this two-way handshake successfully verifies. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST enforce automated two-way association verification during mini-app package review. Mini-app submissions specifying cross-origin `scope_extensions` MUST be validated by store crawlers verifying the presence and signature of `/.well-known/web-app-origin-association` on all declared auxiliary origins. Unverified origins are stripped from the runtime routing manifest.

title: web-app-origin-association Protocol: JSON Schema, Same-Entity Validation, and Anti-Spoofing Rules
standard_reference: WICG Scope Extensions Explainer § Origin Association File Specification
summary: The origin association handshake prevents unauthorized mini-apps from claiming high-reputation domains (such as banking login portals or social networks) within their navigation scope. It defines a standardized JSON schema and TLS verification protocol for mutual domain endorsement.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The target origin hosts `https://target.com/.well-known/web-app-origin-association` served with `Content-Type: application/json` over valid TLS. The JSON structure contains `web_apps: [ { manifest: 'https://app.com/manifest.webmanifest', details: { ... } } ]`. Wildcard subdomains (`*.domain.com`) require the association file to reside at the root apex domain. HTTP redirects are strictly prohibited when fetching the association file to prevent SSRF and DNS rebinding attacks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] The super-app package build pipeline MUST perform daily automated health checks on all registered `web-app-origin-association` files. If an external partner origin deletes the association file or updates its manifest pointer, the store runtime MUST immediately revoke extended scope permissions and revert navigations to isolated sandboxed tabs.

title: Cross-Platform Site Association Parity: Google Digital Asset Links & Apple App Site Association Integration
standard_reference: Google Digital Asset Links Protocol / Apple Universal Links Associated Domains / WICG Scope Extensions Alignment
summary: Native mobile operating systems enforce cross-origin app binding via Google Digital Asset Links (`assetlinks.json`) and Apple Universal Links (`apple-app-site-association`). Super-app containers must harmonize W3C Web App Manifest scope extensions with native OS association protocols to deliver seamless in-app navigation and deep linking.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Google Digital Asset Links queries `https://domain/.well-known/assetlinks.json` specifying package names and SHA-256 certificate fingerprints with `delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls`. Apple Universal Links queries `https://domain/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` with appID prefixes. When a mini-app inside a super app attempts to capture native deep links across multiple domains, the super-app container must map the web-based `scope_extensions` declarations directly into its native App Link / Universal Link routing tables. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store submission pipelines MUST validate that mini-apps requesting native universal link capture across partner web domains provide matching entries in the native host app's asset association tables. The store gateway maintains a unified association registry ensuring no two mini-apps claim overlapping link-capturing routes.

title: WICG Link Capturing & handle_links: Declarative In-App Navigation vs External Browser Dispatch
standard_reference: WICG Manifest Incubations § Link Capturing (`handle_links`) / W3C Web Applications Working Group
summary: When a user clicks a hyperlink within a super app or adjacent mini-app, the container must deterministically decide whether to navigate within the existing mini-app view, open a new mini-app instance tab, or launch an external system browser. The `handle_links` manifest member provides declarative developer control over link capturing behaviors.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WICG Manifest Incubations, the `handle_links` member accepts `'auto'`, `'preferred'`, or `'not-preferred'`. When configured to `'preferred'`, clicking any link that falls within the mini-app's primary `scope` or validated `scope_extensions` captures the navigation into the standalone mini-app window rather than an external webview. Conversely, links outside the extended scope trigger host container interception, prompting the user or routing to a hardened sandboxed webview with restricted JSAPI privileges. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app manifests submitted to the store MUST explicitly declare link capturing expectations. Host container routing engines MUST intercept all `window.open()` and `<a>` navigations, evaluating target URLs against validated `scope_extensions` before executing native navigation transitions. Navigations to unknown third-party domains MUST display an interstitial warning dialog.

title: Cross-Origin Security Isolation: Storage Partitioning, Process Boundaries, and JSAPI Attenuation for Extended Scopes
standard_reference: WICG Scope Extensions Security Considerations / OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide
summary: While `scope_extensions` allows unified window chrome and navigation flow across related domains, extending scopes must not break the fundamental web security boundary. Auxiliary origins must remain isolated regarding cookies, local storage, and privileged native JSAPIs.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG specification strictly mandates that extending the navigation scope does NOT collapse origins into a single security principal. Each origin within `scope_extensions` retains its own distinct origin, storage partitioning, and Content Security Policy. Crossing between origins within an extended scope remains a cross-origin navigation, resetting document globals while preserving the enclosing PWA/mini-app window frame. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host platforms implementing scope extensions MUST NOT grant native bridge JSAPI privileges to secondary extended origins unless those auxiliary origins undergo independent store code auditing. The native container MUST attenuate bridge capabilities when navigations transition from the primary mini-app origin to secondary domains, preventing compromised partner sites from executing sensitive host methods.

title: WICG Performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory(): Cross-Origin Isolated Client RAM Telemetry and Memory Leak Forensics
standard_reference: WICG Performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() Specification / W3C Web Performance Working Group
summary: Unbounded memory consumption in long-running mini-apps causes catastrophic Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes, native mobile Application Not Responding (ANR) events, and abrupt OS termination of the host super app. Standard JavaScript heap profiling APIs (like legacy `performance.memory`) are inaccurate, unstandardized, and leak cross-origin data. The WICG `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` API provides a secure, privacy-preserving, breakdown of client-side RAM allocation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under the WICG specification, `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` returns a Promise resolving to a structured memory report: `{ bytes, breakdown: [ { bytes, attribution: [ { url, scope } ], types } ] }`. Crucially, to prevent side-channel memory timing attacks (Spectre/Meltdown), the API is strictly gated behind Cross-Origin Isolation (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`). Memory measurements are aggregated by origin, and sub-window memory is attributed only when permitted by security headers. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app containers operating long-lived background mini-apps (navigation, music streaming, POS terminals) MUST run scheduled `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` probes. Store automated crash watchdogs MUST enforce maximum client RAM thresholds (e.g. 150MB per mini-app instance). Mini-apps demonstrating progressive memory growth exceeding 20MB/hour are flagged for memory leak remediation.

title: Memory Breakdown Structure & Automated Leak Detection: Tracking DOM, JS Heap, and WebAssembly Allocations
standard_reference: WICG Performance Memory Specification § Memory Measurement Result
summary: Diagnosing whether memory growth stems from DOM detachment, JavaScript object retention, or WebAssembly linear memory requires detailed attribution categorization. The WICG memory measurement breakdown taxonomy enables automated client-side heap classification.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `breakdown` array returned by `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` categorizes memory usage into standardized `types`: `'JavaScript'`, `'DOM'`, `'Shared'`, and `'Canvas'`. Each entry contains an `attribution` array identifying the document URL and context scope (`'Window'`, `'DedicatedWorker'`, `'ServiceWorker'`). By executing periodic measurements after garbage collection cycles and calculating regression slopes across routing events, monitoring scripts identify retained detached DOM trees and un-disposed WebGL/Wasm memory buffers. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Enterprise store SDKs MUST embed lightweight telemetry agents that sample `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` during route transitions. If the 'DOM' or 'JavaScript' memory slice fails to return to baseline after view unmounting, the SDK generates a memory leak violation report sent to the super-app crash forensics gateway.

title: W3C/WICG Element Timing API: Granular Render Timestamps for Critical Hero Images, Text Elements, and CTA Buttons
standard_reference: WICG Element Timing / W3C Web Performance Working Group Draft
summary: While Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures when the single largest visual element renders, it fails to capture when domain-critical business elements (such as an e-commerce 'Purchase Now' button, a banking balance display, or a ride-hailing map viewport) become visible. The Element Timing API provides explicit, opt-in programmatic measurement for designated DOM elements.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Developers add the `elementtiming='identifier'` HTML attribute to critical ``, `` (inside SVG), or text-containing block elements. A `PerformanceObserver` observing type `'element'` receives `PerformanceElementTiming` entries containing `identifier`, `renderTime` (hardware display swap timestamp), `loadTime` (network completion timestamp), `intersectionRect` (element viewport coordinates), and `naturalWidth`/`naturalHeight`. If an element is rendered before user gesture, `renderTime` provides sub-millisecond precision. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app review quality standards SHOULD require developers of transactional mini-apps to annotate core conversion elements with `elementtiming='primary-cta'`. Automated store synthetic auditing bots evaluate whether the primary interactive element renders within 1,200ms on 4G network profiles, rejecting applications where hero content exhibits blank render delays.

title: PerformanceElementTiming: Image Render Timestamps, Cross-Origin Timing-Allow-Origin (TAO), and Resource Metrics
standard_reference: WICG Element Timing § 4 Security and Privacy Considerations
summary: Measuring exact image render times across subresource CDNs introduces microarchitectural side channels if timing attributes leak cross-origin image content. The Element Timing specification defines rigorous Timing-Allow-Origin (TAO) validation rules for image render timestamps.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WICG Element Timing § 4, for cross-origin images to expose non-zero `renderTime` and exact resource timing details, the image server MUST include the `Timing-Allow-Origin` HTTP response header authorizing the mini-app origin. If TAO validation fails, `renderTime` is coerced to zero, and only `loadTime` (the network fetch completion time) is reported. This prevents untrusted scripts from measuring pixel complexity or cache status of cross-origin assets via high-resolution paint timers. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app CDN hosting infrastructures MUST automatically inject appropriate `Timing-Allow-Origin: *` or authorized super-app origin headers on hosted mini-app asset bundles. Developer documentation MUST instruct mini-app creators on TAO compliance to ensure real-user monitoring (RUM) agents capture accurate visual render milestones.

title: Super-App Client Runtime SLA: Synthesizing Memory Limits, Element Timing, and Automated De-Listing Governance
standard_reference: W3C Web Performance Standards / Super-App Operational Governance Framework
summary: Maintaining a premium super-app ecosystem requires continuous, automated enforcement of client runtime SLAs. Mini-apps that degrade host performance, cause memory thrashing, or freeze rendering must be systematically detected and penalized.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern web performance architectures combine `PerformanceObserver` instances tracking `'element'`, `'largest-contentful-paint'`, `'long-animation-frame'`, and periodic `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` calls. Aggregating these metrics yields a composite Client Health Score (CHS). Real-world data shows that mini-apps with memory footprints exceeding 120MB exhibit a 4.2x higher crash frequency on budget Android hardware (devices with <=4GB RAM). [STORE REQUIREMENT] The mini-app store governance policy MUST define strict runtime SLA thresholds: (1) 95th percentile Hero Element Timing < 1.5s; (2) Maximum steady-state client RAM < 100MB; (3) Zero memory growth across 5 consecutive route cycles. Apps violating runtime SLAs across >1% of active production sessions trigger automated developer alerts, demotion in catalog search rankings, and eventual suspension if unresolved within 14 business days.

title: W3C MiniApp Manifest: Standardized JSON Metadata, Page Routing, and Display Directives
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Manifest Candidate Recommendation / W3C MiniApps Working Group
summary: The W3C MiniApp Manifest specification standardizes the centralized metadata format required to discover, route, configure, and execute a mini-app inside a hybrid container host. It unifies disparate vendor formats (WeChat app.json, Alipay app.json, Baidu app.json) into a single interoperable schema.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C MiniApp Manifest defines top-level JSON members including 'app_id', 'name', 'version', 'pages' (ordered routing array of page file paths), 'window' (global window style configuration such as 'navigationBarTitleText', 'navigationBarBackgroundColor', 'navigationBarTextStyle', and 'backgroundColor'), 'orientation' ('portrait', 'landscape', 'auto'), and 'req_permissions' declaring explicit capability requirements. It also introduces 'widgets' declarations for companion micro-interfaces. The document parsing algorithm enforces strict JSON schema validation, discarding unrecognized vendor extensions without aborting execution. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store submission pipelines MUST validate mini-app packages against the W3C MiniApp Manifest JSON Schema. The automated store linter MUST reject submissions missing required 'pages' mappings, verifying that every declared path corresponds to an existing file bundle within the package. Furthermore, store permission managers MUST extract 'req_permissions' during ingest to generate user-facing security declarations in the store catalog.

title: W3C MiniApp Packaging: Zip Container Structure, Subpackage Splitting, and Dynamic Dependency Resolution
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Packaging Candidate Recommendation / W3C MiniApps Working Group
summary: To balance instant cold-start launch times with rich multi-feature business logic, the W3C MiniApp Packaging specification standardizes single-package and multi-package distribution formats. It provides formal semantics for independent subpackage splitting and dynamic on-demand loading.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A W3C MiniApp package is an archive based on the ZIP format containing 'manifest.json' at root, application-level logic/styling ('app.js', 'app.css'), page directories, and static assets. For complex applications, the packaging specification defines subpackages: the 'main package' contains initial launch pages and global resources (capped typically at 2MB-4MB for instant network fetch), while 'subpackages' define isolated route roots. The container runtime executes dynamic subpackage prefetching and on-demand streaming when navigation transitions to secondary route boundaries. Digital signatures and checksum hashes (SHA-256) embedded in the package header guarantee artifact integrity. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store packaging gateways MUST enforce size limits: main packages MUST NOT exceed 4MB compressed, and total aggregate subpackages MUST NOT exceed 20MB. Package review pipelines MUST verify the cryptographic signature of the zip container against the developer's registered public key, ensuring zero binary alteration between submission and edge CDN delivery.

title: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle: Dual-Level Application and Page State Machines with Background Resource Governance
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle Working Group Note / W3C MiniApps Working Group
summary: Mini-apps operate in a dual-threaded architecture (logical thread running business JavaScript and rendering thread displaying UI). The W3C MiniApp Lifecycle specification defines formal state machines and event models for both application-level and page-level transitions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The specification defines two decoupled state machines: (1) Application Lifecycle: 'launch' (initial container cold boot with launch query params), 'show' (entering foreground visibility), 'hide' (transitioning to background), and 'error' (uncaught exception trap); (2) Page Lifecycle: 'load' (DOM compilation and route data injection), 'show' (page visible), 'ready' (first visual paint completed and interactive), 'hide' (navigating to another page in stack), 'unload' (popped from back-stack), and 'pullDownRefresh' (user scroll gesture). When an application transitions to 'hide', the container pauses rendering threads, clamps timers, and restricts background execution unless persistent background capabilities (e.g. background audio or location) are approved. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store SDK runtime frameworks MUST strictly adhere to the W3C lifecycle dispatch order. Mini-apps that fail to release heavy resources (camera, audio streams, WebGL contexts) upon receiving the 'hide' lifecycle event are subject to automated runtime termination by the host container watchdog if background CPU usage exceeds 5% for more than 30 seconds.

title: W3C MiniApp Addressing: Standardized miniapp:// URI Scheme, Path Resolution, and Inter-App Invocation
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Addressing Recommendation / W3C MiniApps Working Group
summary: Navigating between mini-apps and resolving internal sub-resources requires a standardized URI syntax. The W3C MiniApp Addressing specification formalizes the 'miniapp' URI scheme, hierarchical path resolution, and parameter serialization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C MiniApp Addressing, URIs follow the generic syntax: 'miniapp://{miniapp-id}/{page-path}?{query}#{fragment}'. The authority component identifies the unique mini-app identifier registered with the platform; the path component specifies the relative route within the mini-app package; and query parameters pass invocation payloads. The specification also defines resource resolution algorithms mapping relative web assets ('/assets/icon.png') to isolated sandbox package directories, preventing directory traversal ('../../') escapes beyond the package root. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app intent routers and deep-link gateways MUST implement the W3C 'miniapp://' URI parser. Deep-link routing engines MUST sanitize all incoming query parameters against URI injection and buffer overflow attacks. Furthermore, cross-mini-app invocations using 'miniapp://' URIs must be validated against the caller's store capability allowlist to prevent unauthorized inter-app data exfiltration.

title: W3C MiniApp Widget Requirements: Glanceable Micro-Cards, Declarative Data Binding, and Sandbox Constraints
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Widget Requirements Working Group Note / W3C MiniApps Working Group
summary: Widgets represent lightweight, glanceable representations of mini-apps embedded directly into host surfaces (home feeds, notification centers, search cards, and lock screens). The W3C Widget Requirements document outlines architectural constraints and data-binding contracts for these micro-interfaces.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C MiniApp Widgets operate under strict resource and runtime constraints: (1) Instant rendering: widgets must render declaratively within <=50ms, relying on lightweight template engines rather than full WebView initialization; (2) Declarative data binding: the widget UI updates reactively via structured JSON state payloads sent by the host or background workers, eliminating direct script execution in high-density feeds; (3) Sandbox boundary: widgets have zero direct access to native device sensors, cameras, or local storage, communicating exclusively via declarative tap actions routed to the host; (4) Memory footprint: widgets are capped at <=5MB RAM per card instance. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms supporting mini-app widget stores MUST enforce strict review gates: widgets MUST NOT execute unconstrained JavaScript, MUST NOT initiate autonomous network connections outside host-mediated data providers, and MUST declare explicit dimensional layouts ('small', 'medium', 'large') conforming to the host design system grid.

title: Web Bluetooth API: User-Mediated Device Discovery, Service Filtering, and Secure Pairing Lifecycles
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Community Group Specification § 3 Device Discovery / W3C Community Group
summary: Connecting mini-apps to short-range physical peripherals (blood pressure monitors, heart rate bands, retail barcode scanners, BLE smart beacons, IoT smart locks) requires secure, sandboxed device access. The Web Bluetooth API establishes a user-mediated, permission-gated BLE communication bridge.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Web Bluetooth execution begins with 'navigator.bluetooth.requestDevice(options)'. To prevent malicious mass scanning or silent physical tracking, the method MUST be triggered by transient user activation (touch or click). The 'options' object requires explicit 'filters' (by Bluetooth service UUIDs, device name prefix, or manufacturer data) or 'acceptAllDevices: true' paired with an 'optionalServices' array. The browser/container displays an unforgeable native picker dialog where the user explicitly selects the physical device. The returned 'BluetoothDevice' instance is origin-bound and scoped to the user session, exposing 'id', 'name', and the 'gatt' server connection handle. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store submission audits MUST inspect mini-app Bluetooth capability declarations. Mini-apps requesting Bluetooth MUST define specific target service UUIDs in their permission manifest; declaring 'acceptAllDevices: true' without documented IoT device vendor requirements is grounds for store rejection. Furthermore, the container picker dialog must present clear mini-app identity branding to prevent spoofed pairing requests.

title: BluetoothRemoteGATTServer: Connection Lifecycle, Service Discovery, MTU Negotiation, and Disconnection Resilience
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Specification § 4.3 BluetoothRemoteGATTServer / MDN Web Docs
summary: Once a physical device is selected, the application communicates over the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) hierarchy. The BluetoothRemoteGATTServer interface governs connection state, service hierarchy resolution, and physical disconnection handling.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Calling 'device.gatt.connect()' initiates the physical BLE connection and resolves to a 'BluetoothRemoteGATTServer' object. Applications discover GATT services via 'server.getPrimaryService(serviceUUID)' or 'server.getPrimaryServices()'. The connection is prone to physical RF drops, user movement, and signal attenuation; the 'device' dispatches the 'gattserverdisconnected' event upon connection loss. Applications must implement idempotent reconnection loops with exponential backoff. In low-power mobile operating systems, GATT connections are aggressively managed by native OS BLE stacks, requiring negotiation of connection intervals and Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) packet sizes. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app runtimes MUST handle unexpected GATT disconnections without UI freezes or unhandled promise rejections. The super-app host container enforces an automated disconnect watchdog: if a mini-app maintains an open GATT connection while idle for >3 minutes with no data transfer, the container automatically invokes 'device.gatt.disconnect()' to conserve device and peripheral battery.

title: GATT Characteristic Operations: Value Read, Chunked Write, Streaming Notifications, and DataView Deserialization
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Specification § 4.4 BluetoothRemoteGATTCharacteristic / MDN Web Docs
summary: Exchanging telemetry, control commands, and sensor data with Bluetooth peripherals occurs through GATT characteristics. The Web Bluetooth API provides strongly typed, asynchronous interfaces for atomic reads, writes, and real-time event streaming.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A 'BluetoothRemoteGATTCharacteristic' exposes read, write, and notification primitives: (1) 'readValue()' returns a Promise resolving to a 'DataView' containing raw binary payload; (2) 'writeValueWithResponse(buffer)' sends an acknowledged command (ensuring peripheral receipt), while 'writeValueWithoutResponse(buffer)' executes low-latency unacknowledged transmission; (3) 'startNotifications()' enables real-time sensor streaming, triggering the 'characteristicvaluechanged' event whenever the peripheral transmits an updated value. To accommodate BLE ATT MTU boundaries (traditionally 20-23 bytes default payload), high-volume transfers must be manually packetized and chunked by the client script. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store review guidelines require mini-apps communicating with medical, payment, or industrial peripherals to use 'writeValueWithResponse()' for all state-changing or transactional commands to prevent silent packet drop. Developers must explicitly call 'stopNotifications()' during component unmounting or navigation transitions to prevent orphaned background BLE radio polling.

title: Web Bluetooth Security Architecture: W3C/Chrome GATT Blocklist, Keystroke Injection Mitigations, and MITM Defenses
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Specification § 8 Security and Privacy Considerations / Chromium GATT Blocklist
summary: Allowing untrusted web scripts to interact with local hardware introduces severe attack vectors, including keystroke injection, unauthorized firmware flashing, and credential extraction from security dongles. The Web Bluetooth security architecture incorporates a non-bypassable GATT Blocklist.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Web Bluetooth specification and browser implementations enforce an immutable GATT Blocklist of restricted UUIDs. Access to Human Interface Device (HID - 0x1812), FIDO/U2F (0xFFFD), Fast Identity Online authentication services, and specific Heart Rate Control Points (0x2A39) is strictly prohibited. Attempting to access blocked services or characteristics immediately throws a 'SecurityError' DOMException. Furthermore, all Web Bluetooth operations are restricted exclusively to Secure Contexts (HTTPS), and cross-origin iframes cannot invoke Bluetooth APIs unless explicitly delegated via the 'bluetooth' Permissions Policy. [STORE REQUIREMENT] The super-app security sandbox MUST integrate the Chromium GATT Blocklist into native container bridge proxies. Mini-app submissions attempting to connect to prohibited GATT UUIDs or bypass blocklists using raw vendor-specific handles are flagged as high-risk malicious payloads and immediately rejected during static code analysis.

title: Super-App Bluetooth Container Governance: Background Disconnection, Peripheral Sharing, and Enterprise IoT Mediation
standard_reference: Super-App Peripheral Governance Framework / W3C MiniApps Hardware Guidance
summary: In a multi-tenant super app where multiple mini-apps (retail store loyalty, smart health monitors, bike-sharing rentals, smart home appliances) share a single physical mobile device, the container must arbitrate Bluetooth radio access, background suspension, and peripheral conflicts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Mobile operating systems (Android and iOS) enforce strict concurrency and background limits on BLE connections. When a mini-app transitions from foreground to background ('hide' lifecycle event), the super-app host container MUST pause BLE notifications and disconnect non-essential GATT sessions to allow other active mini-apps and host services to utilize the Bluetooth radio. If a shared peripheral (e.g. an in-store POS printer or beacon) is requested by multiple mini-apps, the host container provides a centralized serialization queue preventing GATT collision errors ('GATT_BUSY' / 'GATT_ERROR'). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store governance policies mandate: (1) Mini-apps must register peripheral hardware requirements (vendor IDs, service profiles) in their store metadata; (2) Mini-apps must not attempt background BLE scanning unless granted an enterprise 'background-iot' entitlement by the store operator; (3) The super-app UI must provide an active Bluetooth indicator in the container header showing connected peripherals and offering an instant 'Disconnect' action for user privacy.

title: Web NFC API: NDEFReader Scan Lifecycle, Event Dispatching, and Permissions Policy Controls
standard_reference: W3C Web NFC Working Draft § 5 NDEFReader Interface / W3C Web Applications Security
summary: Near Field Communication (NFC) enables touch-to-pay, smart posters, inventory scanning, transit ticketing, and access badges. The Web NFC API exposes the NDEFReader interface for reading and writing NFC Data Exchange Format (NDEF) payloads in web and mini-app contexts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Web NFC operations require a Secure Context (HTTPS) and top-level browsing context with active document focus. Developers instantiate 'new NDEFReader()' and call 'ndef.scan({ signal: abortSignal })'. When an NFC tag enters the RF field, the reader dispatches the 'reading' event (event of type 'NDEFReadingEvent') carrying 'serialNumber' and a structured 'message' ('NDEFMessage' containing an array of 'NDEFRecord' objects). If transmission fails or invalid data is detected, the reader dispatches 'readingerror'. The API is strictly gated behind the 'nfc' Permissions Policy and requires user permission prompt on first use. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store security policies require mini-apps utilizing NFC to declare the 'nfc' capability in their manifest. The super-app host container MUST wrap native NFC adapters: (1) NFC scanning is automatically paused when the mini-app loses foreground focus or screen locks; (2) The container displays a native NFC scanning indicator card while 'scan()' is active; (3) Store static analysis scans for proper AbortController signal handling to ensure NFC polling is cleanly aborted upon task completion.

title: NDEF Record Anatomy: Record Types, Binary Payload Parsing, Text/URI Decoding, and Security Filtering
standard_reference: W3C Web NFC § 6 NDEF Record / NFC Forum NDEF Technical Specification
summary: NFC messages consist of one or more NDEF records. Decoding these records reliably while safeguarding against malicious payloads (malicious URLs, malformed MIME types, executable payloads) requires standardized record handling.
detail: [SPEC FACT] An 'NDEFRecord' exposes: (1) 'recordType': standard types include 'text', 'url', 'mime', 'empty', or external vendor types; (2) 'mediaType': valid MIME type string when 'recordType' is 'mime'; (3) 'id': optional record identifier string; (4) 'encoding' & 'lang': character encoding ('utf-8', 'utf-16') and BCP 47 language tag for 'text' records; (5) 'data': a 'DataView' containing the raw binary payload. Parsing text records is performed via 'new TextDecoder(record.encoding).decode(record.data)', while URL records require parsing as valid absolute URIs. The Web NFC specification explicitly prohibits parsing or executing active content (such as raw HTML or executable scripts) from NDEF records. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app SDK bridge layers MUST enforce payload validation on all incoming NDEF records. URLs extracted from NFC smart posters MUST be sanitized and evaluated against the mini-app's Content Security Policy and navigation allowlist before executing navigation. Super-app stores reject mini-apps that attempt to execute raw eval() or dynamically inject script blocks parsed from untrusted NFC tag payloads.

title: Web NFC Tag Writing: NDEF Write Protocols, Overwrite Protection, and Contactless POS Tagging Controls
standard_reference: W3C Web NFC § 5.2 Writing NDEF Messages / Chrome Capabilities Documentation
summary: In addition to reading tags, enterprise mini-apps (warehouse inventory tagging, retail product provisioning, customer loyalty badge programming) require write capabilities. Web NFC governs tag writing through asynchronous write promises with explicit overwrite safeguards.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Writing is initiated via 'ndef.write(message, { overwrite: boolean, signal: abortSignal })'. The 'message' parameter can be a string, a URL, a buffer, or a structured NDEF message array. Setting 'overwrite: false' ensures the write operation rejects if the physical tag already contains existing NDEF records, preventing accidental data erasure. Writing requires transient user activation and active physical proximity. The promise resolves only after the physical RF write handshake is verified, or rejects with 'NetworkError' (tag lost during write) or 'NotAllowedError' (user denied permission or tag is read-only). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store review guidelines classify Web NFC tag writing as a high-privilege commercial capability. Mini-apps requesting write access MUST demonstrate an explicit business use case (e.g. logistics tracking or access pass programming). The store review pipeline requires developers to handle write timeouts gracefully and present visual confirmations preventing users from withdrawing devices prematurely during write operations.

title: W3C Generic Sensor API Framework: Lifecycle State Machine, Sampling Frequency Clamping, and Battery Governance
standard_reference: W3C Generic Sensor API Recommendation / W3C Devices and Sensors Working Group
summary: Modern smart devices contain diverse physical sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, ambient light, orientation, gravity). The W3C Generic Sensor API defines the base foundation and standardized lifecycle state machine for all high-level sensor interfaces.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The base 'Sensor' interface defines a 4-state lifecycle: 'idle' (initial state), 'activating' (requesting hardware subsystem), 'activated' (emitting readings), and 'errored' (hardware failure or permission denial). Calling 'sensor.start()' transitions the sensor to 'activating' and dispatches 'activate', while 'sensor.stop()' returns it to 'idle'. Sensor instances expose 'hasReading', 'timestamp', and dispatch the 'reading' event when updated data arrives. To prevent battery drain and side-channel eavesdropping (keystroke acoustic snooping), user agents clamp maximum sampling frequencies (typically <=60Hz) and automatically suspend all sensor updates when document visibility changes to hidden ('visibilitychange'). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container architectures MUST extend the Generic Sensor state machine to native bridge sensors. Mini-apps MUST NOT run continuous sensor polling loops without explicit sampling rate declarations. Runtimes must enforce strict background auto-suspension, terminating active sensor subscriptions whenever a mini-app is concealed or minimized.

title: W3C Geolocation Sensor API: Modern Sensor-Integrated GNSS Telemetry, Accuracy Thresholds, and Privacy Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Geolocation Sensor Specification / W3C Devices and Sensors Working Group
summary: Building upon the Generic Sensor framework, the W3C Geolocation Sensor specification modernizes location telemetry, replacing callback-based legacy geolocation with a robust sensor lifecycle, Promise-based reads, and precision privacy controls.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'GeolocationSensor' extends the base 'Sensor' class. It provides 'latitude', 'longitude', 'altitude', 'accuracy', 'altitudeAccuracy', 'heading', and 'speed' directly on the sensor object. It introduces the static asynchronous method 'GeolocationSensor.read({ accuracy: 'high' | 'low' })' for single-shot location retrieval, resolving directly to coordinate properties without setting up persistent event listeners. Continuous tracking is managed via 'sensor.start()', emitting 'reading' events synchronized with GNSS hardware updates. The specification integrates with the W3C Permissions Policy ('geolocation') and mandates coarsened location rounding for privacy-sensitive contexts. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST enforce privacy-preserving location governance: (1) Delivery and ride-hailing mini-apps are permitted 'high' accuracy GNSS streaming only during active trip navigation; (2) Retail and weather mini-apps are restricted to coarsened regional coordinates (accuracy coarsened to 1km radius); (3) Container watchdogs verify that GeolocationSensor instances are stopped immediately upon order completion or navigation exit.

title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 6.4.3: Mandatory Script Authorization, Inventory, and Integrity Assurance on Payment Pages
standard_reference: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 6.4.3 / PCI Security Standards Council
summary: Mandates that all scripts loaded and executed in the consumer's browser on payment pages are authorized, tracked with written business justification, and assured for cryptographic integrity.
detail: [SPEC FACT] PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 6.4.3 (effective March 31, 2025) requires entities to manage all scripts executed in the consumer's browser on payment pages. The requirement mandates: (1) A method to confirm that each script is authorized; (2) A method to assure the integrity of each script (e.g., Subresource Integrity hashes or Content Security Policy hashes); and (3) An inventory of all scripts with documented business justification for each. In single-page applications (SPAs) where a single DOM context is maintained, any script loaded throughout the application lifecycle may be in scope unless segmented. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST enforce strict script inventory controls: (1) Mini-apps invoking payment flows MUST NOT inject arbitrary third-party analytics or tracker scripts into the payment execution context; (2) The platform container must maintain a cryptographically verified manifest of all permitted checkout SDK scripts; (3) Container runtime gates reject unapproved dynamic script evaluation (<script> tag injection or eval()) on checkout views.

title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 11.6.1: Change and Tamper Detection for Payment Page Scripts and Security HTTP Headers
standard_reference: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 11.6.1 / PCI Security Standards Council
summary: Requires deploying mechanisms to detect unauthorized changes and tampering of payment page scripts and security-impacting HTTP headers (CSP, HSTS) as rendered in the consumer's browser at least weekly or periodically as defined in targeted risk analysis.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Requirement 11.6.1 mandates change- and tamper-detection mechanisms to alert personnel to unauthorized modification to the HTTP headers and script contents of payment pages as received by the consumer browser. Security-impacting HTTP headers include Content-Security-Policy (CSP), Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), and X-Frame-Options. Tamper detection mechanisms include synthetic transaction monitoring, Content Security Policy reporting endpoints (report-uri / report-to), script hash verification, and DOM mutation auditing to prevent Magecart-style digital skimming. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app runtime architectures MUST implement proactive client-side tamper detection: (1) The container Webview injects a tamper-watchdog monitoring MutationObserver events on the payment document DOM; (2) Strict CSP violation reporting is wired directly to super-app SecOps telemetry pipelines; (3) Any detected deviation in script hashes or unexpected network exfiltration channels triggers immediate transaction abort and security incident logging.

title: PCI SSC SAQ A vs SAQ A-EP Architecture: Scoping Boundaries and Connected-to Intermediary Pages
standard_reference: PCI SSC Self-Assessment Questionnaire A (SAQ A) v4.0.1 / PCI SSC E-commerce Guidance
summary: Defines architectural scoping criteria distinguishing SAQ A (full outsourcing via isolated iframe/redirect) from SAQ A-EP (merchant-controlled scripts impacting payment rendering), establishing container segmentation best practices.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In January 2025, PCI SSC updated SAQ A for PCI DSS v4.0.1. While Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 remain fully mandatory in the underlying standard, SAQ A requires merchants to confirm that their site is not susceptible to script-based attacks that compromise payment systems. Merchants qualify for SAQ A only when all cardholder data functions are completely outsourced to a PCI DSS compliant Third-Party Service Provider (TPSP) via an isolated iframe or redirect. If merchant-controlled JavaScript creates or manipulates the payment iframe, or if scripts reside on the same DOM origin, the environment expands into SAQ A-EP, bringing the entire origin and all executing scripts into full PCI audit scope. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app architectures MUST enforce architectural descoping: (1) Mini-app merchant frontends MUST NOT instantiate direct payment input fields; (2) Checkout MUST transition to a super-app native payment sheet or a isolated TPSP sandbox iframe with sandbox='allow-scripts allow-forms' (explicitly omitting allow-same-origin and allow-top-navigation); (3) Merchant mini-apps remain strictly out-of-scope for card data, qualifying for simplified SAQ A compliance.

title: Client-Side Payment Defense: Subresource Integrity (SRI) and Strict CSP Level 3 Hash Governance
standard_reference: PCI SSC Payment Page Security Guidance / W3C CSP Level 3 & SRI
summary: Details cryptographic enforcement of script integrity using Subresource Integrity (integrity='sha384-...') and CSP script-src directives to satisfy PCI DSS 6.4.3 technical requirements.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Subresource Integrity (SRI) enables browsers to verify that resources fetched (such as payment SDK scripts) are delivered without unexpected manipulation. By pairing SRI ('integrity=sha384-...') with strict Content Security Policy ('script-src require-sri-for script' or nonce/hash-based 'strict-dynamic'), browsers reject executed scripts if a single byte is altered at rest or in transit. This cryptographically enforces Requirement 6.4.3's integrity assurance. Furthermore, CSP connect-src directives restrict unauthorized data exfiltration endpoints, thwarting form-jacking and memory-scraping payloads. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container gateways MUST: (1) Mandate SRI attributes on all external payment bridge scripts loaded in web-based checkout views; (2) Inject a strict Content-Security-Policy header restricting script-src to pre-approved origin hashes; (3) Prohibit 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' directives on all payment-related surfaces.

title: Super-App Native Payment Sheet vs Mini-App Context: Out-of-Process Payment Boundary Architecture
standard_reference: Super-App Architecture Pattern / PCI SSC E-commerce Guidance
summary: Establishes a hardened out-of-process native payment architecture that physically isolates merchant mini-app JavaScript runtime threads from sensitive payment authorization channels.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To eliminate client-side script tampering and achieve the highest level of regulatory segregation under PCI DSS v4.0.1, leading super-apps decouple the mini-app runtime from payment collection. Instead of embedding payment iframes inside the mini-app's DOM, the mini-app invokes a native JSAPI (e.g., 'superApp.requestPayment(orderPayload)'). The container intercepts this call, suspends mini-app rendering, and presents a dedicated, tamper-proof native bottom sheet or isolated process payment modal. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store compliance policies MUST mandate: (1) Zero direct cardholder data entry in mini-app webviews; (2) All payments must resolve via the platform's unified payment gateway JSAPI; (3) The native payment sheet executes in an independent OS process with memory encryption, completely out of reach of mini-app DOM introspection, prototype poisoning, or event sniffing; (4) The super-app payment gateway handles tokenization, 3-D Secure 2.0 biometric verification, and bank reconciliation.

title: RFC 9842 Compression Dictionary Transport: 'Use-As-Dictionary' Response Header Semantics and URLPattern Matching
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9842 Section 2.1 (Use-As-Dictionary) / IETF HTTP Working Group
summary: Specifies the 'Use-As-Dictionary' HTTP response header, establishing how origin servers designate cacheable responses as compression dictionaries for future matching requests via URLPattern rules.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 9842 defines the 'Use-As-Dictionary' response header, formatted as an RFC 8941 Structured Field Dictionary. It supports four core parameters: (1) 'match' (mandatory string providing a URLPattern path match without regular expressions); (2) 'match-dest' (optional inner list of Fetch RequestDestinations, such as 'script', 'style', 'document'); (3) 'id' (optional opaque server identifier up to 1024 characters); and (4) 'type' (token indicating dictionary format, defaulting to 'raw'). To prevent cross-origin leaks, the dictionary and future target requests MUST share the exact same origin, and compression dictionary transport is strictly restricted to secure contexts (HTTPS). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app distribution CDNs MUST deploy 'Use-As-Dictionary' on core runtime packages: (1) When a mini-app downloads its baseline framework bundle (e.g., 'framework.v1.0.js'), the CDN response sets 'Use-As-Dictionary: match="/app/*/bundle.js", match-dest=("script"), id="framework-v1-0"'; (2) Container cache engines store this payload in an indexed dictionary cache keyed by origin and URLPattern.

title: Client-Side Dictionary Advertisement: 'Available-Dictionary' SHA-256 Hashes and 'Dictionary-ID' Synchronization
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9842 Section 2.2 & 2.3 / IETF HTTP Working Group
summary: Specifies the client request headers 'Available-Dictionary' and 'Dictionary-ID', enabling user agents to advertise available local dictionaries to origin servers using cryptographic SHA-256 byte digests.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a client requests a resource matching a stored dictionary's 'match' and 'match-dest' criteria, it transmits an 'Available-Dictionary' header containing an RFC 8941 Byte Sequence with the SHA-256 hash of the local dictionary bytes (e.g., 'Available-Dictionary: :pZGm1Av0...FG4=:'). If the dictionary was established with an 'id' parameter, the client also echoes 'Dictionary-ID: "..."'. The server must validate the hash before compressing. When multiple dictionaries match a request, RFC 9842 Section 2.2.3 mandates deterministic precedence: (1) matching 'match-dest' takes precedence over wildcards; (2) longest 'match' URL string takes precedence; (3) most recently fetched dictionary wins ties. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app package loaders MUST implement RFC 9842 client negotiation: (1) The container package manager inspects local cache for previously unpacked mini-app version n-1; (2) When fetching version n updates, the container sends 'Available-Dictionary' with version n-1's SHA-256 hash; (3) The CDN edge immediately recognizes the delta baseline without requiring complex bespoke patch protocols.

title: Negotiated Dictionary Encodings: Shared Brotli ('dcb') and Shared Zstandard ('dcz') Algorithms
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9842 Section 6 (Negotiating Content Encoding) & IANA HTTP Field Registry
summary: Establishes content-encoding tokens 'dcb' (Dictionary-compressed Brotli) and 'dcz' (Dictionary-compressed Zstandard), providing order-of-magnitude bandwidth reduction over standard gzip/br compression.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 9842 registers two standard dictionary-aware content encodings with IANA: 'dcb' (Shared Brotli, RFC 7932) and 'dcz' (Shared Zstandard, RFC 8878). When an available dictionary is advertised, the client appends 'dcb, dcz' to its 'Accept-Encoding' header (e.g., 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd, dcb, dcz'). If the server compresses the response using the indicated dictionary, it returns 'Content-Encoding: dcb' (or 'dcz') and MUST include 'Vary: Available-Dictionary' to prevent intermediate proxy cache pollution. Because external dictionaries provide extensive shared symbol tables and pre-existing code tokens, compression efficiency increases dramatically compared to standalone Brotli. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app CDN release pipelines MUST enable 'dcb' and 'dcz' encoders: (1) Mini-app JavaScript bundles compressed against standard host SDK dictionaries achieve 85% to 92% size reduction; (2) Mobile client runtime decoders leverage hardware-accelerated Zstandard and Brotli shared-memory buffers, cutting mobile cold-start download times from seconds to under 150ms on 3G/4G networks.

title: Proactive Cache Warming: The 'compression-dictionary' Link Relation Type (<link rel='compression-dictionary'>)
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9842 Section 3 (Link Relation Type) / IANA Link Relations
summary: Defines the 'compression-dictionary' link relation type allowing HTML documents and HTTP Link headers to proactively trigger background prefetching and caching of external compression dictionaries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 9842 Section 3 establishes the standard link relation type 'compression-dictionary' (registered in the IANA Link Relations Registry). Origin servers advertise dictionaries via the HTTP response header 'Link: </dict/app-shared.dict>; rel="compression-dictionary"' or via HTML '<link rel="compression-dictionary" href="/dict/app-shared.dict">'. When encountered, the user agent schedules an idle background fetch for the dictionary resource. The fetched response must include valid 'Use-As-Dictionary' directives and standard caching headers (e.g. Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable) to be stored in the dictionary cache for subsequent navigation requests. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store catalog pages MUST utilize proactive dictionary warming: (1) When a user browses a store category (e.g., e-commerce mini-apps), the catalog view issues 'Link: rel="compression-dictionary"' for the common e-commerce UI component dictionary; (2) The container downloads and commits the dictionary during idle network cycles; (3) When the user subsequently launches any individual mini-app within that category, subsequent chunk downloads immediately benefit from 90% delta compression.

title: Super-App Incremental Release Architecture: Delta Package Streaming via Shared Runtime Dictionaries
standard_reference: Super-App Release Standard / IETF RFC 9842
summary: Establishes a standardized super-app delta packaging pipeline using RFC 9842 Shared Brotli/Zstandard dictionaries, eliminating proprietary diffing daemons while slashing cellular data consumption.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Traditional mobile super-apps often rely on proprietary binary diff utilities (such as bsdiff or custom zip patchers) to deliver mini-app updates, creating brittle container dependencies, risk of memory corruption during patching, and complex cache invalidation. RFC 9842 standardizes dictionary-based delta transport natively over HTTP. By designating the existing installed version bundle as the dictionary ('Use-As-Dictionary: match="/miniapp/1004/*"') or pre-installing a standardized super-app framework dictionary directly into the native host app assets ('asset://shared-dict.bin'), all remote updates behave as standard HTTP GET requests with transparent edge decompression. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store packaging guidelines MUST mandate: (1) Host containers expose the pre-installed super-app JS SDK as a local registered dictionary; (2) Developer CI/CD pipelines compile mini-app production builds against the official SDK dictionary; (3) Incremental subpackage updates are capped at <50KB transfer size across cellular networks, ensuring sub-second over-the-air hot updates.

title: W3C CSS View Transitions Level 2: Cross-Document Navigations via '@view-transition' Rule and Render-Blocking Controls
standard_reference: W3C CSS View Transitions Module Level 2 Section 2 (Cross-document view transitions)
summary: Standardizes declarative cross-document animations between distinct same-origin web documents using the '@view-transition { navigation: auto; }' CSS rule and render-blocking synchronization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSS View Transitions Level 2 extends the View Transition API to multi-page architectures (cross-document navigations). To activate cross-document view transitions: (1) Both the outbound and inbound documents must belong to the exact same origin; (2) Both documents must opt in via the '@view-transition { navigation: auto; }' CSS rule; (3) The navigation must be user-initiated or a session history traversal (excluding URL-bar typing and cross-origin redirects); (4) The document must remain visible throughout the transition. Unlike SPA transitions governed by JavaScript callback promises, cross-document transitions leverage the browser's render-blocking mechanism (<link rel='expect' blocking='render'>) to ensure the inbound DOM is stabilized before snapshot capture. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app multi-page mini-app runtimes MUST support declarative transitions: (1) Container webviews enable the '@view-transition' CSS rule by default; (2) Mini-app page-to-page transitions must declare standard view transition animations (such as slide-left, push, or fade); (3) Container watchdogs enforce a strict 300ms maximum transition animation ceiling to prevent frozen UI states during slow network navigations.

title: Cross-Document View Transition Lifecycle: Window 'pageswap' and 'pagereveal' Event Orchestration
standard_reference: W3C CSS View Transitions Module Level 2 / MDN Web APIs (PageSwapEvent & PageRevealEvent)
summary: Specifies the dual-event lifecycle governing cross-document transitions: 'pageswap' on the outbound unloading document and 'pagereveal' on the inbound rendering document.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Cross-document view transitions introduce two complementary Window lifecycle events: (1) 'pageswap' fires on the outbound window immediately before document unload, exposing 'event.viewTransition' and 'event.activation' (with navigation type and destination URL). Authors use 'pageswap' to tag active elements with dynamic 'view-transition-name' properties and configure transition types before snapshots are frozen; (2) 'pagereveal' fires on the inbound window immediately before its first rendering opportunity. The inbound document accesses 'event.viewTransition' to inspect parameters, assign matching 'view-transition-name' properties to inbound DOM nodes, or invoke 'skipTransition()' if navigation conditions changed. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app navigation routers MUST integrate with 'pageswap' and 'pagereveal': (1) Mini-app list-to-detail views utilize 'pageswap' to capture the tapped product card thumbnail; (2) 'pagereveal' pairs the incoming detail hero image to the tapped thumbnail, achieving native-tier shared element transitions; (3) The container automatically cleans up dynamic 'view-transition-name' inline styles upon transition completion to prevent back-forward cache (BFCache) naming collisions.

title: Selective Transitions and 'view-transition-class': Reusable Styling and Collision-Free Animation Scoping
standard_reference: W3C CSS View Transitions Module Level 2 Section 3 & 4 (Selective Transitions & view-transition-class)
summary: Introduces 'view-transition-class' and active transition types (':active-view-transition-type()') to allow reusable animation styles across hundreds of dynamic DOM items without requiring unique per-element CSS rules.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In Level 1, every animated element required a unique 'view-transition-name' and dedicated CSS pseudo-element selectors (e.g. '::view-transition-group(item-1)'), resulting in massive CSS bloat for long lists. Level 2 solves this by introducing 'view-transition-class: <ident>'. A single CSS rule (e.g., '::view-transition-group(.card-item)') applies styles to any captured pseudo-element whose DOM node has that class. Additionally, Level 2 introduces selective transitions via 'viewTransition.types.add("back-transition")' and the CSS selector ':active-view-transition-type(back-transition)', enabling completely different animations for forward vs backward navigation. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app UI design systems MUST adopt 'view-transition-class': (1) Component libraries (buttons, modal dialogs, product grids) define standardized transition classes; (2) Mini-apps applying these classes inherit fluid, 60fps GPU-accelerated transition animations without custom CSS keyframes; (3) The container platform enforces ':active-view-transition-type(slide-back)' when Android Predictive Back or iOS swipe-back gestures are detected.

title: W3C Audio Session API: Operating System Audio Focus Arbitration and Audio Session Types
standard_reference: W3C Audio Session Specification / W3C Audio Working Group
summary: Defines the 'navigator.audioSession' interface for communicating audio intent ('auto', 'playback', 'transient', 'play-and-record', 'ambient') to the underlying mobile operating system audio focus manager.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Audio Session API introduces 'navigator.audioSession', representing the document's audio session parameters mapped directly to mobile OS audio focus managers (such as Android AudioManager and iOS AVAudioSession). The 'type' attribute supports: (1) 'auto' (default UA policy); (2) 'playback' (continuous audio playback, pauses other background media); (3) 'transient' (short alert sounds or sound effects, mixing or ducking existing media without permanent focus loss); (4) 'transient-solo' (short alerts pausing background media); (5) 'ambient' (non-essential sound effects, silenced when device hardware mute switch is engaged); (6) 'play-and-record' (bidirectional audio communication, routing to microphone and earpiece/speaker). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store audio governance MUST enforce strict audio session type declarations: (1) Casual gaming mini-apps MUST set 'type = ambient', ensuring in-game sound effects do not hijack or stop user background podcast/music playback; (2) VoIP and conference mini-apps must declare 'play-and-record' and release focus immediately upon call termination; (3) Mini-apps violating audio etiquette (e.g. playing ads with 'playback' focus) face automated policy rejection.

title: Audio Interruption Resilience: 'onstatechange' Event Handling, Hardware Mute Synchronization, and Ducking
standard_reference: W3C Audio Session Specification Section 5 & 9 / W3C Media Working Group
summary: Specifies audio interruption state handling via the 'statechange' event ('active', 'inactive', 'interrupted'), establishing graceful recovery protocols for incoming calls and container audio ducking.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When high-priority system audio events occur (such as incoming cellular calls, alarm clocks, or voice navigation prompts), the mobile operating system suspends application audio focus. The Audio Session API reflects this by updating 'navigator.audioSession.state' to 'interrupted' and firing an 'onstatechange' event. Well-behaved applications must pause media playback pipelines, suspend AudioContext nodes to avoid wasting CPU cycles, and update UI state. When the interruption clears, the state transitions back to 'active', allowing the application to resume playback seamlessly if desired. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app multimedia certification criteria MUST mandate: (1) All audio-capable mini-apps implement 'navigator.audioSession.addEventListener("statechange", ...)'; (2) Upon 'interrupted' state, mini-apps must cleanly freeze audio synthesis and video playback; (3) AudioContext instances MUST call 'ctx.suspend()' when interrupted to prevent battery drain in background threads; (4) Super-app host container enforces transient audio ducking (reducing mini-app audio volume by 80%) whenever super-app voice assistants or push alerts chime.

title: WICG Topics API: Ephemeral, Coarse-Grained On-Device Interest Personalization Without Covert Fingerprinting
standard_reference: WICG Topics API / MDN Web APIs Topics API
summary: Replaces third-party tracking cookies with an on-device, privacy-preserving topic classification system where the browser/host calculates interest categories without transmitting browsing history.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Topics API provides a privacy-preserving mechanism for interest-based advertising without tracking user activity across disparate websites. The browser or host runtime maps page hostnames to a public, curated taxonomy of coarse categories (e.g., 'Fitness', 'Travel', 'Consumer Electronics'). At the end of each weekly epoch, the device calculates the user's top five topics based on browsing frequency, plus one random topic drawn with 5% probability to provide differential privacy and plausible deniability. Topics are retained for three epochs (weeks) before deletion. A caller (relying party) can observe a topic only if that caller was active on a site associated with that topic during the epoch. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app ad networks and recommendation engines MUST migrate from legacy fingerprinting/IMEI/UUID tracking to the Topics API: (1) Container webviews gate topic retrieval via 'browsing-topics' Permissions Policy; (2) Mini-app callers access topics via 'document.browsingTopics()' or HTTP request header 'Sec-Browsing-Topics'; (3) Super-app analytics gateways audit topic taxonomy access to ensure mini-apps cannot synthesize cross-epoch fingerprint graphs.

title: JavaScript Interface 'document.browsingTopics()': Observation, Filtering, and Epoch Rotation Governance
standard_reference: WICG Topics API Section 3 (Browsing Topics JavaScript Interface) / MDN Document.browsingTopics
summary: Specifies the client-side JavaScript method 'document.browsingTopics({skipObservation: boolean})' returning a Promise resolving to an array of Topic objects.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'document.browsingTopics()' method returns a promise resolving to an array of objects representing the caller's observable topics for the past three completed epochs. Each Topic object exposes: 'configVersion' (taxonomy and classifier model version), 'modelVersion' (ML classifier model identifier), 'taxonomyVersion' (standardized taxonomy integer), 'topic' (integer ID mapping to human-readable taxonomy), and 'version' (composite execution string). Passing '{skipObservation: true}' allows ad bidders to inspect current topics without recording the current page visit as an observation event, preventing unintended topic dilution during background prefetching. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app container runtimes MUST implement structured filtering for 'document.browsingTopics()': (1) Unauthenticated or guest mini-apps receive empty arrays; (2) Store review validates that mini-apps declare their intention to read topics in 'manifest.json' under 'privacy_sandbox.topics: true'; (3) If user engages 'Private Browsing / Incognito' mode in the super-app, 'document.browsingTopics()' immediately returns empty promises, guaranteeing total isolation from stored user personas.

title: Topics Taxonomy & Machine Learning Classification: Hierarchical Categorization and Sensitive Exclusion Policies
standard_reference: Chrome Privacy Sandbox Topics Classification Architecture / WICG Topics Taxonomy
summary: Establishes a human-curated hierarchical taxonomy of topics that strictly excludes sensitive categories (health, race, religion, sexual orientation, financial distress).
detail: [SPEC FACT] Topics classification operates using a public, versioned hierarchical taxonomy (Taxonomy v2 contains ~469 topics). Classification uses a lightweight client-side TensorFlow Lite model or static domain mapping table. Crucially, the taxonomy design enforces absolute exclusion of sensitive categories defined by GDPR Article 9 and international privacy regulations: topics related to medical conditions, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, and sexual orientation are prohibited from ever existing in the taxonomy. If a mini-app domain cannot be classified or belongs to an unmapped niche, it is categorized under generic parent categories or excluded entirely. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app marketplace catalog taxonomy MUST align with the Privacy Sandbox taxonomy: (1) Mini-app categories declared in the developer portal map directly to standardized topic IDs; (2) Sensitive mini-app categories (telemedicine, religious devotion, political discourse, debt relief) are marked as 'no-topics' origins, exempting them from classification and observation; (3) Host runtime blocks any attempt by ad SDKs to infer sensitive health/financial status from adjacent non-sensitive topic clusters.

title: HTTP Header-Based Topic Negotiation: 'Sec-Browsing-Topics' and 'Observe-Browsing-Topics' Network Flow
standard_reference: WICG Topics API HTTP Fetch Integration / Fetch Standard Sec-Browsing-Topics
summary: Defines out-of-band declarative topic negotiation via HTTP request/response headers, enabling low-latency ad bidding without client-side script execution overhead.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In addition to the JavaScript DOM API, the Topics API integrates natively into HTTP network fetch requests. A developer or ad partner initiates a request with 'fetch(url, {browsingTopics: true})' or declares '<iframe src="..." browsingtopics>'. The browser calculates eligible topics and appends the 'Sec-Browsing-Topics' request header containing structured comma-separated topic IDs. If the server wishes to register an observation event on the user, it responds with the 'Observe-Browsing-Topics: ?1' HTTP response header. This header handshake completely decouples topic delivery from DOM JavaScript execution, saving critical main-thread compute. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app network proxies and webview resource interceptors MUST govern 'Sec-Browsing-Topics' propagation: (1) Container ensures 'Sec-Browsing-Topics' is stripped from requests to external cross-origin domains unless explicitly allowlisted in the mini-app manifest; (2) Host network layer throttles and inspects 'Observe-Browsing-Topics: ?1' responses to prevent ad aggregators from flooding observation history; (3) Header injection is strictly forbidden during payment or KYC authentication flows.

title: Store Privacy Governance: 'browsing-topics' Permissions Policy Delegation and Transparent User Opt-Out
standard_reference: WICG Topics API Security & Privacy Considerations / W3C Permissions Policy 'browsing-topics'
summary: Establishes container-level Permissions Policy controls ('browsing-topics=(self "https://ad.example")') and native super-app settings allowing end users to inspect, block, or reset calculated topics.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Topics API is strictly gated by the W3C Permissions Policy feature identifier 'browsing-topics'. Top-level documents control delegation to embedded iframes and third-party scripts via HTTP header 'Permissions-Policy: browsing-topics=()' to disable topics entirely, or 'browsing-topics=(self)' to restrict topics to first-party code. Furthermore, privacy standards mandate that user agents provide accessible user controls displaying the active list of calculated topics, enabling users to remove specific unwanted topics or disable the API completely, resetting observation state across all epochs. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store privacy controls MUST provide native transparency tools: (1) Super-app Privacy Settings panel contains an 'Ad Interests & Topics' dashboard visualizing currently active topics; (2) Users can delete individual topics or toggle global ad personalization off; (3) Mini-app manifest allows developers to declare 'browsing_topics: false' to opt their entire mini-app out of observation by external SDKs; (4) Super-app security scanner flags mini-apps attempting to bypass Permissions Policy restrictions via side-channel storage.

title: W3C CSS Color Module Level 4: Wide-Color-Gamut 'color(display-p3 r g b)' and sRGB Boundary Expansion
standard_reference: W3C CSS Color Module Level 4 Section 10 (Specifying Colors in Predefined Color Spaces)
summary: Standardizes the 'color(display-p3 ...)' functional notation, expanding color reproduction by ~50% over sRGB to leverage modern OLED, mini-LED, and mobile display hardware.
detail: [SPEC FACT] CSS Color 4 introduces the 'color()' function allowing authoring in predefined color spaces beyond standard sRGB, prominently 'display-p3', 'a98-rgb', 'prophoto-rgb', and 'rec2020'. The Display P3 color space, native to modern Apple Retina and Android OLED screens, covers a significantly wider green-red gamut (approx. 50% larger volume than sRGB). In CSS Color 4, coordinates are authored as unitless percentages or floats between 0 and 1 (e.g. 'color(display-p3 1 0.1 0.2)'). When rendered on wide-gamut hardware, UI elements achieve hyper-vibrant brand colors that sRGB physically cannot represent. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app design systems and asset compilers MUST support Display P3: (1) Store UI library exports brand tokens with Display P3 fallbacks; (2) Mini-app asset upload pipelines accept wide-gamut SVG/PNGs without downsampling color profiles to sRGB; (3) Container webviews enable wide-color rendering buffers on supported hardware without incurring double-conversion color banding.

title: W3C CSS Color 4 'oklch()' Functional Notation: Perceptually Uniform Palette Generation and Accessible Contrast
standard_reference: W3C CSS Color Module Level 4 Section 8 (Perceptually Uniform Color Spaces: OKLab and OKLCH)
summary: Specifies 'oklch(L C H [/ A])' (Lightness, Chroma, Hue, Alpha), providing a cylindrical color model with true perceptual uniformity for predictable UI theming and accessibility contrast.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Traditional cylindrical color models like HSL suffer from severe perceptual non-uniformity: yellow at 50% lightness appears blindingly bright while blue at 50% lightness is dark and illegible. CSS Color 4 standardizes OKLCH (Lightness 0-1 or 0-100%, Chroma 0-0.4+, Hue 0-360deg), created by Björn Ottosson. In OKLCH, perceived lightness is mathematically decoupled from hue and chroma. Changing hue across a 360-degree wheel maintains identical perceived luminance, allowing algorithmic generation of UI state themes (hover, focus, disabled, active) and guaranteed contrast ratios without manual tuning per color. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app design systems MUST mandate OKLCH for dynamic theming: (1) Host container's dark/light mode engine uses OKLCH arithmetic to generate consistent contrast tokens; (2) Automated store accessibility scanners evaluate mini-app WCAG 2.2 AA contrast ratios using OKLCH perceived lightness values; (3) Dynamic color themes injected into mini-app CSS custom properties adhere to predictable Chroma ceilings to prevent gamut clipping.

title: Media Query '@media (color-gamut)': Progressive Enhancement for Wide-Gamut Hardware Displays
standard_reference: W3C Media Queries Level 4 / CSS Color Module Level 4 / MDN @media/color-gamut
summary: Enables responsive CSS styling based on the display hardware's color gamut support ('srgb', 'p3', 'rec2020'), ensuring backward compatibility without color distortion.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The '@media (color-gamut: ...)' media feature queries the range of colors supported by the user agent and output device. Values include: (1) 'srgb' (supported by nearly all displays); (2) 'p3' (supported by modern mobile flagships, tablets, and creative laptops); (3) 'rec2020' (ultra-wide gamut, professional broadcast monitors). Authors progressively enhance graphics by serving standard sRGB rules first, enclosed by '@media (color-gamut: p3) { ... }' or '@supports (color: color(display-p3 1 1 1)) { ... }' for wide-gamut devices. This prevents older screens from clipping vibrant colors or producing muddy, out-of-gamut banding.
