Crucially: (1) Methods 'readAsArrayBuffer()', 'readAsText()', and 'readAsDataURL()' operate asynchronously, emitting 'loadstart', 'progress', 'load', 'error', and 'loadend' events; (2) The 'progress' event provides verifiable 'loaded' and 'total' byte counters enabling reliable progress visualization; (3) Reading can be cleanly aborted via 'abort()', freeing underlying buffer allocations; (4) Large data reads via 'readAsDataURL()' introduce severe memory overhead (base64 ~33% bloat) which can cause Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes in mobile webviews. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDKs and store review scanners MUST enforce safe binary ingestion: (1) Mini-apps processing media files over 10MB MUST use 'readAsArrayBuffer()' or streaming ReadableStreams rather than 'readAsDataURL()'; (2) Automated store static analyzers flag excessive base64 serialization in mini-app codebases; (3) Long-running file ingestion must attach 'abort()' handlers tied to page lifecycle unload events.

title: W3C URL.createObjectURL & URL.revokeObjectURL: Blob URL Lifecycle & Memory Deallocation Governance
standard_reference: W3C File API Specification Section 8 (URL for Blob and File Objects)
summary: Governs the minting and lifecycle of 'blob:https://...' URLs via 'URL.createObjectURL' and enforces deterministic memory reclamation via 'URL.revokeObjectURL'.
detail: [SPEC FACT] 'URL.createObjectURL(blob)' generates a unique, opaque URI with the 'blob:' scheme bound to the document's origin (e.g. 'blob:https://example.com/uuid'). The underlying binary Blob data is retained in memory by the browser engine for the entire lifetime of the creating document until explicitly revoked via 'URL.revokeObjectURL(url)'. In single-page applications and long-lived mini-apps, failure to invoke 'revokeObjectURL' after displaying an image, audio clip, or document leads to massive memory leaks, eventually causing the host OS to terminate the webview process via low-memory kills (OOM). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app container frameworks MUST implement deterministic Blob URL lifecycle management: (1) Host container hooks 'URL.createObjectURL' and maintains an origin-scoped registry of active Blob URLs; (2) Mini-app runtime automatically revokes temporary object URLs when the presenting component unmounts or navigates away; (3) Store dynamic scanners audit memory retention curves, flagging any mini-app that retains unrevoked Blob URLs across view transitions.

title: W3C Blob.slice(): Zero-Copy Binary Chunking, Resilient Multi-Part Uploads & Memory Ceilings
standard_reference: W3C File API Specification Section 3.2 (The slice method)
summary: Specifies 'Blob.slice(start, end, contentType)' enabling zero-copy sub-chunking of massive files, providing the foundation for resilient chunked uploads and media streaming.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'Blob.slice([start, [end, [contentType]]])' method returns a new Blob object containing data in the specified byte range of the source Blob. Crucially, the slice operation creates an immutable view/slice over the underlying storage without eagerly duplicating binary bytes in memory (zero-copy pointer offset). This allows applications running in constrained environments (such as mobile webviews with 128MB RAM limits) to partition multi-gigabyte video or backup archives into uniform 1MB-5MB chunks for reliable, resumable HTTP chunked uploads or incremental cryptographic hashing without triggering memory exhaustion. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app developer SDKs and upload bridges MUST leverage Blob slicing: (1) Mini-app upload utilities chunk large media assets (>10MB) into uniform 2MB slices; (2) Each slice is transmitted with cryptographic digests (RFC 9530 Content-Digest) and byte-range offsets, enabling resumption after network drops; (3) Host memory watchdogs verify that binary chunking does not allocate redundant duplicate heap buffers.

title: W3C File API Security Considerations: Cross-Origin Leakage, File System Masking & Origin Isolation
standard_reference: W3C File API Specification Section 10 (Security and Privacy Considerations)
summary: Mandates strict origin isolation for Blob URLs, total masking of underlying host filesystem directory hierarchies, and defense against cross-origin file resource theft.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Section 10 of the W3C File API details critical security and privacy considerations: (1) Path masking: User agents MUST NOT disclose full underlying system path structures (e.g. /home/user/... or C:\Windows\...) in File.name or any exposed metadata, as path structures reveal operating systems, user identities, and directory layouts; (2) Origin isolation: A 'blob:origin/uuid' URL must only be fetchable by contexts sharing the exact same origin as the creating context; (3) Cross-origin access: If an image or media element loads a Blob URL from another origin, CORS must be enforced, or the request fails; (4) Drag-and-drop / picker isolation: File handles granted via user selection must be restricted strictly to the chosen files, preventing directory traversal attacks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app containers MUST enforce strict File API security boundaries: (1) File picker bridges sanitize all returned File objects, truncating paths to basename only; (2) Host webview security managers block cross-mini-app access to Blob URLs minted by other applications; (3) Storage sandboxing guarantees that mini-app file caches remain completely isolated on disk.

title: WICG HTML Sanitizer API: Native Browser-Driven DOM XSS Elimination & Safe HTML Parsing
standard_reference: WICG Sanitizer API Specification (Living Document)
summary: Specifies native browser-level HTML parsing and sanitization via 'new Sanitizer()' and 'Element.setHTML()', replacing vulnerable userland regex/DOMPurify libraries with engine-native C++ DOM tree sanitization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG Sanitizer API introduces a native browser primitive to eliminate DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS). Unlike userland libraries (e.g. DOMPurify) that parse strings into intermediate detached DOM trees susceptible to parser-mutation XSS (mXSS) and bypasses, the Sanitizer API operates directly within the browser's HTML parser pipeline. Invoking 'element.setHTML(untrustedString, { sanitizer: new Sanitizer() })' strips executable scripts (<script>), inline event handlers (onload, onerror, onclick), dangerous protocol schemes (javascript:, data:text/html), and hazardous elements (<object>, <embed>, <iframe>) by default. The API allows configurable allowlists and blocklists for elements, attributes, and comments, providing deterministic, engine-enforced memory safety. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app developer frameworks and container WebViews MUST enforce the Sanitizer API: (1) Deprecate and audit raw 'innerHTML' and 'outerHTML' assignments in mini-app templates, migrating all dynamic rendering to 'Element.setHTML()'; (2) Container bridge injects polyfilled/native Sanitizer configurations matching store security baselines; (3) Static review scanners reject mini-app packages invoking raw DOM injection sinks unless guarded by verified Sanitizer instances.

title: SanitizerConfig: Granular Element, Attribute, and Namespace Filtering Controls
standard_reference: WICG Sanitizer API Section 2 (The Sanitizer Interface & Configuration)
summary: Defines SanitizerConfig dictionary structures ('elements', 'removeElements', 'attributes', 'removeAttributes') allowing host platforms to tailor safe HTML subsets for rich-text mini-app content.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'Sanitizer' constructor accepts a 'SanitizerConfig' object defining precise sanitization rules: 'elements' (allowlist of allowed tag names), 'removeElements' (blocklist of tags stripped along with their children), 'dropElements' (strips tags while preserving text children), 'attributes' (per-element or global attribute allowlists), and 'removeAttributes' (attribute blocklists). Furthermore, the configuration explicitly strips dangerous SVG/MathML script execution vectors and protects namespace boundaries. Unknown or non-standard HTML elements are safely dropped or escaped depending on configuration flags. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST define standard platform Sanitizer profiles: (1) 'StoreStrictProfile': allows only structural and formatting tags (p, div, span, b, i, ul, li, a[href=https]), dropping all forms, embeds, and dynamic nodes for user reviews and publisher descriptions; (2) 'StoreRichTextProfile': permits media tags (img[src=https], video[controls]) with mandatory HTTPS URL sanitization and responsive styling attributes; (3) Mini-app review pipeline validates that mini-apps do not override default sanitizer configs to re-enable executable event handlers.

title: Element.setHTML(): Safe In-Place DOM Replacement & Parser-Mutation (mXSS) Defense
standard_reference: WICG Sanitizer API Section 3 (Extensions to the Element Interface)
summary: Establishes 'Element.setHTML(input, options)' as the standardized replacement for innerHTML, performing parsing, sanitization, and tree insertion in a single atomic, mutation-proof browser step.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In traditional web architectures, calling 'element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(input)' involves a multi-stage workflow: parsing string to DOM, serializing back to string, and re-parsing into the target element. Attackers exploit subtle differences between the parsing contexts (e.g. mathematical markup, foreign elements, malformed comments) to execute parser-mutation XSS (mXSS). 'Element.setHTML(input, { sanitizer })' completely neutralizes mXSS by performing string tokenization, tree construction, sanitization filtering, and live document insertion in a single unified C++ pass directly within the target element's actual parsing context. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app container engines MUST: (1) Expose 'Element.setHTML()' natively in container WebViews (Chromium / Gecko / WebKit); (2) Combine 'setHTML' with W3C Trusted Types ('require-trusted-types-for script') to ensure that raw string assignment to legacy sinks is rejected with runtime TypeError exceptions; (3) Provide automated code transform utilities in mini-app CLI build tools that rewrite legacy 'innerHTML' calls to 'setHTML'.

title: Document.parseHTML(): Detached Safe Fragment Parsing & Off-DOM Content Inspection
standard_reference: WICG Sanitizer API Section 4 (Extensions to Document and DocumentFragment)
summary: Specifies 'Document.parseHTML(input, options)' returning a sanitized DocumentFragment, allowing off-DOM manipulation and inspection before layout or node attachment.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Sanitizer specification provides 'Document.parseHTML(input, { sanitizer })' which returns a sanitized 'DocumentFragment' rather than inserting directly into an attached DOM node. This enables complex mini-app components (e.g. virtualized lists, template renderers, rich-text markdown previewers) to inspect, traverse, and transform nodes (such as rewriting outbound links or verifying image dimensions) in an inert, off-screen fragment without triggering premature network requests, layout recalculations, or security side-effects. Nodes within the returned fragment are guaranteed free from active scripts or unauthorized attributes. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app frameworks MUST utilize 'Document.parseHTML()' for pre-rendering pipelines: (1) Virtualized feed components parse external markdown/HTML payloads into DocumentFragments, validating layout constraints prior to mounting; (2) Inbound content scanners verify node counts and nesting depths to defend against deeply nested DOM Denial-of-Service (DOM DoS) attacks; (3) All image links within the parsed fragment are validated against the super-app's CSP image domain allowlist before insertion into the active document.

title: Sanitizer API & W3C Trusted Types Interoperability: Defense-in-Depth Injection Architecture
standard_reference: WICG Sanitizer API Section 6 (Interaction with Content Security Policy and Trusted Types)
summary: Defines the integration between the Sanitizer API and W3C Trusted Types, allowing TrustedTypePolicy factories to return sanitized HTML strings and satisfying strict CSP injection policies.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a super-app container enforces strict Content Security Policy directives ('require-trusted-types-for script'), assigning raw strings to any DOM sink throws a CSP violation exception. The Sanitizer API is architected to seamlessly interoperate with Trusted Types. Developers can construct a default Trusted Types policy that routes untrusted strings through 'new Sanitizer().sanitizeToString(input)' (or uses 'Element.setHTML()'), creating a cryptographically attested, type-safe path from untrusted network payloads to the DOM. This dual-layer defense-in-depth architecture ensures that even if a developer inadvertently attempts a string assignment, the Trusted Types enforcement blocks execution unless routed through the verified Sanitizer pipeline. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store compliance policies MUST mandate: (1) Host container injects a pre-configured, immutable 'TrustedHTML' default policy backed by the engine Sanitizer API; (2) Mini-app submissions targeting financial, health, or high-privilege transactional categories MUST activate 'require-trusted-types-for script'; (3) Automated review pipeline verifies zero raw string assignments to DOM sinks across all mini-app bundles.

title: WasmGC: Garbage-Collected Memory Primitives & Host V8/JavaScript Engine Integration
standard_reference: WebAssembly Garbage Collection (WasmGC) Specification (W3C WebAssembly Community Group)
summary: Standardizes managed heap objects ('struct', 'array', 'anyref') in WebAssembly, enabling languages with automatic memory management (Dart/Flutter, Kotlin, Java) to compile to Wasm while directly sharing the browser's native garbage collector.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebAssembly 1.0 was restricted to linear memory (untyped byte arrays), requiring languages with garbage collection (like Dart/Flutter or Kotlin Multiplatform) to ship their own complete GC runtime embedded inside the Wasm binary. This inflated binary footprints by 1MB-3MB, caused memory fragmentation, and introduced stop-the-world GC pauses that degraded frame rates. WasmGC introduces native GC types directly into WebAssembly bytecodes: 'struct' types for heterogeneous structured records, 'array' types for typed homogeneous buffers, and reference hierarchies rooted in 'anyref'/'eqref'. WasmGC modules allocate managed memory directly within the host JavaScript engine's native garbage collector (e.g. V8's Oilpan/Orinoco, JavaScriptCore), sharing heap tracing, generational collection, and memory compaction without overhead. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app container engines MUST enable WasmGC: (1) Flutter-based and Kotlin-based mini-app frameworks MUST compile to WasmGC targets rather than shipping embedded userland garbage collectors; (2) Mini-app startup latency benchmarks require sub-100ms initialization for WasmGC binaries; (3) Store package scanners verify that Wasm binaries utilize native WasmGC bytecodes to minimize bundle download footprints on mobile devices.

title: WasmGC Binary Footprint Reduction: Eliminating Redundant Runtime Overhead in Mobile Super-Apps
standard_reference: Chrome Developers: WebAssembly Garbage Collection (WasmGC) Technical Analysis
summary: Documents the 60-70% payload compression and 2x cold-start acceleration achieved by compiling modern mini-apps (Flutter web, Kotlin Wasm) directly to WasmGC, removing duplicated memory managers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Production benchmarks from Chrome and Flutter teams demonstrate that compiling Dart/Flutter applications to WasmGC reduces gzipped bundle sizes by up to 60-70% compared to legacy js_of_wasm or emscripten-compiled GC runtimes. Startup performance improves up to 2x because the host engine can tier-compile WasmGC bytecodes incrementally (via Liftoff/TurboFan in V8) without parsing megabytes of polyfilled heap management code. Furthermore, memory footprint during execution decreases significantly because heap allocation cycles are synchronized with the host WebView's main garbage collection pipeline, preventing duplicate heap caching and out-of-memory crashes on resource-constrained mobile hardware. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app stores MUST enforce binary footprint guidelines: (1) Mini-app distribution bundles compiled from managed languages must leverage WasmGC optimization pipelines (e.g. 'dart compile wasm --optimization-level=4'); (2) Initial download bundle limit for Wasm mini-apps is capped at 4MB gzipped; (3) Automated review tooling runs differential bytecode analysis to ensure WasmGC instructions are utilized and redundant runtime code is stripped.

title: WasmGC Bidirectional JavaScript Interop: Zero-Copy Object Sharing & Fast Host Bridge Calls
standard_reference: V8 Engine Architecture: Porting Languages to WebAssembly Garbage Collection
summary: Establishes zero-copy bi-directional interoperability between WasmGC managed structs and JavaScript DOM/Host objects via 'externref' and typed casts, eliminating serialization overhead in bridge calls.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Traditional Wasm-to-JS bridge interactions required complex serialization schemes (such as passing strings or JSON through linear memory offsets via pointer-length pairs and UTF-8 decoders). This created massive CPU overhead when mini-apps interacted with host APIs, DOM nodes, or platform plugins. WasmGC introduces high-speed interoperability where JavaScript objects are passed directly into WebAssembly functions as 'externref', and WasmGC structs can be wrapped and exposed to JavaScript without copying. Type conversions are verified at the bytecode level via 'ref.cast' and 'ref.test' instructions. Cross-boundary function invocations execute at near-native C++ function pointer speeds. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host container SDKs MUST provide zero-copy WasmGC bridge bindings: (1) Host container APIs (biometrics, payments, location, storage) provide typed externref bindings for direct invocation from WasmGC mini-apps; (2) Mini-app SDKs eliminate JSON stringify/parse cycles for high-frequency bridge telemetry; (3) Host bridge security filters validate externref capabilities, preventing arbitrary memory reference leakage across mini-app boundaries.

title: WasmGC Type-Safe Memory Safety: Eliminating Pointer Arithmetic Vulnerabilities & Buffer Overflows
standard_reference: WebAssembly GC Security Model (Formal Type System & Memory Safety)
summary: Analyzes the formal type system of WasmGC which prohibits arbitrary pointer arithmetic on managed references, eliminating buffer overflows and use-after-free exploits in mini-app runtimes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In WebAssembly linear memory, unsafe languages (C/C++) can suffer from spatial and temporal memory safety issues (buffer overflows, heap corruption, use-after-free) within the 4GB linear memory boundary. While linear memory is isolated from the host OS, internal memory corruption can allow malicious payloads to hijack control flow inside the Wasm module. WasmGC completely eliminates this attack surface for managed code by enforcing a sound static type system. References to structs and arrays cannot be forged, cast to arbitrary integer memory addresses, or subjected to pointer arithmetic. Array accesses are guaranteed bounds-checked at runtime with hardware-accelerated traps. Managed objects are freed only when all references are dropped, preventing use-after-free conditions entirely. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app security architectures MUST prioritize WasmGC for untrusted third-party computational modules: (1) High-risk computational tasks (e.g. client-side financial calculations, cryptography preprocessing, document rendering) must compile to WasmGC targets to ensure memory safety; (2) Store submission pipeline verifies that WasmGC modules contain no unauthorized raw linear memory exports; (3) Host memory watchdogs monitor WasmGC allocation rates to prevent allocation-bomb denial of service.

title: Super-App Multi-Tenant Heap Governance: WasmGC Memory Quotas & OOM Watchdog Safeguards
standard_reference: V8 Engine Multi-Tenant Memory Isolation & WebAssembly Heap Boundaries
summary: Defines runtime memory limits, heap growth boundaries, and proactive garbage collection triggers for WasmGC mini-apps running concurrently within a mobile super-app host container.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When multiple mini-apps or background widgets run inside a single super-app host container, unconstrained heap allocations by a single rogue WasmGC module can starve host processes and trigger operating system Low-Memory Killer (LMK) events. Modern JavaScript engines provide mechanisms to isolate and monitor WasmGC heap consumption. By configuring isolate-level memory limits and instrumenting GC epilogue callbacks, host containers can track the live heap size of managed Wasm structures. If a mini-app's WasmGC heap exceeds pre-allocated tenant quotas (e.g. 64MB for lightweight micro-apps, 128MB for full mini-apps), the engine can trigger aggressive incremental garbage collection cycles, invoke cooperative downscaling, or safely terminate the misbehaving module. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app operational resilience standards MUST mandate: (1) Host container sets strict maximum heap allocations (max 128MB) for third-party WasmGC runtimes; (2) Backgrounded mini-apps trigger an immediate major GC sweep releasing unreferenced WasmGC structures; (3) Continuous telemetry monitors VRAM and RAM footprint, automatically flagging mini-apps exhibiting unbounded heap expansion in the developer dashboard.

title: WHATWG File System Living Standard: Origin Private File System (OPFS) Sandboxed Root & Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard Section 5 (Origin Private File System)
summary: Establishes 'navigator.storage.getDirectory()' providing a private, fully sandboxed, high-performance hierarchical filesystem for each mini-app origin, inaccessible to the user and other origins.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG File System standard defines the Origin Private File System (OPFS) accessed via 'navigator.storage.getDirectory()'. OPFS provides a dedicated, highly optimized directory hierarchy that is strictly origin-partitioned. Unlike public file pickers, the contents of OPFS are entirely invisible to the user and host operating system file managers, eliminating accidental user modification, malicious file tampering by neighboring apps, and path traversal vulnerabilities. OPFS operations are subject to standard browser storage quota management and origin eviction rules. The directory structure supports full asynchronous folder and file handle creation ('getDirectoryHandle', 'getFileHandle'), renaming, and deletion, providing a native POSIX-like foundation for client-side databases. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app storage architectures MUST enforce OPFS for application state: (1) All persistent transactional records, local databases (SQLite), and cached media MUST reside in the mini-app's OPFS sandbox; (2) Host container isolates OPFS disk directories per mini-app package ID; (3) Store compliance policies mandate that uninstalling or resetting a mini-app triggers an atomic purge of the associated OPFS directory structure.

title: FileSystemSyncAccessHandle: In-Worker Zero-Overhead Synchronous I/O for Embedded Engines
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard Section 7 (FileSystemSyncAccessHandle)
summary: Specifies synchronous in-place byte-level I/O methods ('read', 'write', 'truncate', 'flush') exclusively within Web Workers, providing raw disk access speeds without blocking the main UI thread.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standard Web APIs for disk storage rely on asynchronous Promises which introduce significant event-loop context-switching overhead and microtask queue latency, rendering them inadequate for high-performance database engines like SQLite. To solve this, the WHATWG File System standard introduces 'FileSystemSyncAccessHandle', created via 'FileSystemFileHandle.createSyncAccessHandle()'. This handle is strictly limited to Dedicated Web Workers. It provides synchronous read and write primitives ('read(buffer, options)', 'write(buffer, options)', 'truncate(newSize)', 'flush()') that map directly to underlying OS synchronous file descriptors (pread/pwrite/fsync). Opening a sync access handle acquires an exclusive OS-level file lock, preventing concurrent read/write races on the same file. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app database runtimes MUST adopt SyncAccessHandle architecture: (1) Client-side database engines (SQLite Wasm, DuckDB Wasm, LevelDB) MUST execute inside Dedicated Web Workers using 'FileSystemSyncAccessHandle'; (2) Exclusive file locking mechanisms must be handled gracefully with timeout safeguards preventing worker deadlocks; (3) Main UI thread must remain 100% free from storage I/O, preserving smooth 60fps/120fps rendering.

title: SQLite Wasm on OPFS: Enterprise-Grade Client Relational Persistence & VFS Crash Resilience
standard_reference: Official SQLite Wasm Documentation: Persistent Storage using the Origin Private File System (OPFS)
summary: Documents the official SQLite Wasm OPFS Virtual File System (VFS) architecture, enabling full ACID compliance, multi-megabyte transaction handling, and crash recovery inside webview sandboxes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The official SQLite project ships a specialized WebAssembly distribution featuring an OPFS-based Virtual File System (opfs VFS). By pairing SQLite's C-compiled core with 'FileSystemSyncAccessHandle' in a dedicated worker, SQLite Wasm achieves performance parity with native mobile SQLite installations. Transactions are fully ACID-compliant; SQLite's rollback journal or Write-Ahead Log (WAL) mode guarantees zero database corruption even if the mobile app process is abruptly killed or loses power during a write operation. Benchmarks demonstrate write throughput up to 10x-50x faster than traditional IndexedDB key-value stores. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app frameworks catering to complex enterprise, fintech, or ERP mini-apps MUST provide standardized SQLite Wasm OPFS scaffolding: (1) Host SDK bundles a vetted, secure SQLite Wasm binary with pre-configured OPFS VFS; (2) Mini-app data synchronization pipelines use WAL mode for concurrent read/write transactions; (3) Store performance guidelines mandate sub-5ms query response times for IndexedDB/OPFS reads under standard workloads.

title: OPFS Storage Quota Governance: Estimations, Storage Pressure, and Eviction Class Policies
standard_reference: Web.dev (Google Chrome Architecture): The Origin Private File System & Storage Quotas
summary: Analyzes storage quota allocation, 'navigator.storage.estimate()' tracking, and persistent vs best-effort eviction rules governing OPFS data under mobile device storage pressure.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Files stored in the Origin Private File System count against the origin's overall storage quota allocated by the browser engine. The storage manager provides 'navigator.storage.estimate()' returning 'quota' and 'usage' byte metrics. Under default conditions, OPFS storage is classified as 'best-effort' (subject to LRU eviction if device storage drops below critical thresholds). However, mini-apps can request 'navigator.storage.persist()', upgrading the origin to 'persistent' storage, which exempts OPFS files from automatic browser eviction during disk pressure. The super-app host container can intercept and mediate these storage requests based on user trust tiers and mini-app permissions. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app storage governance standards MUST enforce: (1) Mini-apps must monitor storage consumption via 'navigator.storage.estimate()' and maintain usage within allocated tier caps (e.g. 50MB for standard mini-apps, 250MB for verified enterprise apps); (2) Automatic storage cleanup handlers must prune temporary cached files when quota utilization exceeds 80%; (3) Store operator consoles provide users with transparent storage breakdowns per mini-app, including one-click cache clearing.

title: OPFS File Locking Architecture: Exclusive vs Shared Lock Arbitration & Deadlock Mitigation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard Section 7.1 (Locking and Concurrency Models)
summary: Governs the concurrency model of FileSystemSyncAccessHandle, specifying exclusive file lock acquisitions and defining graceful collision handling across concurrent worker threads.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a worker invokes 'createSyncAccessHandle()' on a FileSystemFileHandle, the user agent acquires an exclusive lock on that specific file. Any subsequent attempt by another worker or document within the same origin to open a sync access handle or writable stream on that file immediately throws a 'NoModificationAllowedError' DOMException. If a worker terminates abnormally without calling 'accessHandle.close()', the browser engine automatically cleans up the handle and releases the file lock during worker teardown. However, to prevent persistent lock starvation, applications must manage handle lifecycles deterministically. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container SDKs MUST incorporate robust lock arbitration: (1) Multi-threaded worker frameworks implement single-writer multiplexing to ensure only one worker accesses the database file handle at any time; (2) Background workers wrap access handle operations in try/finally blocks guaranteeing that 'accessHandle.close()' is executed even upon unhandled exceptions; (3) Host watchdog monitors long-lived locks, terminating hung worker threads if lock retention exceeds 30 seconds.

title: OpenFeature Evaluation API: Standardized Typed Resolution & Mini-App Dynamic Feature Gating
standard_reference: OpenFeature Specification v1.0 Section 1 (Flag Evaluation API)
summary: Establishes a vendor-neutral, strongly typed client API ('getBooleanValue', 'getStringValue', 'getNumberValue', 'getObjectValue') and detailed evaluation structures ('value', 'variant', 'reason', 'errorCode') governing dynamic feature activation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OpenFeature specifies a standard evaluation interface decoupling application code from proprietary feature flag backends. The Flag Evaluation API exposes typed primitives: boolean, string, numeric, and arbitrary structured JSON object evaluations. Rather than simple binary returns, evaluation details structures encapsulate: 'value' (the resolved flag payload), 'variant' (the specific semantic variant identifier such as 'canary-v2' or 'control'), 'reason' (e.g. 'TARGETING_MATCH', 'DEFAULT', 'STATIC', 'SPLIT', 'CACHED', 'ERROR'), and 'errorCode' ('FLAG_NOT_FOUND', 'TYPE_MISMATCH', 'PARSE_ERROR', 'TARGETING_KEY_MISSING'). This rich metadata enables runtime transparency and self-healing error fallbacks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host platforms MUST standardize mini-app runtime capability toggles using OpenFeature: (1) Host container exposes an isolated OpenFeature client to each mini-app sandbox; (2) Experimental host bridge APIs (e.g. biometrics, WebTransport, hardware peripherals) must be gated behind typed boolean/object flags evaluated at runtime; (3) Store operator consoles provide instant kill-switches capable of toggling compromised or buggy mini-app features in under 1 second without redeploying the mini-app package.

title: OpenFeature EvaluationContext: Hierarchical Scoping & Privacy-Preserving Targeting Rules
standard_reference: OpenFeature Specification v1.0 Section 3 (Evaluation Context)
summary: Governs the contextual data structures used for dynamic rule evaluation, defining an exact 5-tier merge precedence (API -> Transaction -> Client -> Invocation -> Before Hooks) while protecting user privacy.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OpenFeature defines 'EvaluationContext' as a dictionary of contextual attributes used by providers to evaluate rules, percentage splits, and user cohort targeting. The specification mandates a strict hierarchical merge order where duplicate keys are overwritten by more specific contexts: API (global container level, lowest precedence) -> Transaction -> Client (per-mini-app level) -> Invocation (per-call level) -> Before Hooks (highest precedence). The context requires an optional 'targetingKey' (identifying the subject for stable hash bucketing). To prevent cross-origin tracking and privacy leaks, contextual attributes must be strictly isolated. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app execution environments MUST enforce privacy boundaries on evaluation contexts: (1) Global context provided to mini-apps must be sanitized to contain only non-sensitive environment attributes (e.g. 'os_version', 'app_channel', 'locale', 'network_type'); (2) User PII (name, phone, real user ID) is strictly forbidden in mini-app evaluation contexts; instead, the host injects an opaque, ephemeral pairwise pseudonymous identifier (PPID) as the 'targetingKey'; (3) Contextual merges ensure mini-apps cannot overwrite or tamper with host-level security attributes (such as compliance status or geographic jurisdiction).

title: OpenFeature Provider Architecture: Dynamic Lifecycle States & OFREP Remote Synchronization
standard_reference: OpenFeature Specification v1.0 Section 2 (Providers) & Appendix C (OFREP)
summary: Defines provider abstraction, lifecycle state machines ('NOT_READY', 'READY', 'STALE', 'ERROR', 'FATAL'), and OpenFeature Remote Evaluation Protocol (OFREP) for low-latency Edge flag resolution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In OpenFeature, 'Providers' implement the actual flag resolution logic and bridge to backend services. Providers follow a strict lifecycle state machine transitioning between 'NOT_READY' (during initialization), 'READY' (connected and serving fresh flags), 'STALE' (network partitioned or serving expired cache), 'ERROR' (transient failure), and 'FATAL' (unrecoverable authentication or configuration fault). Providers emit standard events ('PROVIDER_READY', 'PROVIDER_CONFIGURATION_CHANGED', 'PROVIDER_ERROR', 'PROVIDER_STALE'). The OpenFeature Remote Evaluation Protocol (OFREP) standardizes HTTP-based bulk evaluation endpoints ('/ofrep/v1/evaluate/flags'), allowing Edge gateways to resolve hundreds of rules in a single round-trip with ETag caching. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app client architectures MUST integrate resilient OpenFeature providers: (1) Host container runs an in-memory cached provider backed by a local SQLite/OPFS persistence store, guaranteeing sub-1ms synchronous flag resolution without blocking network requests; (2) Provider subscribes to host WebSocket/SSE channels to receive push notifications of flag invalidations; (3) When offline or during cold starts, the provider operates in 'STALE' or 'READY' mode with zero-latency cached defaults, preventing mini-app launch blocking.

title: OpenFeature Hooks Pipeline: 4-Stage Lifecycle Interception for Security Auditing & Safe Fallbacks
standard_reference: OpenFeature Specification v1.0 Section 4 (Hooks)
summary: Specifies middleware-style lifecycle hooks ('before', 'after', 'error', 'finally') executing across global, client, and invocation scopes to enforce compliance, telemetry, and automated remediation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OpenFeature Hooks provide deterministic lifecycle interception during flag evaluation across four stages: 'before' (executes immediately prior to flag resolution, capable of mutating context or aborting execution), 'after' (executes after successful evaluation, receiving evaluation details for telemetry), 'error' (executes when resolution fails or throws, allowing custom logging or remediation), and 'finally' (unconditionally executes upon completion for resource cleanup). Hooks can be attached at API, Client, or Invocation levels. Hooks execute in a defined order: before hooks run in registration order, while after, error, and finally hooks run in reverse registration order (onion model). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platform governance MUST deploy standard host hooks: (1) Global 'SecurityAuditHook' validates that evaluation contexts do not leak sensitive session tokens or raw credentials; (2) 'MetricsTelemetryHook' records evaluation latency, cache hits/misses, and evaluation reasons into OpenTelemetry streams; (3) 'ResilienceFallbackHook' catches provider exceptions and injects pre-certified safe fallbacks, ensuring mini-app execution never halts due to feature flag gateway downtime.

title: OpenFeature Eventing & Tracking: Real-Time Canary Analysis & Automated Rollback Triggers
standard_reference: OpenFeature Specification v1.0 Section 5 (Events) & Section 6 (Tracking)
summary: Standardizes event handlers and the 'track' API to correlate runtime feature flag evaluations with mini-app crash rates, conversion metrics, and automated release rollbacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OpenFeature standardizes event-driven configuration updates via 'client.addHandler(ProviderEvents.ConfigurationChanged, handler)' enabling instant reaction when feature rules mutate on the server. Furthermore, the Tracking specification defines 'client.track(trackingEventName, evaluationContext, trackingEventDetails)', establishing a standardized telemetry bridge that connects feature variant exposures directly with business and reliability outcomes (e.g. crashes, conversion events, latency spikes). This allows automated experimentation engines and progressive delivery systems to compute real-time statistical variance between canary cohorts and control cohorts. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app release automation MUST bind OpenFeature tracking to store health gates: (1) Mini-app version canary rollouts (e.g. 5% -> 25% -> 100%) MUST be coupled to OpenFeature cohort tracking; (2) If a canary cohort exhibits a statistically significant increase in crash rates (>0.1% delta) or API latency (>200ms delta), the store automated orchestrator instantly flips the feature flag variant back to control; (3) Event streams notify connected active mini-app sessions to reload state or drop deprecated features without forcing full app restarts.

title: OpenID Shared Signals Framework (SSF 1.0) & RFC 8417 Security Event Tokens Architecture
standard_reference: OpenID Shared Signals Framework (SSF) 1.0 Specification & IETF RFC 8417 (Security Event Token)
summary: Establishes a standardized framework for real-time security signal sharing between identity providers and relying parties using cryptographically signed RFC 8417 Security Event Tokens (SET).
detail: [SPEC FACT] The OpenID Shared Signals Framework (SSF 1.0) profiles IETF RFC 8417 (Security Event Token) to allow asynchronous, cross-domain security event communication. A Security Event Token (SET) is a specialized JSON Web Token (JWT) encapsulating an 'events' claim dictionary containing standardized event URIs and event-specific payloads. SSF standardizes transmitter metadata discovery (via '/.well-known/sse-configuration'), dynamic event stream management APIs, stream status verification, and subject identifier schemas (such as 'iss_sub', 'email', 'phone', 'jwt_id', 'opaque'). The framework enables an identity provider or risk engine to emit tamper-proof, non-repudiable security assertions to federated services without polling. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app ecosystems operating distributed enterprise or commerce mini-apps MUST implement SSF: (1) Super-App Identity Provider acts as an SSF Transmitter broadcasting security events to running mini-app backends; (2) All SET tokens MUST be signed using JWS (RFC 7515) with asymmetric keys published in the super-app's JWKS; (3) Mini-app backends maintain stream verification and validate token signatures, issuer validity, and audience claims before processing events.

title: OpenID CAEP 1.0: Real-Time Session Revocation & Device State Compliance Synchronization
standard_reference: OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile (CAEP) Specification 1.0
summary: Standardizes event types ('session-revoked', 'token-claims-change', 'credential-change', 'assurance-level-change', 'device-compliance-change') enabling zero-trust continuous session evaluation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OpenID CAEP 1.0 standardizes critical event schemas that bridge the gap between static OAuth token lifetimes and dynamic runtime risk. Key event types include: (1) 'session-revoked' (invalidates a specific session ID or all user sessions across services); (2) 'device-compliance-change' (notifies services when a device status changes between compliant and non-compliant, e.g. root detection or jailbreak); (3) 'assurance-level-change' (indicates step-up authentication or downgrades, carrying 'current_level' and 'previous_level'); (4) 'credential-change' (signals password reset or passkey revocation); and (5) 'token-claims-change' (updates roles or permissions dynamically). This allows relying parties to terminate access immediately rather than waiting up to 60 minutes for OAuth access tokens to expire. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app security architectures MUST implement CAEP receiver hooks: (1) Upon receiving a 'session-revoked' or 'device-compliance-change: non-compliant' event, the super-app native container immediately freezes the active WebView and terminates mini-app local storage and cached tokens; (2) Mini-app microservice backends must register webhooks to invalidate active refresh tokens within 500ms of event ingestion; (3) High-assurance transactions in mini-apps verify CAEP stream health prior to dispatching payments.

title: OpenID RISC 1.0: Cross-Domain Fraud & Account Compromise Threat Coordination
standard_reference: OpenID Risk Incident Sharing and Coordination (RISC) Profile Specification 1.0
summary: Profiles cross-organization security event sharing for credential stuffing, account takeover, account purging, and credential compromise recovery across federated super-app partners.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The RISC 1.0 profile defines standardized event types targeting identity fraud and malicious compromise: 'account-credential-change-required' (forces user password/biometric reset due to exposure in data dumps), 'account-purged' (notifies services of permanent account deletion under privacy laws or abuse ban), 'account-disabled' (temporarily freezes account activities), and 'identifier-changed' (alerts services when email/phone changes, preventing takeover chaining). RISC events enable federated applications to take coordinated defensive action even when an attack originates on an external partner's portal. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app marketplace risk governance MUST mandate RISC integration: (1) When the super-app central security operations center (SOC) detects credential stuffing or device compromise, it broadcasts RISC 'account-credential-change-required' to all third-party mini-apps where the user has active account links; (2) Mini-apps receiving this signal must force re-authentication or biometric step-up before processing financial orders or sensitive profile updates; (3) Super-app operator console maintains an immutable audit log of all RISC event deliveries for forensic analysis.

title: RFC 8935 Push-Based SET Delivery: High-Throughput HTTP Transport & Mutual Authentication
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8935: Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
summary: Specifies push delivery of Security Event Tokens over HTTP POST with mandatory TLS, mutual authentication, delivery acknowledgments, and error-handling semantics.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8935 defines push-based delivery of SETs where the transmitter acts as an HTTP client sending POST requests to the receiver's pre-configured delivery endpoint. Requests carry the content type 'application/secevent+jwt'. The receiver acknowledges successful delivery by returning HTTP 202 Accepted. If verification fails, the receiver returns HTTP 400 Bad Request with standardized error JSON schemas ('invalid_key', 'invalid_issuer', 'invalid_audience', 'authentication_failed'). To prevent spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks, RFC 8935 mandates TLS 1.3 and specifies transmitter authentication via OAuth 2.0 Bearer tokens (RFC 6750) or mutual TLS (mTLS RFC 8705). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app push delivery gateways MUST implement RFC 8935 standards: (1) High-priority CAEP events (such as session termination) must be dispatched via RFC 8935 push to achieve sub-second delivery latency; (2) Transmitter implements exponential backoff retry mechanisms with dead-letter queueing for unresponsive mini-app webhook endpoints; (3) Push endpoints must enforce mTLS or HMAC signature verification to prevent rogue entity injection.

title: RFC 8936 Poll-Based SET Delivery: Resilient Queue Consumption for Constrained Mini-App Runtimes
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8936: Poll-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
summary: Specifies poll-based delivery of Security Event Tokens over HTTP POST, enabling firewall-protected enterprise mini-apps to reliably pull and acknowledge security events without public webhooks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8936 provides a pull-based alternative to push delivery, specifically designed for receivers behind strict enterprise firewalls, NATs, or internal VPC networks that cannot expose public HTTP endpoints. The receiver issues an HTTP POST to the transmitter's poll endpoint with JSON payload requesting queued SETs: '{"maxEvents": 10, "returnImmediately": false, "ack": ["token-jti-1", "token-jti-2"]}'. The transmitter supports long-polling, holding the request open until new security events arrive or a timeout occurs, returning a batch of SETs. The receiver explicitly acknowledges processed tokens in subsequent requests, ensuring at-least-once delivery semantics and preventing event loss. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app enterprise store infrastructure MUST support RFC 8936 poll streams: (1) On-premise enterprise mini-app backends (e.g. core banking, internal HR, ERPs) connect via RFC 8936 long-polling to consume security signals safely; (2) Transmitter maintains partitioned, persistent event buffers per mini-app client for a minimum retention window of 24 hours; (3) Store monitoring surfaces unacknowledged event lag to detect stalled enterprise event consumers.

title: EU Digital Services Act Article 30: Mandatory KYBC Verification & Developer Identity Attestation
standard_reference: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 30 (Traceability of traders)
summary: Mandates online marketplaces to collect, verify, and store verifiable Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) identification from all commercial developers before permitting mini-app distribution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Article 30 of the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) establishes strict statutory obligations for intermediary platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders. Online platforms MUST obtain prior to onboarding: (a) trader legal name, address, telephone number, and email address; (b) a copy of an official identification document or equivalent electronic identification; (c) payment account details; (d) trade register and registration number (e.g. EU Business Registers or national registries); and (e) a self-certification by the trader committing to offer only compliant products and services. Platforms are legally obligated to make 'best efforts' to assess the reliability of this information through freely accessible official online databases (such as VIES for VAT numbers or national commercial registries) before granting marketplace distribution rights. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app stores facilitating commercial transactions, IAPs, or paid services MUST implement automated KYBC verification: (1) Developer registration workflow enforces cryptographic submission of company registration documents, tax IDs, and official representative ID; (2) Automated integration with government business registries validates developer status prior to app submission review; (3) Failure to provide verifiable corporate documentation results in immediate block of publishing privileges.

title: DSA Article 30(3) Rectification Governance: Inaccurate Trader Data, Grace Periods & Mandatory Suspension
standard_reference: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 30 Paragraph 3 & 4
summary: Governs platform enforcement when trader data is discovered to be inaccurate, establishing formal notification mechanisms, rectification deadlines, and mandatory suspension of non-compliant mini-apps.
detail: [SPEC FACT] DSA Article 30(3) dictates that where an online platform obtains sufficient indications or has reason to believe that any item of information provided by a trader is inaccurate, incomplete, or not up to date, it MUST request that the trader remedy that situation without delay, or within the time period set by Union and national law. If the trader fails to remedy the information within that period, the platform MUST immediately suspend the provision of its service to that trader for the offering of products or services to consumers until the request is fully complied with. Furthermore, Article 30(4) requires platforms to retain trader identification records securely for the duration of their contractual relationship and for exactly six months thereafter for regulatory audit purposes. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app catalog governance engines MUST automate DSA compliance workflows: (1) Periodic re-validation checks (minimum annually) audit developer active business status against company registers; (2) Automated notice and cure timers give developers a strict statutory grace period (e.g. 14 to 30 calendar days) upon detection of invalid credentials; (3) If the cure period lapses without verified remediation, the store backend automatically executes a soft-suspension, disabling mini-app discovery and payment checkout in affected jurisdictions.

title: DSA Article 31: Compliance by Design for Storefront Interfaces & Mandatory Public Trader Disclosures
standard_reference: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 31 (Compliance by design for online interfaces)
summary: Requires online marketplace UIs to be designed and structured so that consumers can clearly inspect the verified trader's identity, contact information, and regulatory credentials before launch or purchase.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Article 31 mandates that online platforms allowing distance contracts must design their user interfaces to enable traders to comply with consumer protection and product safety information duties. The storefront interface must present to consumers, in a clear, easily accessible, and comprehensible manner: the trader's name, registered business address, telephone number, email address, trade registry and registration number, and clear indication of consumer cancellation/withdrawal rights. The platform must ensure that third-party traders cannot distribute mini-apps or publish listings without populating these mandatory disclosure fields in the platform UI schema. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app store interfaces MUST implement standardized compliance-by-design UI modules: (1) Mini-app product detail pages (PDP) MUST render a dedicated 'Developer Information & Legal Entity' card displaying verified trader attributes; (2) The host payment sheet dynamically renders the legal entity name and contact details prior to user payment confirmation; (3) Catalog submission validators reject mini-app packages that fail to map required trader metadata to the localized storefront presentation layer.

title: Apple App Store DSA Implementation: D-U-N-S Corporate Verification, Self-Declaration & EU Listing Visibility
standard_reference: Apple Developer Documentation: Manage Trader Status for the EU Digital Services Act
summary: Examines Apple's operational enforcement of DSA Article 30 requiring Dun & Bradstreet (D-U-N-S) enterprise validation, phone/email two-factor verification, and mandatory storefront disclosures for EU distribution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple enforces DSA Article 30 across all developer accounts distributing in 27 EU member states. Developers must declare their status as a 'Trader' (an entity acting for commercial, trade, or professional purposes) or 'Non-Trader'. For Organizations, Apple leverages existing verified Dun & Bradstreet (D-U-N-S) data to automatically populate the legal entity name, address, and registry numbers, while requiring two-step SMS and email verification for public contact channels. For Individuals, Apple requires legal proof of address, telephone verification, and national identification. Failure to complete Trader Status verification by statutory deadlines leads to automated suppression of app availability across all EU storefronts. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app operator portals MUST emulate enterprise registry federation models: (1) Organizations registering to distribute commercial mini-apps must authenticate via verified corporate registry identifiers (e.g. D-U-N-S number, national corporate registry APIs, or LEI - Legal Entity Identifier); (2) Host console verifies phone numbers via OTP SMS and email addresses via cryptographic magic links before listing; (3) Storefront catalog dynamically filters mini-app availability, hiding non-compliant commercial mini-apps from users located within regulated jurisdictions.

title: Google Play Developer Verification & DSA Article 30(5) Random Sampling Architecture
standard_reference: Google Play Console Help: Provide Trader Information for the European Union (DSA)
summary: Analyzes Google Play's developer identity verification infrastructure and the implementation of DSA Article 30(5) random compliance checks against official commercial and consumer safety registries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Google Play mandates full developer identity verification (including official government ID, D-U-N-S number for businesses, and proof of address) coupled with DSA Trader status declarations. In compliance with DSA Article 30(5), Google Play and marketplace operators must make reasonable efforts to conduct random checks on products and services offered on their platforms to detect whether they have been identified as illegal in any official database (such as the EU Safety Gate / RAPEX). When an irregularity is identified or developer status is invalidated, Google Play immediately removes the listing and initiates a formal compliance audit. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app marketplace compliance pipelines MUST incorporate continuous automated verification and sampling: (1) Automated scrapers and API connectors periodically check developer business standing against national commercial registries (e.g. EU Business Registers, VIES, state tax bureaus); (2) Compliance engine runs weekly random sampling of active mini-app catalogs (minimum 5% random cohort inspection) to verify that publisher contact info, legal terms, and payment pathways remain operational and authentic; (3) Real-time integration with consumer protection safety feeds immediately flags and quarantines flagged mini-app vendors.

title: WICG Signature-Based Subresource Integrity: Cryptographic Provenance vs Bit-Exact Content Hashing
standard_reference: WICG Signature-based Resource Loading Restrictions Explainer & W3C Subresource Integrity
summary: Establishes cryptographic provenance validation for subresources using digital signatures, decoupling integrity enforcement from brittle bit-exact content hashing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Subresource Integrity (SRI) has historically relied on exact cryptographic digests (e.g., sha256, sha384, sha512) over the full byte stream of a resource. While this guarantees bit-level immutability, it introduces severe operational brittleness: any legitimate upstream patch, localized asset recompilation, or edge cache compression variation alters the hash, breaking client verification and causing denial of service. WICG Signature-Based SRI introduces signature-based integrity checks by requiring origin servers or trusted publishers to cryptographically sign resources using a narrow profile of HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). Rather than verifying that resource content matches a pre-shared digest, the user agent validates that the resource was signed by an authorized entity holding a trusted public key. This allows publishers to deploy non-breaking patches and dynamic CDN assets while guaranteeing provenance. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST adopt signature-based integrity verification for dynamic subresources: (1) Package ingestion tools permit mini-apps to declare trusted publisher Ed25519 public keys in the mini-app manifest or CSP headers; (2) The container runtime verifies the digital signature of third-party SDKs, dynamically loaded script modules, and remote style bundles against trusted developer/platform keys; (3) Host caches and edge networks can serve updated, localized, or dynamically compressed assets without requiring manual hash re-registration in the store catalog.

title: WICG Signature-Based SRI RFC 9421 Profile: Ed25519 Algorithms & Canonical Component Constraints
standard_reference: WICG Signature-based Resource Loading Restrictions & IETF RFC 9421 (HTTP Message Signatures)
summary: Specifies the strict RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures profile enforced for Signature-Based SRI, restricting cryptographic primitives to Ed25519 and standardizing signature base generation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To prevent algorithmic downgrade attacks, canonicalization ambiguities, and intermediary tampering, WICG Signature-Based SRI establishes a strict, constrained profile of RFC 9421. The profile mandates the 'ed25519' signature algorithm and requires that the public key portion of the verification key material be explicitly referenced or included via the 'keyid' signature parameter. The signature base construction strictly serializes request and response derived components: request components (using the 'req' flag) include '@authority', '@method', '@path', '@target-uri', '@query', and arbitrary specified headers; response components include '@status' and response headers. Furthermore, the signature parameters MUST include 'created' (an integer representing a time in the past), 'expires' (an integer representing a future expiration timestamp to prevent replay of revoked versions), and a unique 'nonce' string. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app package and gateway pipelines MUST enforce RFC 9421 compliance for hosted subresources: (1) Build and release pipelines sign mini-app script bundles using Ed25519 signing keys bound to developer organizational identities; (2) The container network stack validates signature base components, rejecting any response where 'expires' is in the past, 'created' is in the future, or required derived components (@status, @authority, @path) are missing; (3) Signatures with weak or legacy algorithms (RSA-PKCS1-v1_5, ECDSA with SHA-1) are rejected at container intake.

title: Signature-Based SRI Client Verification Pipeline: Integrity-Digest & Two-Stage Handover
standard_reference: WICG Signature-based Resource Loading Restrictions (Section 2: Verification Requirements)
summary: Details the client-side execution gate verifying the Integrity-Digest response body hash and Signature-Input reconstruction prior to script execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In Signature-Based SRI, user agents perform a two-stage verification process before releasing downloaded bytes for script execution: (1) First, the user agent reconstructs the signature base from the 'Signature-Input' header and verifies the signature in the 'Signature' header against the public key declared for that resource. This verification can execute immediately upon receiving HTTP response headers, without waiting for the complete body payload. (2) Second, the user agent computes a cryptographic digest over the fully decoded HTTP response body and asserts that it matches the digest specified in the 'Integrity-Digest' (or RFC 9530 'Content-Digest') response header. The resource is passed to the script execution engine if and only if both the signature over the headers/digest validates and the decoded body matches the asserted digest. If either check fails, the user agent halts execution and fires an 'error' event on the invoking HTML script/link element. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Container WebView and native mini-app runtimes MUST implement two-stage integrity verification: (1) The container network client inspects 'Signature', 'Signature-Input', and 'Integrity-Digest' headers on subresource downloads; (2) Body verification runs synchronously upon download completion in a memory-safe buffer; (3) Mismatched digests or invalid cryptographic signatures trigger immediate resource dropping, preventing DOM insertion, and log structured security violation events to the super-app audit telemetry pipeline.

title: CSP Level 3 Integration & Accept-Signature Proactive Negotiation Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 & WICG Signature-Based SRI (Fetch Integration)
summary: Defines the integration of Signature-Based SRI into CSP Level 3 directives and the automatic client negotiation of signature requirements via Accept-Signature headers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Signature-Based SRI integrates natively with Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3) by introducing the 'ed25519-<public-key-base64>' source expression into script-src and style-src directives. This allows pages to enforce provenance constraints alongside traditional nonce and hash directives: for example, 'script-src https://trusted-cdn.com/ ed25519-abc123... nonce-xyz'. When a resource request is initiated from an element or context that mandates a signature, the browser's Fetch algorithm automatically appends an 'Accept-Signature' HTTP request header (e.g. 'Accept-Signature: sig1;keyid="ed25519-abc123..."'). This signals to origin servers and intermediary proxies that the response must include RFC 9421 signature metadata. If a server responds without the required signature or with an untrusted key, the resource is blocked under CSP violation rules. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST configure default CSP policies supporting signature-based source expressions: (1) Host containers inject CSP headers enforcing 'script-src' with trusted super-app root public keys; (2) The container network client automatically injects 'Accept-Signature' into outbound subresource requests destined for authorized partner domains; (3) Third-party scripts lacking a valid signature from an authorized developer or platform key are quarantined and denied execution.

title: Enterprise Mini-App Store Architecture: Dynamic Subresource Attestation & Edge Caching
standard_reference: Super-App Security Architecture Blueprint: Subresource Provenance and Supply-Chain Governance
summary: Establishes reference operational architecture for signing, distributing, and caching mini-app subresources across multi-tenant enterprise super-app environments.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Super-app ecosystems routinely rely on dynamic subresources: financial charting libraries, localization strings, micro-frontends, and regional payment widgets. Traditional SRI requires the top-level mini-app package to update its HTML markup and manifest whenever a subresource changes, leading to release churn. Signature-Based SRI eliminates this friction by binding trust to cryptographic keys rather than ephemeral file digests. Developers or vetted vendor partners register their public signing keys with the Super-App Developer Console. The store publishes an authenticated key directory (or embeds keys in the signed manifest). Edge CDNs can then cache, optimize, and rotate subresource versions seamlessly, provided each release is signed with the developer's registered private key. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store architectures MUST establish key-based subresource trust management: (1) The developer console provides self-service Ed25519 public key enrollment with hardware security module (HSM) attestation; (2) Release pipelines verify that all external script references match enrolled publisher keys; (3) The runtime container caches verified public keys per mini-app origin, verifying dynamic subresource signatures without querying remote trust anchors on every invocation.

title: WICG Network Efficiency Guardrails: Replacing Fragmented Heuristics with Document Policy Constraints
standard_reference: WICG Network Efficiency Guardrails Specification & W3C Document Policy
summary: Establishes a unified, browser-enforced document policy framework that detects and reports network inefficiencies such as uncompressed transfers and oversized assets.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Web developers and mobile application containers have historically struggled with policing network efficiency: developers either invent complex ad-hoc JavaScript interceptors (monkey-patching window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest) or deploy heavyweight Service Worker proxies to inspect response sizes and headers. These custom heuristics introduce CPU overhead, runtime fragility, and inconsistent thresholds across different device form factors. The WICG Network Efficiency Guardrails specification solves this by defining a standardized Document Policy feature. When enabled, the User Agent's native C++ network stack directly monitors network resource requests initiated by the document, evaluating whether transfers meet efficiency baselines without burdening the application layer with runtime monitoring code. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST integrate Network Efficiency Guardrails into the mini-app hosting runtime: (1) Host containers inject default Document Policy headers into mini-app webviews to activate browser-level network auditing; (2) Inefficient network transactions (e.g. uncompressed JSON responses, raw bitmaps) are caught at the platform boundary rather than requiring mini-app developers to bundle proprietary telemetry SDKs; (3) Performance grading is performed uniformly across all third-party mini-apps using standardized platform heuristics.

title: Document Policy Header Integration: Coarse Thresholding Against Uncompressed & Oversized Transfers
standard_reference: W3C Document Policy Specification (Configuration Points and Header Syntax)
summary: Specifies Document-Policy HTTP header syntax, iframe policy delegation, and coarse, non-parametric thresholds for HTTP compression and asset sizing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Network Efficiency Guardrails is configured via the 'Document-Policy' HTTP response header (or the 'policy' attribute on iframe elements). Rather than exposing micro-configurable thresholds that could be weaponized for high-precision side-channel fingerprinting, the policy groups related criteria into coarse, non-parametric categorical boundaries: (1) Mandatory HTTP compression for text-based resources (requiring gzip, brotli, or zstd); (2) Utilization of modern compressed file formats for images and fonts (blocking raw uncompressed payloads); (3) Standardized size-based thresholds that prevent accidental unbounded payload transfers. The policy operates strictly within the scope of the declaring document: monitoring and reporting are active only when explicitly enabled, and child iframes inherit or refine these constraints based on container configuration. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store gateways and container SDKs MUST enforce Document Policy headers: (1) Gateway reverse proxies serve mini-app HTML shells with 'Document-Policy: network-efficiency-guardrails' to activate native guardrails; (2) Embedded iframes and sub-views inherit network efficiency constraints, preventing third-party ad tags or analytics scripts from bypassing compression standards; (3) In development and staging environments, violations can be configured in enforcement mode to block non-compliant subresources directly.

title: W3C Reporting API Out-of-Band Telemetry & ReportingObserver Integration
standard_reference: W3C Reporting API (Reporting-Endpoints & ReportingObserver Interfaces)
summary: Details out-of-band asynchronous JSON violation delivery to server endpoints and in-browser monitoring via ReportingObserver.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a network efficiency threshold is violated, the user agent generates a structured violation report via the W3C Reporting API without stalling the critical rendering path. Reports are dispatched in two complementary ways: (1) Out-of-band JSON payloads sent to reporting endpoints defined by the 'Reporting-Endpoints' HTTP response header (e.g. 'Reporting-Endpoints: net-report="https://superapp.com/api/net-reports"'); (2) In-document JavaScript notification via the 'ReportingObserver' interface, allowing client-side performance diagnostics code to capture violation events in real time. The report payload provides the full URL of the violating resource, the specific efficiency category violated (e.g. uncompressed-text, oversized-image), and contextual disposition information. Because reporting is asynchronous, monitoring does not degrade UI frame rates or page responsiveness. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app operational pipelines MUST implement centralized violation collection: (1) Super-app runtime configures the 'Reporting-Endpoints' header pointing to the platform's telemetry collector; (2) The client SDK initializes a ReportingObserver to feed network violation events into local breadcrumb buffers; (3) Telemetry ingestion pipelines aggregate reports per mini-app ID and release version, surfacing automated efficiency regressions in the developer portal.

title: Cross-Origin Subresource Diagnostics & Timing Side-Channel Fingerprinting Mitigations
standard_reference: WICG Network Efficiency Guardrails (Security & Privacy Self-Assessment)
summary: Analyzes the privacy trade-offs of inspecting cross-origin subresources and the side-channel protections built into coarse violation classifications.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A critical challenge in web network monitoring is that documents frequently load cross-origin subresources (e.g. third-party APIs, CDNs, social widgets). Exposing exact byte sizes or precise transfer metrics across origins can create dangerous side channels, enabling cross-site search leaks (XS-Leaks) or user profiling based on cached payload lengths. Network Efficiency Guardrails balances diagnosability with privacy by ensuring the exposed signal is intentionally coarse and non-parametric. The policy reports that a browser-defined threshold was exceeded, but strictly conceals exact byte sizes, transfer durations, or protocol headers. Furthermore, violation reports are delivered exclusively to the document that initiated the request and its pre-configured reporting endpoints; no cross-document correlation or ambient persistent tracking state is created. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app security architectures MUST enforce privacy-safe diagnostic boundaries: (1) Mini-app network diagnostics MUST NOT log exact byte lengths for cross-origin third-party resources unless explicit Timing-Allow-Origin (TAO) headers are present; (2) Telemetry processors sanitize URL query parameters containing user-specific tokens before persisting violation reports; (3) Container sandboxes isolate diagnostic logs per mini-app session, preventing cross-tenant information leaks.

title: Store Ingestion Performance Grading & Cellular Data Preservation Standards
standard_reference: Super-App Marketplace Operating Standard: Automated Quality Assurance and Mobile Bandwidth Governance
summary: Establishes automated store ingestion gates and cellular data preservation policies based on Document Policy efficiency violations.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Mobile super-app users frequently operate under constrained cellular network environments (metered 3G/4G/5G connections with strict data caps). Uncompressed API responses, raw PNG/JPEG images, and bloated web fonts unnecessarily drain mobile data allowances, accelerate battery exhaustion, and inflate cloud egress costs for the super-app operator. By leveraging standardized Network Efficiency Guardrails during pre-release automated testing (e.g. via headless browser runners like WebDriver BiDi), the app store review pipeline can automatically execute simulated end-to-end user journeys and capture violation reports. Mini-apps that generate repeated violations for uncompressed payloads or oversized subresources are flagged for remediation before receiving release approval. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app store review and governance pipelines MUST enforce bandwidth preservation gates: (1) Automated CI/CD review runners execute mini-app flows with Document-Policy enforcement enabled; (2) Release gates require zero critical network efficiency violations (e.g. all text resources >10KB must be compressed via gzip/brotli/zstd); (3) Dynamic store ranking penalizes mini-apps with high real-world violation frequencies reported by field telemetry; (4) The host container dynamically tightens network guardrails when the operating system signals 'Save-Data' or low battery mode.

title: WICG Autofill Event API: Pre-Fill Intent Signals & Document-Targeted Dispatch Architecture
standard_reference: WICG Autofill Event Specification (DOM Interface & Event Dispatch Lifecycle)
summary: Defines the DOM 'autofill' event dispatched prior to field population, exposing intention signals and filled element mappings without breaking custom form logic.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Web and mini-app autofill frequently breaks modern web applications that rely on dynamic JavaScript state, virtualized forms, or multi-step checkout dialogs. Conventional autofill mechanisms simulate input and change events after modifying the DOM, leading to race conditions with client frameworks (React, Vue) and silent data truncation. The WICG Autofill Event API addresses this by dispatching a dedicated DOM event of type 'autofill' directly to the target Document before fields are physically modified. The event is non-bubbling and non-cancelable. Its 'values' property provides an immutable list of key-value tuples mapping each targeted HTMLElement to its intended fill value (as a string or boolean). This provides the web application with advance notice of user intent, enabling proactive state synchronization and dynamic UI adjustments before field mutations take effect. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host webviews and mini-app frameworks MUST support the Autofill Event API: (1) Host container webviews fire the 'autofill' DOM event whenever the user selects a stored profile (identity, payment address, shipping details) from the super-app wallet; (2) Mini-app framework runtimes listen for 'autofill' events to synchronize reactive component state with incoming form values; (3) Forms embedded inside custom web components or shadow DOM roots receive properly targeted event dispatching.

title: Programmatic Refill Lifecycle: AutofillEvent.refill() Dynamic Re-Filling & Recursion Defense
standard_reference: WICG Autofill Event (Section: Programmatic Refills & Refill Methods)
summary: Specifies the async AutofillEvent.refill() method enabling dynamic DOM modification (e.g. country/state dropdowns) followed by coordinated browser re-population.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A fundamental flaw in multi-country checkout forms is dynamic field dependency: selecting a country (e.g., United States or Vietnam) dynamically injects new input elements (such as state/province dropdowns or postal code inputs) that did not exist when the browser initially scanned the form. The WICG Autofill Event API introduces the 'AutofillEvent.refill()' method to resolve this cleanly. Within the 'autofill' event handler, application script can inspect incoming values (e.g. discovering the user selected a US address), dynamically insert required regional inputs into the DOM, and call 'await e.refill()'. The browser re-evaluates the form, populates the newly injected fields with corresponding profile data, and resolves the promise. To prevent denial-of-service loops and exploit conditions, 'refill()' can only be invoked once per event; subsequent calls reject immediately, and 'refill' evaluates to null if refills are unsupported for sensitive data types (such as banking credentials). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app checkout workflows MUST leverage programmatic refill contracts: (1) Super-app commerce mini-apps utilize 'e.refill()' to dynamically render localized tax, shipping, and administrative province fields based on user location; (2) Container webviews enforce strict time-window boundaries (max 2 seconds) on refill promises to prevent unresponsiveness; (3) Repeated or re-entrant refill calls are automatically suppressed by the container bridge to guard against infinite render loops.

title: 'full-address' Autocomplete Scoping: Holistic Profile Delegation & Privacy Sandboxing
standard_reference: WICG Autofill Event ('full-address' Proposal & WHATWG HTML Autocomplete)
summary: Establishes declarative 'full-address' form scoping that enables explicit user authorization for comprehensive profile sharing while preventing hidden-field data harvesting.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A long-standing privacy vulnerability on the web has been autofill abuse, where malicious sites include hidden form fields (e.g. hidden email, telephone, or home address inputs) that browsers blindly populate when a user autofills a visible name field. The WICG Autofill proposal addresses this via the declarative 'full-address' autocomplete attribute on the enclosing '<form>' element. Declaring 'autocomplete="full-address"' signals that the form legitimately requires a holistic address entity. The browser presents an explicit, transparent user consent modal showing exactly which attributes will be shared across the origin boundary. Concurrently, the specification establishes browser restrictions deprecating the automatic filling of hidden, obscured, or non-visible form elements, neutralizing covert data harvesting. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app store privacy guidelines MUST enforce transparent autofill consent: (1) Mini-apps requesting user contact or delivery information MUST declare standard autocomplete tokens ('shipping address-line1', 'shipping postal-code', or form-level 'full-address'); (2) The super-app native container displays an explicit permission sheet detailing every field transferred from the user's host profile; (3) Host webviews strictly block autofill population of any DOM element that is hidden via 'display: none', 'visibility: hidden', or clipped out of view, automatically failing privacy audit gates for deceptive designs.

title: WICG Managed Configuration API: Enterprise Policy Injection & Asynchronous Key-Value Distribution
standard_reference: WICG Managed Device Web API: Managed Configuration API Specification
summary: Specifies navigator.managed.getManagedConfiguration() for asynchronous retrieval of enterprise administrator configuration and dynamic policy synchronization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In enterprise and managed kiosk environments, web and mini-applications require out-of-band configuration (e.g. internal server endpoints, corporate tenant IDs, telemetry reporting toggles, feature entitlements) that cannot be hardcoded in public application packages. The WICG Managed Configuration API defines 'navigator.managed.getManagedConfiguration(keys)', an asynchronous JavaScript interface that retrieves administrator-provisioned key-value configuration. Configuration payloads are defined by enterprise administrators in central device management consoles (e.g. via ManagedConfigurationPerOrigin policies). When policies are updated remotely, the browser dispatches an 'onmanagedconfigurationchange' event to the document, allowing applications to re-read updated settings without requiring an application restart or cache invalidation.
